lesson.content:
# Distributed Unique ID Generation

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Once more than one machine can create new rows at the same time, a single **auto-incrementing counter** stops being possible, so distributed systems need an ID scheme that many machines can generate correctly without ever talking to each other.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Snowflake-style ID generation across shards

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    w1["Worker 1 (server A)"]:::server
    w2["Worker 2 (server B)"]:::server
    coord["Worker ID assignment"]:::server
    db[("Sharded Database")]:::db
    coord -->|"assigns worker_id=1"| w1
    coord -->|"assigns worker_id=2"| w2
    w1 -->|"generates ID locally, no round trip"| db
    w2 -->|"generates ID locally, no round trip"| db
```

#### UUID v4 vs Snowflake-style ID

| UUID v4 | Snowflake-style ID |
| :--- | :--- |
| 128 bits, fully random, effectively zero collision risk | 64 bits, packs timestamp + worker ID + sequence |
| No inherent time ordering, sorts randomly | Roughly sortable by creation time |
| Zero coordination needed, not even a worker ID to assign | Needs a scheme to assign unique worker IDs to each generator |

#### Two workers generating IDs, same millisecond, no coordination

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant W1 as Worker 1
  participant W2 as Worker 2
  W1->>W1: timestamp + worker_id=1 + seq=0
  W2->>W2: timestamp + worker_id=2 + seq=0
  W1->>W1: ID = ...worker_id 1
  W2->>W2: ID = ...worker_id 2
  Note over W1,W2: Same millisecond, no collision
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Trying to keep auto-increment IDs after sharding by having each shard start at a different offset, which works briefly but breaks the moment you add another shard or run out of the allocated range.
- ⚠️ Using UUID v4 as a primary key on a huge, high-write table without realizing the random insert order fragments the index and hurts write throughput compared to a roughly sequential key.
- ⚠️ ==Assuming Snowflake-style IDs are perfectly globally ordered==, they're only roughly ordered, clock skew between machines and network delay mean two IDs close in time aren't a guaranteed strict ordering.
- ⚠️ Forgetting to plan worker ID assignment before deploying a Snowflake-style generator, then having two machines accidentally reuse the same worker ID and start colliding.
- ⚠️ Exposing an auto-increment-style ID publicly (like in a URL) and inadvertently leaking how many total records exist or letting users guess adjacent IDs, a problem neither UUIDs nor Snowflake-style IDs have to the same degree.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you just keep using auto-increment IDs once you shard your database across multiple machines?**

> **Model Answer:** Auto-increment relies on a single counter that every insert goes through, which is exactly what sharding removes, each shard would generate its own sequence independently and eventually produce duplicate IDs across shards, making merges, joins, and global uniqueness impossible to guarantee.

**Q: What does a Snowflake-style ID offer that a UUID doesn't, and what does it cost to get that?**

> **Model Answer:** A Snowflake-style ID is roughly sortable by creation time and fits in a compact 64-bit integer, both useful for pagination, debugging, and index locality, which a random UUID can't offer. The cost is that you need a scheme to assign each ID-generating machine a unique worker ID, some coordination UUIDs don't require at all.

**Q: Why can inserting UUID v4 primary keys into a B-tree index hurt write performance at scale, compared to a roughly sequential ID?**

> **Model Answer:** B-tree indexes perform best when new keys land near the existing high end of the tree, which sequential or roughly time-ordered IDs naturally do. Fully random UUIDs scatter inserts across the entire key space, causing far more page splits and index fragmentation, which shows up as slower writes and a larger, less cache-friendly index over time.

lesson.content:
# Distributed Consensus Basics

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **Consensus** is how a group of machines that don't fully trust each other's timing or health still agree on one true answer, and the whole difficulty comes from never being able to tell the difference between 'that node is slow' and 'that node is dead'.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Quorum write across five replicas

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    leader["Leader"]:::server
    n1[("Replica 1")]:::db
    n2[("Replica 2")]:::db
    n3[("Replica 3")]:::db
    n4[("Replica 4 (unreachable)")]:::db
    client -->|"write request"| leader
    leader -->|"ack"| n1
    leader -->|"ack"| n2
    leader -->|"ack"| n3
    leader -.->|"no response, quorum already reached"| n4
```

#### Paxos vs Raft

| Paxos | Raft |
| :--- | :--- |
| Prepare then accept phases, proven correct, foundational | Explicit leader election as a first-class, separate phase |
| Deliberately general, doesn't prescribe a single leader model | Log replication and safety rules kept clearly distinct |
| Notoriously hard to reason about and implement correctly | Designed from the start to be understandable and implementable |

#### Raft-style leader failover

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant L as Leader (term 1)
  participant A as Node A
  participant B as Node B
  L->>A: heartbeat
  L->>B: heartbeat
  Note over L: Leader crashes
  A->>B: request vote (term 2)
  B-->>A: vote granted
  Note over A: Majority reached, A becomes leader
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming a quorum of any size works, when W + R > N is specifically what guarantees read and write quorums overlap, ==get that math wrong== and you can read stale data with full confidence it's current.
- ⚠️ Treating an unreachable node as definitely dead, when the entire point of consensus design is that you can never actually know that, only that a majority proceeded without it.
- ⚠️ Building a system with two nodes each able to independently accept writes without a real leader election mechanism, which is exactly how split-brain happens.
- ⚠️ Assuming Paxos or Raft guarantees ==zero downtime==, they guarantee the group never agrees on conflicting values, but a period with no elected leader is genuinely unavailable for writes until election completes.
- ⚠️ Confusing consensus (agreeing on one value or order of operations) with simple replication (copying data to multiple places), replication without a consensus mechanism can still end up with conflicting versions of the truth.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does requiring a majority for both reads and writes guarantee a read always sees the latest write?**

> **Model Answer:** Any two majorities out of N nodes are mathematically guaranteed to share at least one common node, because two disjoint majorities would together need more than N nodes to exist. That shared node participated in the latest successful write, so it's guaranteed to be included in any subsequent read quorum, meaning the read is guaranteed to see the latest value somewhere among the nodes it queries.

**Q: What problem does leader election actually solve in a consensus protocol like Raft?**

> **Model Answer:** Without a leader, every node would need to negotiate the order of every operation with every other node, which is slow and complex. Electing one leader for a period of time lets that leader unilaterally decide the order of operations and replicate them to followers, dramatically simplifying agreement, while the protocol still safely detects a failed leader and elects a new one with a higher term to take over.

**Q: Why is it wrong to say Paxos or Raft guarantees a system will never be unavailable?**

> **Model Answer:** These protocols guarantee safety, the group will never agree on two conflicting values, not liveness in every situation. If a leader fails, there is a real window where no writes can be accepted until a new leader is elected, and in some network partition scenarios a minority side of the cluster can't make progress at all, by design, since it can't reach quorum.

topics.description: A search engine answers 'which documents contain this word' in milliseconds by flipping the obvious data structure inside out ahead of time, from document-to-words into **word-to-documents**.

lesson.summary: A search engine answers 'which documents contain this word' in milliseconds by flipping the obvious data structure inside out ahead of time, from document-to-words into **word-to-documents**.
lesson.content:
# Search Indexing & Inverted Indexes

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A search engine answers 'which documents contain this word' in milliseconds by flipping the obvious data structure inside out ahead of time, from document-to-words into **word-to-documents**.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### From raw document to a searchable inverted index

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Raw document ('The quick fox runs fast')"]:::step
    step_2["2. Tokenize (split into words, lowercase)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Remove stop words (drop 'the')"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Stem ('runs' becomes 'run')"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Update postings lists (term -> list of doc IDs)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Query time: intersecting postings lists

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Search Query"]:::client
    gateway["Search API"]:::server
    idx["Inverted Index (shard 1)"]:::server
    idx2["Inverted Index (shard 2)"]:::server
    client -->|"'quick fox'"| gateway
    gateway -->|"lookup postings for 'quick', 'fox'"| idx
    gateway -->|"lookup postings for 'quick', 'fox'"| idx2
```

#### Inverse document frequency drops as a term gets more common

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming search relevance is just about whether a term is present, and ignoring that frequency and rarity across the corpus (TF-IDF or similar) are what actually separate a strong match from a coincidental one.
- ⚠️ Expecting newly written data to be instantly searchable, when most search systems batch and periodically refresh the index rather than updating it synchronously on every write.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that stop word removal and stemming are lossy, sometimes deliberately dropping or merging distinctions that matter for a specific use case, like exact legal or code search where 'running' and 'run' should not be treated as the same term.
- ⚠️ Treating a search index as a replacement for the primary database, when it's typically a derived, denormalized view built for read performance, not the durable source of truth for the data.
- ⚠️ Underestimating storage cost, a full inverted index with positions for phrase search can be comparable in size to, or larger than, the original text it was built from.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is a full inverted index dramatically faster to search than scanning every document's raw text at query time?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the expensive work, reading and tokenizing every document, happens once at index time, not on every query. At query time, the search only has to look up the already-built postings list for each search term and intersect a small number of sorted lists, work proportional to the number of matching documents, not the size of the entire corpus.

**Q: How does an inverted index support phrase search, like matching the exact phrase 'quick fox' and not just documents containing both words separately?**

> **Model Answer:** The postings list for each term stores not just which documents contain it but the specific positions within each document. A phrase query checks that the position of 'fox' in a candidate document is exactly one more than the position of 'quick', confirming adjacency, not just co-occurrence anywhere in the document.

**Q: Why do most search systems refresh their index periodically instead of making every write instantly searchable?**

> **Model Answer:** Updating an inverted index for one new or changed document can mean touching the postings list of every distinct term in that document, which is expensive to do synchronously on every single write. Batching updates and refreshing the searchable index on an interval trades a small amount of write-to-search latency for much better indexing throughput.

```mermaid
    idx2["Inverted Index (shard 2)"]:::server
    client -->|"'quick fox'"| gateway
    gateway -->|"lookup postings for 'quick', 'fox'"| idx
    gateway -->|"lookup postings for 'quick', 'fox'"| idx2
```

#### Inverse document frequency drops as a term gets more common

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming search relevance is just about whether a term is present, and ignoring that frequency and rarity across the corpus (TF-IDF or similar) are what actually separate a strong match from a coincidental one.
- ⚠️ Expecting newly written data to be instantly searchable, when most search systems batch and periodically refresh the index rather than updating it synchronously on every write.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that stop word removal and stemming are lossy, sometimes deliberately dropping or merging distinctions that matter for a specific use case, like exact legal or code search where 'running' and 'run' should not be treated as the same term.
- ⚠️ Treating a search index as a replacement for the primary database, when it's typically a derived, denormalized view built for read performance, not the durable source of truth for the data.
- ⚠️ Underestimating storage cost, a full inverted index with positions for phrase search can be comparable in size to, or larger than, the original text it was built from.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is a full inverted index dramatically faster to search than scanning every document's raw text at query time?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the expensive work, reading and tokenizing every document, happens once at index time, not on every query. At query time, the search only has to look up the already-built postings list for each search term and intersect a small number of sorted lists, work proportional to the number of matching documents, not the size of the entire corpus.

**Q: How does an inverted index support phrase search, like matching the exact phrase 'quick fox' and not just documents containing both words separately?**

> **Model Answer:** The postings list for each term stores not just which documents contain it but the specific positions within each document. A phrase query checks that the position of 'fox' in a candidate document is exactly one more than the position of 'quick', confirming adjacency, not just co-occurrence anywhere in the document.

**Q: Why do most search systems refresh their index periodically instead of making every write instantly searchable?**

> **Model Answer:** Updating an inverted index for one new or changed document can mean touching the postings list of every distinct term in that document, which is expensive to do synchronously on every single write. Batching updates and refreshing the searchable index on an interval trades a small amount of write-to-search latency for much better indexing throughput.

callout.text: A search engine answers 'which documents contain this word' in milliseconds by flipping the obvious data structure inside out ahead of time, from document-to-words into **word-to-documents**.

lesson.content:
# Object / Blob Storage Systems

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **Object storage** gives up the filesystem's folder-and-edit model entirely in exchange for something that scales to trillions of files across thousands of machines: every object is a whole, immutable blob addressed by a flat key, never a path you partially edit.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Uploading and replicating an object

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client (upload)"]:::client
    gateway["Object Storage API"]:::server
    s1["Storage node (rack A)"]:::server
    s2["Storage node (rack B)"]:::server
    s3["Storage node (rack C)"]:::server
    client -->|"PUT object"| gateway
    gateway -->|"replica 1"| s1
    gateway -->|"replica 2"| s2
    gateway -.->|"replica 3"| s3
```

#### Filesystem vs object storage

| Traditional filesystem | Object storage |
| :--- | :--- |
| Nested folder hierarchy, in-place partial edits | Flat key space inside buckets, objects are whole and immutable |
| Optimized for one machine's local or attached disk | Built to scale across thousands of machines and data centers |
| Fine-grained, low-latency small reads and writes | Replace-the-whole-object updates, durability via replication or erasure coding |

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Trying to use object storage like a shared network filesystem==, expecting fast partial edits or fine-grained locking that its whole-object, immutable model was never designed to provide.
- ⚠️ Assuming the folder-like structure implied by slashes in an object's key is a real, efficiently-navigable directory tree, when it's typically just a flat namespace with string prefix matching for listing.
- ⚠️ Storing huge numbers of very small, frequently-updated objects in object storage when a database or filesystem would fit that access pattern far better, and paying per-request costs that add up fast at that shape.
- ⚠️ Choosing an archive or cold tier for data that turns out to need frequent access, then absorbing large, repeated retrieval costs and multi-hour latency that a warmer tier would have avoided.
- ⚠️ ==Forgetting that object storage durability is about surviving hardware failure, not about protecting against a bad application deleting or overwriting the wrong object==, versioning or backups are still needed for that.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you efficiently edit a single byte in the middle of an object stored in something like S3, and why is that actually a feature, not a limitation?**

> **Model Answer:** Object storage treats every object as a whole, immutable unit, updates mean uploading an entirely new version rather than modifying bytes in place. This removes the need to coordinate concurrent partial writes to the same object across a massively distributed system, which is exactly the kind of coordination problem that makes traditional shared filesystems hard to scale to the size object storage systems operate at.

**Q: What's the practical trade-off between full replication and erasure coding for object durability?**

> **Model Answer:** Full replication stores multiple complete copies of an object, simple and fast to read or reconstruct from, but uses several times the object's actual size in raw storage. Erasure coding splits the object into data and parity fragments and can tolerate losing some fragments while using meaningfully less total storage than full replication, at the cost of extra CPU work to reconstruct the object when fragments are missing.

**Q: Why is object storage considered the backbone of media-heavy systems specifically, rather than a general-purpose replacement for a database?**

> **Model Answer:** Media files like photos and video are large, written once (or replaced wholesale on edit), and read very often, exactly the access pattern object storage is optimized for: whole-object writes, massively parallel whole-object reads, and cheap-per-gigabyte durable storage. A database is optimized for small, frequent, partial updates and complex queries, a completely different shape of workload that object storage deliberately doesn't try to serve.

topics.description: Sending one notification is trivial, sending the same event to millions of devices reliably, and quietly retrying the ones that fail, is a **fan-out** and queueing problem wearing a friendly UI.

lesson.summary: Sending one notification is trivial, sending the same event to millions of devices reliably, and quietly retrying the ones that fail, is a **fan-out** and queueing problem wearing a friendly UI.
lesson.content:
# Notification Delivery Systems

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Sending one notification is trivial, sending the same event to millions of devices reliably, and quietly retrying the ones that fail, is a **fan-out** and queueing problem wearing a friendly UI.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Fan-out from one event to millions of push notifications

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    trigger["Triggering Service"]:::server
    queue>"Notification Queue"]:::queue
    worker["Delivery Workers"]:::server
    dlq>"Dead Letter Queue"]:::queue
    apns["Push Provider (APNs/FCM)"]:::server
    trigger -->|"one event"| queue
    queue -->|"fan out per device"| worker
    worker -->|"deliver"| apns
    worker -.->|"repeated failure"| dlq
```

#### Retry with exponential backoff and jitter

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Attempt 1 fails (wait ~1s + jitter)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Attempt 2 fails (wait ~2s + jitter)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Attempt 3 fails (wait ~4s + jitter)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Attempt 4 fails (max retries reached)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Send to dead letter queue (stop retrying, alert or inspect)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Retry delay growth: exponential backoff vs backoff with jitter

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Sending notifications synchronously inside the request that triggered them==, which makes the triggering action's latency scale with the number of recipients instead of staying constant.
- ⚠️ ==Retrying failed deliveries immediately and aggressively without backoff==, which can turn a brief provider hiccup into a self-inflicted traffic spike that makes the outage worse.
- ⚠️ Retrying every failed delivery forever with no dead letter queue, quietly burning worker capacity on tokens or endpoints that will never succeed again.
- ⚠️ Treating push delivery as guaranteed and instant, when devices can be offline, apps uninstalled, or tokens stale, delivery is inherently best-effort even when the system itself is working correctly.
- ⚠️ Building a webhook or push system without idempotency on the receiving side, then getting duplicate notifications or duplicate side effects the moment an at-least-once retry succeeds after the original attempt actually landed.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does a notification system need a queue between the triggering event and actual delivery, instead of just delivering directly?**

> **Model Answer:** One event, like a viral post, can require delivering to millions of devices, and doing that synchronously would make the triggering request's latency scale with the number of recipients, an unbounded and unacceptable cost. A queue absorbs the fan-out asynchronously, letting the triggering request return immediately while a pool of workers handles the actual per-device delivery at its own pace.

**Q: A downstream push provider starts failing intermittently. Why is retrying immediately and repeatedly a bad idea, and what should happen instead?**

> **Model Answer:** Immediate, repeated retries add exactly the same load pattern back onto a provider that's already struggling, which can turn a brief hiccup into a sustained outage. Exponential backoff with jitter spaces retries out with increasing, randomized delays, giving the provider room to recover and avoiding a synchronized wave of retries all landing at once.

**Q: What's the difference between at-most-once and at-least-once delivery for notifications, and why do most systems pick at-least-once?**

> **Model Answer:** At-most-once fires a delivery attempt once and doesn't retry, so a transient failure means the notification is simply lost. **At-least-once** retries until success or a dead letter queue, guaranteeing delivery eventually happens if the target is reachable, at the cost of ==possible duplicates==, which is why most systems choose at-least-once and rely on idempotency on the receiving side rather than accept silent message loss.

topics.title: Design a URL Shortener
topics.description: A URL shortener is really just a distributed key-value store (short code -> long URL) with one extremely **read-heavy access pattern**, so almost every real design decision is about making that one lookup fast and that one code generation ==collision-free==.

lesson.summary: A URL shortener is really just a distributed key-value store (short code -> long URL) with one extremely **read-heavy access pattern**, so almost every real design decision is about making that one lookup fast and that one code generation ==collision-free==.
lesson.content:
# Design a URL Shortener

> **Difficulty:** `EASY` | **Target Companies:** `Bitly • TinyURL • Twitter (t.co)` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A URL shortener is really just a distributed key-value store (short code -> long URL) with one extremely **read-heavy access pattern**, so almost every real design decision is about making that one lookup fast and that one code generation ==collision-free==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a service like Bitly: a user submits a long URL and gets back a
short one (like short.ly/aZ9k2). Visiting the short URL redirects the
visitor to the original long URL. Design the system that makes this work
at scale.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many URLs do we need to shorten per day, and what's the read:write ratio?
*Why it matters:* URL shorteners are read-heavy by nature, usually 100:1 or more redirects to creations. That ratio decides whether you even need a cache layer, and how aggressively.

#### Q: Do short URLs need to be unguessable/random, or is a short, possibly predictable code acceptable?
*Why it matters:* This decides between a counter-based approach (predictable, simpler, sequential) and a random-generation approach (needs collision checking, but codes can't be enumerated by an attacker).

#### Q: Do users need custom aliases (choose their own short code), and do links expire?
*Why it matters:* Custom aliases mean you must handle uniqueness conflicts at write time with a clear error, not silently. Expiry means you need a background cleanup job or TTL-based storage, not just a table that grows forever.

#### Q: Do we need click analytics (how many times a link was visited, from where)?
*Why it matters:* Analytics turns this from 'one write path, one read path' into a system with an additional high-volume event-logging pipeline that must not slow down the redirect itself.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Given a long URL, generate and return a unique short URL.
- Given a short URL, redirect the visitor to the original long URL with low latency.
- Support optional custom aliases chosen by the user.
- Support optional expiration dates on shortened links.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Redirects must be fast: well under 100ms, since a slow redirect is a bad experience on every single click.**
- **High availability for redirects specifically: a URL shortener being briefly unable to accept new links is tolerable, being unable to redirect existing ones is not.**
- **Short codes must be effectively unique with no user-visible collisions, even under concurrent writes.**
- **The system must scale to billions of stored URLs and tens of thousands of redirects per second at peak.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 100 million new short URLs created per day
- 100:1 read-to-write ratio (10 billion redirects per day)
- Each stored URL record is roughly 500 bytes (long URL + short code + metadata)
- Links are kept for 5 years by default

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Write QPS:** 100,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 1,160 writes/sec average; design for 5-10x that at peak, so ~10,000 writes/sec
- **Read QPS:** 100:1 ratio means ≈ 116,000 reads/sec average, well over 500,000/sec at peak, this is the number that actually drives the architecture
- **Storage over 5 years:** 100M/day * 365 * 5 * 500 bytes ≈ 91 TB total, which comfortably fits a horizontally sharded relational or key-value store, not a single machine
- **Short code space needed:** 100M/day * 365 * 5 ≈ 182 billion codes; base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) with 7 characters gives 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations, comfortably enough

*Capacity Takeaway:* This is a read-dominated system by roughly two orders of magnitude, so the entire architecture should be optimized around making redirects fast and cacheable, while writes can tolerate slightly more latency.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A client hits a load balancer, which routes to a stateless fleet of app
servers. Writes (POST /shorten) go to the app server, which generates a
short code and writes it to a sharded database, the source of truth. Reads
(GET /{shortCode}) first check a distributed cache (like Redis); on a cache
hit the redirect happens immediately, on a miss the app server reads from
the database and populates the cache before redirecting. Because reads
outnumber writes by roughly 100 to 1, the cache is doing almost all of the
real work in this system, the database mostly needs to be correct and
durable, not blazing fast on every single read.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### High-level design: redirect (read) path dominates

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    cache["Cache (Redis)"]:::cache
    db[("Sharded DB")]:::db
    queue>"Click Events Queue"]:::queue
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"read (hot path)"| cache
    cache -.->|"miss -> read"| db
    app -->|"write"| db
    app -.->|"log click"| queue
```

#### A redirect request, step by step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Client requests /{shortCode} (GET)"]:::step
    step_2["2. App server checks cache (Redis lookup)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Cache hit (return long_url immediately)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Cache miss -> DB read (then populate cache)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. 301/302 redirect (browser follows to long_url)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Short code generation, hash vs counter

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["New long URL submitted"] --> b{"Custom alias given?"}
  b -->|"yes"| c["Check alias uniqueness"]
  b -->|"no"| d["Generate code"]
  d --> e{"Hash or counter?"}
  e -->|"hash"| f["Base62-encode hash, check collision"]
  e -->|"counter"| g["Base62-encode counter value"]
  c --> h["Store mapping"]
  f --> h
  g --> h
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/shorten` | Body: { long_url, custom_alias?, expires_at? }. Returns the generated (or validated custom) short code and full short URL. |
| `GET` | `/{shortCode}` | Looks up shortCode, returns an HTTP 301/302 redirect to the original long URL, or 404 if not found or expired. |
| `GET` | `/api/urls/{shortCode}/stats` | Returns click count and basic analytics for a given short URL, if analytics are enabled. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/urls/{shortCode}` | Deletes or deactivates a short URL before its natural expiry, owner-authenticated. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `urls`
- `short_code (string, primary key, e.g. base62, indexed)`
- `long_url (text, the original destination)`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
- `expires_at (timestamp, nullable)`
- `owner_id (nullable, if user accounts exist)`
*Notes:* The entire hot path only ever needs short_code -> long_url, which is exactly why this fits a key-value store as well as a relational one.

### Entity: `click_events`
- `short_code (string, indexed)`
- `timestamp (timestamp)`
- `referrer (string, nullable)`
- `approx_location (string, nullable, derived from IP)`
*Notes:* Written asynchronously via a queue, never on the synchronous redirect path, so analytics can never slow down a redirect.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you generate the short code itself?
Two real approaches exist. Approach one: hash the long URL (e.g. MD5) and take the first 7 characters, base62-encoded, then check for collisions and re-hash with a salt if one occurs, this is stateless but needs a collision check on every write. Approach two: use a centralized counter (or pre-generated range of counter values handed out to each app server) and base62-encode the counter value itself, guaranteeing uniqueness by construction with zero collision checks, at the cost of needing that counter to be a reliable, available service itself.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Hash-based: no shared state needed between servers, but requires a collision check (an extra database read) on every single write
- Counter-based: zero collision checks ever, but the counter service becomes a new component that must itself be highly available and not become a bottleneck
- A common middle ground: give each app server a pre-allocated range of counter values (e.g. server A gets 1,000,001 to 2,000,000) so most writes never even need to talk to the counter service

### Why cache redirects instead of always hitting the database?
With a 100:1 read:write ratio, the redirect path is where nearly all system load lives, so it's the one path worth optimizing hardest. A cache (Redis or Memcached) holding the hottest short codes in memory turns a database round trip into an in-memory lookup, cutting redirect latency from tens of milliseconds to sub-millisecond, and taking almost all read load off the database entirely.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Cache-aside (read from cache, populate on miss): simple, works well since URL mappings almost never change after creation, so stale cache data is a non-issue
- Skipping the cache entirely would mean every one of the ~500,000 peak reads/sec hits the database directly, which no single database (or even a modest shard count) comfortably survives
- Because a short_code's long_url essentially never changes once created, there's no meaningful cache-invalidation problem here, which is what makes caching this particular system unusually easy compared to most

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The database is the eventual bottleneck for writes at very high scale; shard by short_code (e.g. hash-based sharding) so writes and the occasional cache-miss read distribute across many machines instead of one.
- A single centralized counter service (if using the counter-based generation approach) can become a bottleneck or single point of failure; solve by handing out pre-allocated ranges to each app server instead of round-tripping to the counter on every write.
- The cache itself needs to be a cluster (not one instance) once traffic is high enough, using consistent hashing to spread hot keys across cache nodes without one node becoming overloaded.
- If analytics volume grows large, the click-event write path needs its own queue and separate storage (e.g. a time-series or analytics-optimized store) so it never competes with the redirect path for resources.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing the short code generator around random generation with retry-on-collision without estimating how often collisions actually occur at scale, when they're rare enough that hashing is usually fine, or common enough that a counter-based approach is clearly better.
- ⚠️ ==Forgetting to cache redirects at all== and assuming a single database can handle hundreds of thousands of reads per second directly.
- ⚠️ Writing click analytics synchronously in the same request path as the redirect, adding latency to every single click for a feature that doesn't need to be real-time.
- ⚠️ Choosing a short code length without doing the math on how many codes are actually needed, either wasting characters (URLs longer than necessary) or running out of code space years earlier than expected.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is a URL shortener a good system to reason about caching with almost no downsides?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a short_code's mapping to a long_url practically never changes once created (there's no 'edit' operation in the core flow), so there's no cache invalidation problem: whatever you cache stays correct indefinitely, which is unusual and makes caching an almost pure win here.

**Q: What happens if two users try to create the same custom alias at the same time?**

> **Model Answer:** This needs a uniqueness constraint enforced at the database level (a unique index on short_code), and the write should be attempted with that constraint, catching the conflict and returning a clear 'alias taken' error to whichever request loses the race, rather than trying to check-then-write in the application layer, which has a race condition window.

# Design a URL Shortener

> **Difficulty:** `EASY` | **Target Companies:** `Bitly • TinyURL • Twitter (t.co)` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A URL shortener is really just a distributed key-value store (short code -> long URL) with one extremely **read-heavy access pattern**, so almost every real design decision is about making that one lookup fast and that one code generation ==collision-free==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a service like Bitly: a user submits a long URL and gets back a
short one (like short.ly/aZ9k2). Visiting the short URL redirects the
visitor to the original long URL. Design the system that makes this work
at scale.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many URLs do we need to shorten per day, and what's the read:write ratio?
*Why it matters:* URL shorteners are read-heavy by nature, usually 100:1 or more redirects to creations. That ratio decides whether you even need a cache layer, and how aggressively.

#### Q: Do short URLs need to be unguessable/random, or is a short, possibly predictable code acceptable?
*Why it matters:* This decides between a counter-based approach (predictable, simpler, sequential) and a random-generation approach (needs collision checking, but codes can't be enumerated by an attacker).

#### Q: Do users need custom aliases (choose their own short code), and do links expire?
*Why it matters:* Custom aliases mean you must handle uniqueness conflicts at write time with a clear error, not silently. Expiry means you need a background cleanup job or TTL-based storage, not just a table that grows forever.

#### Q: Do we need click analytics (how many times a link was visited, from where)?
*Why it matters:* Analytics turns this from 'one write path, one read path' into a system with an additional high-volume event-logging pipeline that must not slow down the redirect itself.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Given a long URL, generate and return a unique short URL.
- Given a short URL, redirect the visitor to the original long URL with low latency.
- Support optional custom aliases chosen by the user.
- Support optional expiration dates on shortened links.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Redirects must be fast: well under 100ms, since a slow redirect is a bad experience on every single click.**
- **High availability for redirects specifically: a URL shortener being briefly unable to accept new links is tolerable, being unable to redirect existing ones is not.**
- **Short codes must be effectively unique with no user-visible collisions, even under concurrent writes.**
- **The system must scale to billions of stored URLs and tens of thousands of redirects per second at peak.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 100 million new short URLs created per day
- 100:1 read-to-write ratio (10 billion redirects per day)
- Each stored URL record is roughly 500 bytes (long URL + short code + metadata)
- Links are kept for 5 years by default

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Write QPS:** 100,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 1,160 writes/sec average; design for 5-10x that at peak, so ~10,000 writes/sec
- **Read QPS:** 100:1 ratio means ≈ 116,000 reads/sec average, well over 500,000/sec at peak, this is the number that actually drives the architecture
- **Storage over 5 years:** 100M/day * 365 * 5 * 500 bytes ≈ 91 TB total, which comfortably fits a horizontally sharded relational or key-value store, not a single machine
- **Short code space needed:** 100M/day * 365 * 5 ≈ 182 billion codes; base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) with 7 characters gives 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations, comfortably enough

*Capacity Takeaway:* This is a read-dominated system by roughly two orders of magnitude, so the entire architecture should be optimized around making redirects fast and cacheable, while writes can tolerate slightly more latency.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A client hits a load balancer, which routes to a stateless fleet of app
servers. Writes (POST /shorten) go to the app server, which generates a
short code and writes it to a sharded database, the source of truth. Reads
(GET /{shortCode}) first check a distributed cache (like Redis); on a cache
hit the redirect happens immediately, on a miss the app server reads from
the database and populates the cache before redirecting. Because reads
outnumber writes by roughly 100 to 1, the cache is doing almost all of the
real work in this system, the database mostly needs to be correct and
durable, not blazing fast on every single read.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### High-level design: redirect (read) path dominates

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    cache["Cache (Redis)"]:::cache
    db[("Sharded DB")]:::db
    queue>"Click Events Queue"]:::queue
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"read (hot path)"| cache
    cache -.->|"miss -> read"| db
    app -->|"write"| db
    app -.->|"log click"| queue
```

#### A redirect request, step by step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Client requests /{shortCode} (GET)"]:::step
    step_2["2. App server checks cache (Redis lookup)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Cache hit (return long_url immediately)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Cache miss -> DB read (then populate cache)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. 301/302 redirect (browser follows to long_url)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Short code generation, hash vs counter

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["New long URL submitted"] --> b{"Custom alias given?"}
  b -->|"yes"| c["Check alias uniqueness"]
  b -->|"no"| d["Generate code"]
  d --> e{"Hash or counter?"}
  e -->|"hash"| f["Base62-encode hash, check collision"]
  e -->|"counter"| g["Base62-encode counter value"]
  c --> h["Store mapping"]
  f --> h
  g --> h
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/shorten` | Body: { long_url, custom_alias?, expires_at? }. Returns the generated (or validated custom) short code and full short URL. |
| `GET` | `/{shortCode}` | Looks up shortCode, returns an HTTP 301/302 redirect to the original long URL, or 404 if not found or expired. |
| `GET` | `/api/urls/{shortCode}/stats` | Returns click count and basic analytics for a given short URL, if analytics are enabled. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/urls/{shortCode}` | Deletes or deactivates a short URL before its natural expiry, owner-authenticated. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `urls`
- `short_code (string, primary key, e.g. base62, indexed)`
- `long_url (text, the original destination)`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
- `expires_at (timestamp, nullable)`
- `owner_id (nullable, if user accounts exist)`
*Notes:* The entire hot path only ever needs short_code -> long_url, which is exactly why this fits a key-value store as well as a relational one.

### Entity: `click_events`
- `short_code (string, indexed)`
- `timestamp (timestamp)`
- `referrer (string, nullable)`
- `approx_location (string, nullable, derived from IP)`
*Notes:* Written asynchronously via a queue, never on the synchronous redirect path, so analytics can never slow down a redirect.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you generate the short code itself?
Two real approaches exist. Approach one: hash the long URL (e.g. MD5) and take the first 7 characters, base62-encoded, then check for collisions and re-hash with a salt if one occurs, this is stateless but needs a collision check on every write. Approach two: use a centralized counter (or pre-generated range of counter values handed out to each app server) and base62-encode the counter value itself, guaranteeing uniqueness by construction with zero collision checks, at the cost of needing that counter to be a reliable, available service itself.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Hash-based: no shared state needed between servers, but requires a collision check (an extra database read) on every single write
- Counter-based: zero collision checks ever, but the counter service becomes a new component that must itself be highly available and not become a bottleneck
- A common middle ground: give each app server a pre-allocated range of counter values (e.g. server A gets 1,000,001 to 2,000,000) so most writes never even need to talk to the counter service

### Why cache redirects instead of always hitting the database?
With a 100:1 read:write ratio, the redirect path is where nearly all system load lives, so it's the one path worth optimizing hardest. A cache (Redis or Memcached) holding the hottest short codes in memory turns a database round trip into an in-memory lookup, cutting redirect latency from tens of milliseconds to sub-millisecond, and taking almost all read load off the database entirely.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Cache-aside (read from cache, populate on miss): simple, works well since URL mappings almost never change after creation, so stale cache data is a non-issue
- Skipping the cache entirely would mean every one of the ~500,000 peak reads/sec hits the database directly, which no single database (or even a modest shard count) comfortably survives
- Because a short_code's long_url essentially never changes once created, there's no meaningful cache-invalidation problem here, which is what makes caching this particular system unusually easy compared to most

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The database is the eventual bottleneck for writes at very high scale; shard by short_code (e.g. hash-based sharding) so writes and the occasional cache-miss read distribute across many machines instead of one.
- A single centralized counter service (if using the counter-based generation approach) can become a bottleneck or single point of failure; solve by handing out pre-allocated ranges to each app server instead of round-tripping to the counter on every write.
- The cache itself needs to be a cluster (not one instance) once traffic is high enough, using consistent hashing to spread hot keys across cache nodes without one node becoming overloaded.
- If analytics volume grows large, the click-event write path needs its own queue and separate storage (e.g. a time-series or analytics-optimized store) so it never competes with the redirect path for resources.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing the short code generator around random generation with retry-on-collision without estimating how often collisions actually occur at scale, when they're rare enough that hashing is usually fine, or common enough that a counter-based approach is clearly better.
- ⚠️ ==Forgetting to cache redirects at all== and assuming a single database can handle hundreds of thousands of reads per second directly.
- ⚠️ Writing click analytics synchronously in the same request path as the redirect, adding latency to every single click for a feature that doesn't need to be real-time.
- ⚠️ Choosing a short code length without doing the math on how many codes are actually needed, either wasting characters (URLs longer than necessary) or running out of code space years earlier than expected.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups

> **Model Answer:** Because a short_code's mapping to a long_url practically never changes once created (there's no 'edit' operation in the core flow), so there's no cache invalidation problem: whatever you cache stays correct indefinitely, which is unusual and makes caching an almost pure win here.

**Q: What happens if two users try to create the same custom alias at the same time?**

> **Model Answer:** This needs a uniqueness constraint enforced at the database level (a unique index on short_code), and the write should be attempted with that constraint, catching the conflict and returning a clear 'alias taken' error to whichever request loses the race, rather than trying to check-then-write in the application layer, which has a race condition window.

lesson.content:
# Design a Rate Limiter

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Stripe • Cloudflare • AWS API Gateway` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A rate limiter is a **distributed counting problem** disguised as an algorithm problem: the hard part was never picking token bucket versus sliding window, it's ==keeping one accurate, low-latency count per client== when a hundred stateless app servers are all trying to enforce the same limit at once.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a rate limiter that protects an API from being overwhelmed by any
single client: each API key or user should be allowed at most N requests
per time window, and requests beyond that limit should be rejected quickly
and cheaply, without slowing down the requests that are still allowed
through.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is the limit per API key/user, per IP address, or both, and does it apply globally or per endpoint?
*Why it matters:* Per-IP limiting breaks down behind NAT or shared corporate proxies, and per-endpoint limits (e.g. a cheap read endpoint vs an expensive write endpoint) need separate counters, not one global counter, which changes the key design entirely.

#### Q: Does the limit need to be hard real-time accurate, or is some slack (a client briefly exceeding the limit) acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Perfectly exact distributed counting requires synchronous coordination on every request, which adds latency to every allowed request too. Tolerating small slack unlocks much cheaper, eventually-consistent counting schemes.

#### Q: What should happen to a rejected request: a hard 429 error, or should it be queued and retried later?
*Why it matters:* A hard rejection means the limiter only needs to answer 'allow or deny' quickly. A queue-and-retry model turns this into a second system (a request queue with its own backpressure), which is a materially different and larger design.

#### Q: How many distinct clients need independent limits, and how many app servers will be enforcing the limit simultaneously?
*Why it matters:* A handful of clients and one app server could get away with an in-memory counter. Millions of clients across hundreds of app servers is what forces the counter into a shared, external store, which is the entire crux of this design.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Allow a client at most N requests within a rolling or fixed time window (e.g. 100 requests per minute).
- Reject requests over the limit with a clear signal (HTTP 429) and, ideally, a Retry-After header.
- Support different limits for different clients or tiers (e.g. free tier vs paid tier).
- Support independent limits per endpoint, not just one global count per client.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **The limiter check itself must add minimal latency, ideally low single-digit milliseconds, since it runs on every single request.**
- **The limiter must work correctly across many app servers enforcing the same limit concurrently, not just on one machine.**
- **The limiter must fail safe under its own infrastructure failure: a rate-limiting outage should not take down the whole API (fail open or fail closed, deliberately chosen, not accidental).**
- **The system must handle at least tens of thousands of rate-limit checks per second at peak without becoming the bottleneck itself.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million active API clients, each with an independent limit
- Average client makes 10 requests/minute, peak clients make up to 1,000 requests/minute
- Every single API request needs a rate-limit check, so check volume equals total request volume
- Total API traffic across all clients averages 50,000 requests/sec at peak

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Rate-limit checks per second at peak:** 50,000 requests/sec means 50,000 rate-limit checks/sec, this is the load the limiter itself must sustain, not just the API behind it
- **Counter storage size:** 5,000,000 clients * ~100 bytes per counter entry (key + count + window timestamp) ≈ 500 MB, comfortably fits in memory on a small Redis cluster
- **Per-check latency budget:** If the total request budget is 100ms and the rate-limit check must stay a small fraction of that, it needs to land under 2-5ms, which rules out a check that does a disk-backed database round trip
- **Redis ops needed:** 50,000 checks/sec each needing 1-2 Redis operations (read/increment) ≈ 50,000-100,000 ops/sec, well within a single well-provisioned Redis instance's typical 100,000+ ops/sec, so one shared counter store is realistic before any sharding is needed

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that drives this architecture isn't the limit value itself, it's that every one of 50,000 requests/sec needs a sub-5ms answer from a counter that many app servers share, which is why the counter has to live in a fast, shared, in-memory store rather than in each app server's own memory.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Every incoming request passes through a rate-limit middleware layer,
typically at the API gateway, before it ever reaches an app server's
business logic. That middleware computes a key from the client ID and
endpoint, then does a single fast read-and-increment against a shared
Redis (or Redis Cluster) counter store, using an algorithm like token
bucket or sliding window log to decide allow or deny. Because the counter
lives in one shared store rather than in each app server's local memory,
every app server enforcing the same client's limit sees the same count, no
matter which server the client's requests happen to land on behind the
load balancer. Allowed requests continue to the app server; denied ones
get a 429 immediately, never touching business logic at all.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Rate limiting at the API gateway, backed by a shared counter store

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["API Client"]:::client
    gateway["API Gateway (limiter)"]:::server
    cache["Redis Counter Store"]:::cache
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    config[("Policy Config DB")]:::db
    client --> gateway
    gateway -->|"check + increment"| cache
    gateway -->|"allowed"| app
    gateway -.->|"load limit policy"| config
```

#### One request through the rate limiter

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Request arrives at gateway (with client API key)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Compute counter key (client_id + endpoint + window)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Read-and-increment in Redis (atomic operation)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Under limit (forward to app server)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Over limit (return 429 + Retry-After)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Token bucket level over time (capacity 10, refill 2/sec)

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/internal/rate-limit/check` | Body: { client_id, endpoint_key }. Internal call made by the API gateway/middleware on every request; returns { allowed: bool, remaining, retry_after_seconds }. |
| `PUT` | `/api/admin/rate-limits/{client_id}` | Body: { limit, window_seconds }. Sets or updates a custom rate limit for a specific client (e.g. a paid-tier override). |
| `GET` | `/api/admin/rate-limits/{client_id}` | Returns the current configured limit and live usage count for a client, for support/debugging purposes. |
| `ANY` | `/{any protected endpoint}` | Every real API endpoint passes through rate-limit middleware first; on rejection returns 429 with a Retry-After header before the request ever reaches business logic. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `rate_limit_counters`
- `key (string, e.g. "client_123:endpoint_orders:window_1699999980", the composite key that scopes a counter to a client, endpoint, and time window)`
- `count (integer, current request count in this window)`
- `ttl (the window's expiry, so stale windows are automatically cleaned up rather than growing forever)`
*Notes:* Lives in an in-memory store (Redis), not the primary relational database, because it needs sub-millisecond reads and writes and the data is disposable once its window expires.

### Entity: `rate_limit_policies`
- `client_id (or tier name)`
- `endpoint_key`
- `limit (max requests per window)`
- `window_seconds`
*Notes:* The relatively small, low-write-volume configuration table read (and cached) by the rate-limit middleware to know what limit applies to a given request; changes rarely compared to the counters themselves.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Which rate-limiting algorithm: token bucket, fixed window, or sliding window?
Fixed window (count resets to zero at each minute boundary) is the simplest to implement but allows a burst of up to 2x the limit right at a window boundary, since a client can use its full quota in the last second of one window and again in the first second of the next. Token bucket (a bucket refills tokens at a steady rate, each request consumes one token) smooths this out and naturally allows small bursts up to the bucket size, which matches real traffic patterns well. Sliding window log (track exact timestamps of recent requests) is the most accurate but the most expensive to store, since it keeps a growing list per client rather than a single integer.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Fixed window: cheapest (one counter, one TTL), but allows boundary bursts up to double the intended limit
- Token bucket: smooths bursts, cheap to compute (just track tokens and a last-refill timestamp), the industry-standard choice for most APIs, but slightly more complex to reason about than a raw counter
- Sliding window log: most precise, no boundary burst problem at all, but storage grows with request volume per client instead of staying constant, making it the most expensive option at scale
- Sliding window counter (a hybrid that weights the previous and current fixed windows): near sliding-window accuracy at near fixed-window cost, the pragmatic middle ground many production systems actually ship

### Where should the limiter live: client SDK, API gateway, or each individual service?
A client-side SDK can self-throttle to be a good citizen, but it can't be trusted as the actual enforcement point since a malicious or buggy client can simply ignore it. Enforcing at the API gateway means one centralized place checks every request before it reaches any backend service, which is simple to operate and consistent. Enforcing inside each individual service allows different services to have very different limit logic, but means every service reimplements (and can inconsistently implement) the same concern.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Client SDK only: cheap, but not enforceable, exists purely as a courtesy for well-behaved clients, never sufficient alone
- API gateway (centralized): one consistent enforcement point, easy to reason about and change limits globally, but every request pays the cost of a gateway hop and the gateway becomes a component every request depends on
- Per-service enforcement: allows service-specific nuance (e.g. an expensive ML inference endpoint wants a stricter limit than a cheap read endpoint), but risks inconsistent implementations and duplicated counter infrastructure across teams
- The common real-world answer: coarse global limiting at the gateway, plus optional finer per-endpoint limits enforced by individual services for their especially expensive operations

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single Redis instance holding all counters becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure at very high request volume; shard counters across a Redis Cluster by hashing the client key, similar to how a cache would be sharded.
- A synchronous round trip to Redis on every request adds latency and a hard dependency; many production limiters batch or approximate counts locally (e.g. count locally and sync to Redis every N requests or M milliseconds) trading small accuracy loss for much lower latency and Redis load.
- If Redis itself becomes unavailable, the system must have a deliberate fail-open (allow all requests, risking overload) or fail-closed (reject all requests, risking a full outage over a rate-limiter failure) policy, chosen explicitly rather than left to whatever the client library does by default.
- Hot clients (a single very high-volume API key) can still create a hotspot on one Redis key even with sharding; this is usually acceptable since it's bounded to one client's traffic, but extreme cases may need that one client's counter further split and merged.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Storing rate-limit counters in each app server's local memory==, which silently breaks the moment there's more than one app server, since a client can just get routed to a different server with its own fresh counter.
- ⚠️ Picking fixed window without realizing it allows up to **double the intended request rate** right at window boundaries, which matters a lot for strict limits.
- ⚠️ Not deciding what happens when the rate-limit store itself goes down, leaving the system to fail open or closed by accident rather than by design.
- ⚠️ Enforcing rate limits after expensive business logic has already run, instead of as early as possible (ideally at the gateway), wasting compute on requests that were always going to be rejected.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does a rate limiter need a shared, external counter store instead of just using each server's local memory?**

> **Model Answer:** Because in any real deployment, a client's requests are load-balanced across many stateless app servers, not pinned to one. If each server kept its own local counter, a client could receive N times the intended limit simply by having requests spread across N servers, since no single server would ever see the client's full request count. A shared store like Redis gives every server the same, consistent view of a client's usage.

**Q: How would you rate-limit fairly when the rate limiter's own Redis backing store is briefly slow or unavailable?**

> **Model Answer:** This requires a deliberate choice: fail open (let requests through when the check can't be performed, protecting availability at the cost of temporarily unenforced limits) or fail closed (reject requests when the check can't be performed, protecting the backend at the cost of availability for legitimate traffic). Most production systems fail open for short blips, since a brief loss of rate limiting is usually less damaging than an outage, but this should be an explicit design decision, documented and tested, not a default nobody chose.
