lesson.content:
# Design a Nearby Search Service (Yelp)

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Yelp • Google Places` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The hard part isn't choosing a single clever geospatial data structure, it's that 'nearby' and 'matches ramen' are answered by two completely different kinds of index, a **spatial structure** and a **text/inverted index**, and naively running one filter then the other throws away most of the other index's power, so the real design question is how to combine them into one fast query.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a service like Yelp: users can search for businesses matching a
text query (e.g. "ramen") within a given distance of their current
location, and results come back ranked by a mix of relevance and
distance. Businesses have relatively static profiles (name, category,
address, rating) that are updated far less often than they're searched.
Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is the search always 'text query plus a distance radius,' or does it also need to support pure category browsing with no text (e.g. 'show me all coffee shops nearby')?
*Why it matters:* Pure category/location browsing with no free text is a much simpler query, essentially just the spatial filter. If free-text relevance search is a first-class, always-present part of the query, the design has to seriously address combining a spatial index with a text index, not just bolt text search on as an afterthought.

#### Q: How static are business locations and profiles, do they change roughly daily (new photos, hours) or almost never (address, category)?
*Why it matters:* This is a read-heavy system regardless, but the update cadence determines whether the combined spatial-plus-text index can be rebuilt in large batches on a comfortable schedule, or needs a more real-time incremental update path. Low write volume means the design can lean toward index structures that are cheap to query but relatively expensive to update, since updates are rare.

#### Q: Does ranking need to account for more than distance and text relevance, like star rating, review count, or sponsored placement?
*Why it matters:* Pure distance-plus-relevance ranking is a two-factor scoring function. Adding rating, popularity, or paid placement turns ranking into a genuinely multi-factor scoring problem that changes how aggressively the system can pre-filter candidates before ranking, since a business slightly farther away but much higher-rated might need to outrank a closer, mediocre one.

#### Q: What's the typical search radius and business density, a dense city block or a 20-mile suburban radius?
*Why it matters:* Dense urban search radii return huge raw candidate counts (thousands of businesses within a mile) that need heavy pre-filtering before text ranking is affordable, while sparse suburban searches might return so few candidates that the spatial filter barely matters and text relevance dominates. The typical case shapes how much the system leans on the spatial index to narrow things down early.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can search for businesses by free-text query (name, category, or description keywords) within a specified radius of a given location.
- Search results are ranked by a combination of text relevance and distance from the search location.
- A user can view a business's full profile: name, address, category, hours, rating, and photos.
- Business owners (or an internal pipeline) can create and update business listings, including their location and category.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Search must return results in well under a second, since this is an interactive, type-and-browse search experience.**
- **The system is overwhelmingly read-heavy: searches vastly outnumber business profile updates, and the design should be optimized accordingly.**
- **Search should remain fast and relevant in both dense urban areas (thousands of candidates within a mile) and sparse areas (a handful of candidates within twenty miles).**
- **Newly added or updated business listings should become searchable within a reasonably short time (minutes, not necessarily seconds), since this isn't a live-inventory system.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50 million business listings globally
- 20 million searches per day, heavily concentrated during lunch and dinner hours
- Business listings change relatively rarely, on average once every few weeks per listing
- A typical urban search radius (1-2 miles) in a dense city can match 2,000-5,000 raw candidate businesses before any text filtering

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Search QPS:** 20,000,000 / 86,400 sec ≈ 230 searches/sec average, several times higher at lunch/dinner peaks
- **Listing update rate:** 50,000,000 listings / (21 days average update interval * 86,400 sec) ≈ 27 updates/sec average, roughly 8-9x lower than search volume
- **Raw spatial candidates before text ranking, dense urban query:** 2,000-5,000 candidates in a 1-2 mile radius; ranking full text relevance across all of them per query, times 230 queries/sec, is the cost the design has to control
- **Read-to-write ratio:** 230 searches/sec vs 27 updates/sec ≈ 8.5:1, confirming this is a read-optimized system where the index can favor fast queries over fast updates

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving fact is the combination of a heavily read-skewed workload (roughly 8.5 reads to 1 write) with a raw candidate count in the thousands for a single dense urban query, which means the system can afford an index structure that's expensive to update but must aggressively narrow the spatial candidate set before running expensive text relevance ranking, rather than text-ranking every business in the radius.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Business profile writes go to a durable primary store and are never
queried directly for search. Every write also enqueues an async indexing
job that updates a separate, purpose-built combined spatial-and-text
index (commonly something like Elasticsearch with a geo_point field, or a
geohash-partitioned structure paired with a per-cell inverted index). A
search request first uses the spatial component of that index to narrow
the full business population down to a bounded, nearby candidate set
(using the search location and radius), and only then runs text
relevance scoring against that already-narrowed candidate set, blending
the resulting relevance score with distance (and rating, if in scope)
into a final ranking. This ordering, spatial filter first, text ranking
second, on a combined index that supports both natively, is what keeps
queries fast even in dense urban areas with thousands of raw candidates
in range.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Search read path over a combined spatial and text index

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    searchsvc["Search Service"]:::server
    geotext["Combined Geo+Text Index"]:::server
    bizdb[("Businesses DB")]:::db
    indexq>"Index Update Queue"]:::queue
    indexer["Async Indexer"]:::server
    cache["Result Cache"]:::cache
    client -->|"search query"| lb
    lb --> searchsvc
    searchsvc -->|"check cache"| cache
    searchsvc -->|"spatial filter, then rank"| geotext
    bizdb -.->|"on write"| indexq
    indexq -.-> indexer
    indexer -.->|"update index"| geotext
```

#### Filter-first ordering: distance-first vs text-first

| Distance-first, then text rank | Text-first, then distance filter |
| :--- | :--- |
| Bounds candidate set immediately regardless of query breadth | Works well for narrow, specific text queries |
| Safer default for dense urban areas with many candidates | Broad/common queries return a huge global set before filtering |
| Still needs a candidate cap in very dense radii | Wastes relevance-ranking work on far-away results |

#### Non-linear distance decay in the ranking score

#### One search query, spatial filter to final rank

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  q["Query: text + lat/lng + radius"] --> spatial["Spatial filter via geohash cells"]
  spatial --> cap{"Candidate set too large?"}
  cap -->|"yes, dense area"| shrink["Tighten effective radius"]
  shrink --> textrank["Text relevance scoring"]
  cap -->|"no"| textrank
  textrank --> blend["Blend relevance + distance decay + rating"]
  blend --> ranked["Ranked results returned"]
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/search` | Query params: q (text), lat, lng, radius_km. Returns ranked businesses matching both the text query and the spatial radius. |
| `GET` | `/api/businesses/{businessId}` | Returns the full profile for a single business: name, address, category, hours, rating, photos. |
| `POST` | `/api/businesses` | Body: { name, category, address, lat, lng, ... }. Creates or updates a business listing; feeds the async indexing pipeline. |
| `GET` | `/api/businesses/{businessId}/reviews` | Returns paginated reviews for a business, used to compute and display its aggregate rating. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `businesses`
- `business_id`
- `name, category, description`
- `address, lat, lng`
- `avg_rating, review_count`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* The durable source of truth for a business profile, in a regular relational or document store, not queried directly for search since it isn't optimized for combined spatial-plus-text lookups.

### Entity: `geo_text_index (combined spatial + inverted index, e.g. Elasticsearch with geo_point field, or a geohash-partitioned text index)`
- `business_id`
- `geohash (or geo_point) (for spatial pre-filtering)`
- `indexed_terms (tokenized name/category/description, for text relevance)`
- `avg_rating, review_count (denormalized, for ranking without a join)`
*Notes:* The actual structure search queries hit. Rebuilt/updated asynchronously from the businesses table, deliberately denormalizing rating so ranking never needs a join at query time.

### Entity: `index_update_queue`
- `business_id`
- `change_type (create, update, delete)`
- `enqueued_at`
*Notes:* Decouples business profile writes from the (comparatively slower) work of re-indexing into the combined geo-text structure, so a profile edit doesn't block on index rebuild.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Geohash vs quadtree vs R-tree for the spatial component
Geohashing encodes lat/lng into a string where geographically close points usually (not always, due to boundary effects) share a prefix, letting 'nearby' become a cheap range query over sorted keys or a lookup across a small set of neighboring cells. A quadtree recursively subdivides space into cells sized to keep point density roughly even, so it adapts automatically to dense downtown blocks versus sparse rural areas, but a moving or newly inserted point can require rebalancing tree nodes. An R-tree groups nearby objects into bounding rectangles in a tree structure, which handles non-point data (like a business's delivery area polygon) more naturally than either geohash or quadtree, at the cost of more complex insert/query logic.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Geohash: simple, cheap range queries, easy to shard and store in an ordinary sorted structure, but fixed-size cells mean uneven density (packed downtown cells vs empty rural ones) and awkward boundary cases where two nearby points land in different-prefix cells
- Quadtree: adapts cell size to actual point density, handling urban/rural skew well, but is a genuine tree structure that's harder to shard across machines and more expensive to update on every insert or move
- R-tree: the natural choice if the data isn't just points (delivery zones, service areas), and query performance is strong, but it's the most complex of the three to implement and tune correctly, overkill for a system where every business is just a single point on a map, which is the actual shape of this problem
- For this problem, since business locations are static points with rare updates, geohash-based indexing (or a managed geospatial index like Elasticsearch's geo_point, which handles this internally) is the pragmatic choice: the simplicity and cheap queries matter more here than the update-time cost quadtrees optimize for, and there's no polygon data to justify an R-tree

### Combining spatial filtering and text relevance in one query, instead of running them as two separate steps
The naive approach picks one filter to run first and the other second: filter to businesses within radius, then linearly scan that set for text matches (fine for a small radius, catastrophic for a large one with thousands of candidates), or filter by text match first, then check distance on the results (misses genuinely nearby businesses that just don't rank in the raw global text results). Both orderings throw away information the other index has. A combined index, spatial data and inverted text index living together over the same document set, lets a single query apply both filters natively: narrow by geohash cell membership first (cheap, bounded), then run relevance scoring only against that already-small candidate set, and finally blend the two into a single ranked list.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Text-first, then filter by distance: works well when the text query is narrow (few matches globally), but a broad or common query (like a popular category) returns a huge global candidate set before distance is even considered, most of which gets thrown away, wasting the relevance engine's work
- Distance-first, then filter/rank by text: bounds the candidate set immediately regardless of query breadth, which is why it's the generally safer default, but a radius that's too large in a dense area can still hand thousands of candidates to the text ranker, so it still needs a hard candidate cap or a tighter effective radius under high density
- A genuinely combined spatial-plus-text index (e.g. Elasticsearch's geo_point combined with its native text scoring in one query): avoids materializing an intermediate candidate list twice and lets the engine optimize the combined filter-and-rank as one operation, at the cost of depending on a more specialized piece of infrastructure than a plain spatial store or a plain text index alone

### Ranking: blending distance, text relevance, and rating into one score
Once a candidate set is narrowed, each candidate needs a single final rank, not three separate ones. A common approach normalizes each signal to a comparable scale (e.g. 0-1) and combines them with tunable weights: relevance score from the text engine, a distance decay function (closer businesses score higher, but not linearly, since the difference between 0.2 and 0.5 miles matters more to a walking user than the difference between 5 and 5.3 miles), and rating/popularity as a smaller boost or tiebreaker.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Pure distance sort, ignoring text relevance strength: simple and predictable, but a barely-matching business 200 meters away can outrank a perfect match 600 meters away, which frequently feels wrong to users typing a specific query
- Pure text relevance sort, distance as a secondary filter only: prioritizes the best textual matches regardless of how much closer a slightly-less-relevant option might be, which can feel wrong for a fundamentally location-driven search like 'coffee near me'
- Weighted blend of relevance, distance decay, and rating: matches user expectations much better in practice, but introduces real tuning work, the weights are a product decision as much as an engineering one, and need to be validated against actual search behavior, not just picked once and left alone

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A dense downtown area during peak search hours can concentrate a disproportionate share of both search traffic and candidate density into a small number of spatial index cells; those cells need to be able to split or replicate independently of quieter regions rather than sharing a fixed geographic partitioning scheme.
- The combined geo-text index needs to be sharded, commonly by geography, so a search only has to fan out to the shard(s) covering its radius rather than every shard globally; a radius that straddles a shard boundary needs a small query fan-out to the neighboring shard too.
- Index rebuild/update latency (the gap between a business editing its listing and that edit becoming searchable) can grow under high update volume if updates go through the same pipeline as bulk reindexing; a live incremental-update path needs to stay separate from any periodic full reindex job.
- Autocomplete or 'search as you type' on top of this system adds a much higher effective query rate than full searches, since it fires on every keystroke; that path typically needs its own lighter-weight, prefix-optimized index rather than reusing the full relevance-plus-distance query for every partial keystroke.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing only the spatial index== and treating text relevance as an afterthought bolted on with a simple substring match, instead of a real inverted index with proper tokenization and scoring.
- ⚠️ ==Running the full text relevance ranking over every business== in a large search radius before applying any spatial narrowing, which is fine in a sparse suburb and catastrophically slow in a dense city center.
- ⚠️ Choosing a complex spatial structure like an R-tree by default without checking whether the data actually needs it (business locations here are static points, not polygons), adding implementation complexity with no real payoff.
- ⚠️ Ranking purely by distance or purely by text relevance instead of a blended score, producing results that technically match the query logic but feel wrong to an actual user.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why not just run the text search first globally, then filter the results by distance?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a broad or common text query (like a popular category or chain name) can match tens of thousands of businesses globally before distance is ever considered, and the relevance engine wastes work ranking businesses that will just get thrown away by the distance filter afterward, most of which aren't even in the user's city. Filtering by distance first bounds the candidate set to a manageable size before the more expensive text ranking work runs, which is why distance-first is the generally safer default ordering.

**Q: The business listings table changes rarely, why not just query it directly for search instead of maintaining a separate index?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a plain relational or document store isn't built to efficiently answer 'nearby AND text-relevant' as a single combined query, it would need either a full scan with a distance calculation per row, or two separate queries stitched together in application code, neither of which scales to tens of millions of listings and hundreds of queries per second. A purpose-built combined spatial-and-text index (or a search engine like Elasticsearch that supports both natively) can answer that combined query efficiently in one pass, which is worth the added complexity of keeping it asynchronously in sync with the source-of-truth table.

**Q: How would ranking need to change if the product added paid/sponsored listings that should appear near the top regardless of distance or relevance?**

> **Model Answer:** Sponsored placement would need to be treated as its own explicit signal in the scoring blend, not just folded into rating or relevance, and typically it's applied as a separate boost or a small number of guaranteed top slots layered on top of the organic ranked list, rather than mixed indistinguishably into the same weighted score. This keeps organic ranking honest and auditable while still letting the business logic control where sponsored results appear.

#### Q: How static are business locations and profiles, do they change roughly daily (new photos, hours) or almost never (address, category)?
*Why it matters:* This is a read-heavy system regardless, but the update cadence determines whether the combined spatial-plus-text index can be rebuilt in large batches on a comfortable schedule, or needs a more real-time incremental update path. Low write volume means the design can lean toward index structures that are cheap to query but relatively expensive to update, since updates are rare.

#### Q: Does ranking need to account for more than distance and text relevance, like star rating, review count, or sponsored placement?
*Why it matters:* Pure distance-plus-relevance ranking is a two-factor scoring function. Adding rating, popularity, or paid placement turns ranking into a genuinely multi-factor scoring problem that changes how aggressively the system can pre-filter candidates before ranking, since a business slightly farther away but much higher-rated might need to outrank a closer, mediocre one.

#### Q: What's the typical search radius and business density, a dense city block or a 20-mile suburban radius?
*Why it matters:* Dense urban search radii return huge raw candidate counts (thousands of businesses within a mile) that need heavy pre-filtering before text ranking is affordable, while sparse suburban searches might return so few candidates that the spatial filter barely matters and text relevance dominates. The typical case shapes how much the system leans on the spatial index to narrow things down early.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can search for businesses by free-text query (name, category, or description keywords) within a specified radius of a given location.
- Search results are ranked by a combination of text relevance and distance from the search location.
- A user can view a business's full profile: name, address, category, hours, rating, and photos.
- Business owners (or an internal pipeline) can create and update business listings, including their location and category.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Search must return results in well under a second, since this is an interactive, type-and-browse search experience.**
- **The system is overwhelmingly read-heavy: searches vastly outnumber business profile updates, and the design should be optimized accordingly.**
- **Search should remain fast and relevant in both dense urban areas (thousands of candidates within a mile) and sparse areas (a handful of candidates within twenty miles).**
- **Newly added or updated business listings should become searchable within a reasonably short time (minutes, not necessarily seconds), since this isn't a live-inventory system.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50 million business listings globally
- 20 million searches per day, heavily concentrated during lunch and dinner hours
- Business listings change relatively rarely, on average once every few weeks per listing
- A typical urban search radius (1-2 miles) in a dense city can match 2,000-5,000 raw candidate businesses before any text filtering

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Search QPS:** 20,000,000 / 86,400 sec ≈ 230 searches/sec average, several times higher at lunch/dinner peaks
- **Listing update rate:** 50,000,000 listings / (21 days average update interval * 86,400 sec) ≈ 27 updates/sec average, roughly 8-9x lower than search volume
- **Raw spatial candidates before text ranking, dense urban query:** 2,000-5,000 candidates in a 1-2 mile radius; ranking full text relevance across all of them per query, times 230 queries/sec, is the cost the design has to control
- **Read-to-write ratio:** 230 searches/sec vs 27 updates/sec ≈ 8.5:1, confirming this is a read-optimized system where the index can favor fast queries over fast updates

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving fact is the combination of a heavily read-skewed workload (roughly 8.5 reads to 1 write) with a raw candidate count in the thousands for a single dense urban query, which means the system can afford an index structure that's expensive to update but must aggressively narrow the spatial candidate set before running expensive text relevance ranking, rather than text-ranking every business in the radius.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Business profile writes go to a durable primary store and are never
queried directly for search. Every write also enqueues an async indexing
job that updates a separate, purpose-built combined spatial-and-text
index (commonly something like Elasticsearch with a geo_point field, or a
geohash-partitioned structure paired with a per-cell inverted index). A
search request first uses the spatial component of that index to narrow
the full business population down to a bounded, nearby candidate set
(using the search location and radius), and only then runs text
relevance scoring against that already-narrowed candidate set, blending
the resulting relevance score with distance (and rating, if in scope)
into a final ranking. This ordering, spatial filter first, text ranking
second, on a combined index that supports both natively, is what keeps
queries fast even in dense urban areas with thousands of raw candidates
in range.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Search read path over a combined spatial and text index

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    searchsvc["Search Service"]:::server
    geotext["Combined Geo+Text Index"]:::server
    bizdb[("Businesses DB")]:::db
    indexq>"Index Update Queue"]:::queue
    indexer["Async Indexer"]:::server
    cache["Result Cache"]:::cache
    client -->|"search query"| lb
    lb --> searchsvc
    searchsvc -->|"check cache"| cache
    searchsvc -->|"spatial filter, then rank"| geotext
    bizdb -.->|"on write"| indexq
    indexq -.-> indexer
    indexer -.->|"update index"| geotext
```

#### Filter-first ordering: distance-first vs text-first

| Distance-first, then text rank | Text-first, then distance filter |
| :--- | :--- |
| Bounds candidate set immediately regardless of query breadth | Works well for narrow, specific text queries |
| Safer default for dense urban areas with many candidates | Broad/common queries return a huge global set before filtering |
| Still needs a candidate cap in very dense radii | Wastes relevance-ranking work on far-away results |

#### Non-linear distance decay in the ranking score

#### One search query, spatial filter to final rank

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  q["Query: text + lat/lng + radius"] --> spatial["Spatial filter via geohash cells"]
  spatial --> cap{"Candidate set too large?"}
  cap -->|"yes, dense area"| shrink["Tighten effective radius"]
  shrink --> textrank["Text relevance scoring"]
  cap -->|"no"| textrank
  textrank --> blend["Blend relevance + distance decay + rating"]
  blend --> ranked["Ranked results returned"]
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/search` | Query params: q (text), lat, lng, radius_km. Returns ranked businesses matching both the text query and the spatial radius. |
| `GET` | `/api/businesses/{businessId}` | Returns the full profile for a single business: name, address, category, hours, rating, photos. |
| `POST` | `/api/businesses` | Body: { name, category, address, lat, lng, ... }. Creates or updates a business listing; feeds the async indexing pipeline. |
| `GET` | `/api/businesses/{businessId}/reviews` | Returns paginated reviews for a business, used to compute and display its aggregate rating. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `businesses`
- `business_id`
- `name, category, description`
- `address, lat, lng`
- `avg_rating, review_count`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* The durable source of truth for a business profile, in a regular relational or document store, not queried directly for search since it isn't optimized for combined spatial-plus-text lookups.

### Entity: `geo_text_index (combined spatial + inverted index, e.g. Elasticsearch with geo_point field, or a geohash-partitioned text index)`
- `business_id`
- `geohash (or geo_point) (for spatial pre-filtering)`
- `indexed_terms (tokenized name/category/description, for text relevance)`
- `avg_rating, review_count (denormalized, for ranking without a join)`
*Notes:* The actual structure search queries hit. Rebuilt/updated asynchronously from the businesses table, deliberately denormalizing rating so ranking never needs a join at query time.

### Entity: `index_update_queue`
- `business_id`
- `change_type (create, update, delete)`
- `enqueued_at`
*Notes:* Decouples business profile writes from the (comparatively slower) work of re-indexing into the combined geo-text structure, so a profile edit doesn't block on index rebuild.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Geohash vs quadtree vs R-tree for the spatial component
Geohashing encodes lat/lng into a string where geographically close points usually (not always, due to boundary effects) share a prefix, letting 'nearby' become a cheap range query over sorted keys or a lookup across a small set of neighboring cells. A quadtree recursively subdivides space into cells sized to keep point density roughly even, so it adapts automatically to dense downtown blocks versus sparse rural areas, but a moving or newly inserted point can require rebalancing tree nodes. An R-tree groups nearby objects into bounding rectangles in a tree structure, which handles non-point data (like a business's delivery area polygon) more naturally than either geohash or quadtree, at the cost of more complex insert/query logic.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Geohash: simple, cheap range queries, easy to shard and store in an ordinary sorted structure, but fixed-size cells mean uneven density (packed downtown cells vs empty rural ones) and awkward boundary cases where two nearby points land in different-prefix cells
- Quadtree: adapts cell size to actual point density, handling urban/rural skew well, but is a genuine tree structure that's harder to shard across machines and more expensive to update on every insert or move
- R-tree: the natural choice if the data isn't just points (delivery zones, service areas), and query performance is strong, but it's the most complex of the three to implement and tune correctly, overkill for a system where every business is just a single point on a map, which is the actual shape of this problem
- For this problem, since business locations are static points with rare updates, geohash-based indexing (or a managed geospatial index like Elasticsearch's geo_point, which handles this internally) is the pragmatic choice: the simplicity and cheap queries matter more here than the update-time cost quadtrees optimize for, and there's no polygon data to justify an R-tree

### Combining spatial filtering and text relevance in one query, instead of running them as two separate steps
The naive approach picks one filter to run first and the other second: filter to businesses within radius, then linearly scan that set for text matches (fine for a small radius, catastrophic for a large one with thousands of candidates), or filter by text match first, then check distance on the results (misses genuinely nearby businesses that just don't rank in the raw global text results). Both orderings throw away information the other index has. A combined index, spatial data and inverted text index living together over the same document set, lets a single query apply both filters natively: narrow by geohash cell membership first (cheap, bounded), then run relevance scoring only against that already-small candidate set, and finally blend the two into a single ranked list.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Text-first, then filter by distance: works well when the text query is narrow (few matches globally), but a broad or common query (like a popular category) returns a huge global candidate set before distance is even considered, most of which gets thrown away, wasting the relevance engine's work
- Distance-first, then filter/rank by text: bounds the candidate set immediately regardless of query breadth, which is why it's the generally safer default, but a radius that's too large in a dense area can still hand thousands of candidates to the text ranker, so it still needs a hard candidate cap or a tighter effective radius under high density
- A genuinely combined spatial-plus-text index (e.g. Elasticsearch's geo_point combined with its native text scoring in one query): avoids materializing an intermediate candidate list twice and lets the engine optimize the combined filter-and-rank as one operation, at the cost of depending on a more specialized piece of infrastructure than a plain spatial store or a plain text index alone

### Ranking: blending distance, text relevance, and rating into one score
Once a candidate set is narrowed, each candidate needs a single final rank, not three separate ones. A common approach normalizes each signal to a comparable scale (e.g. 0-1) and combines them with tunable weights: relevance score from the text engine, a distance decay function (closer businesses score higher, but not linearly, since the difference between 0.2 and 0.5 miles matters more to a walking user than the difference between 5 and 5.3 miles), and rating/popularity as a smaller boost or tiebreaker.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Pure distance sort, ignoring text relevance strength: simple and predictable, but a barely-matching business 200 meters away can outrank a perfect match 600 meters away, which frequently feels wrong to users typing a specific query
- Pure text relevance sort, distance as a secondary filter only: prioritizes the best textual matches regardless of how much closer a slightly-less-relevant option might be, which can feel wrong for a fundamentally location-driven search like 'coffee near me'
- Weighted blend of relevance, distance decay, and rating: matches user expectations much better in practice, but introduces real tuning work, the weights are a product decision as much as an engineering one, and need to be validated against actual search behavior, not just picked once and left alone

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A dense downtown area during peak search hours can concentrate a disproportionate share of both search traffic and candidate density into a small number of spatial index cells; those cells need to be able to split or replicate independently of quieter regions rather than sharing a fixed geographic partitioning scheme.
- The combined geo-text index needs to be sharded, commonly by geography, so a search only has to fan out to the shard(s) covering its radius rather than every shard globally; a radius that straddles a shard boundary needs a small query fan-out to the neighboring shard too.
- Index rebuild/update latency (the gap between a business editing its listing and that edit becoming searchable) can grow under high update volume if updates go through the same pipeline as bulk reindexing; a live incremental-update path needs to stay separate from any periodic full reindex job.
- Autocomplete or 'search as you type' on top of this system adds a much higher effective query rate than full searches, since it fires on every keystroke; that path typically needs its own lighter-weight, prefix-optimized index rather than reusing the full relevance-plus-distance query for every partial keystroke.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing only the spatial index== and treating text relevance as an afterthought bolted on with a simple substring match, instead of a real inverted index with proper tokenization and scoring.
- ⚠️ ==Running the full text relevance ranking over every business== in a large search radius before applying any spatial narrowing, which is fine in a sparse suburb and catastrophically slow in a dense city center.
- ⚠️ Choosing a complex spatial structure like an R-tree by default without checking whether the data actually needs it (business locations here are static points, not polygons), adding implementation complexity with no real payoff.
- ⚠️ Ranking purely by distance or purely by text relevance instead of a blended score, producing results that technically match the query logic but feel wrong to an actual user.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why not just run the text search first globally, then filter the results by distance?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a broad or common text query (like a popular category or chain name) can match tens of thousands of businesses globally before distance is ever considered, and the relevance engine wastes work ranking businesses that will just get thrown away by the distance filter afterward, most of which aren't even in the user's city. Filtering by distance first bounds the candidate set to a manageable size before the more expensive text ranking work runs, which is why distance-first is the generally safer default ordering.

**Q: The business listings table changes rarely, why not just query it directly for search instead of maintaining a separate index?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a plain relational or document store isn't built to efficiently answer 'nearby AND text-relevant' as a single combined query, it would need either a full scan with a distance calculation per row, or two separate queries stitched together in application code, neither of which scales to tens of millions of listings and hundreds of queries per second. A purpose-built combined spatial-and-text index (or a search engine like Elasticsearch that supports both natively) can answer that combined query efficiently in one pass, which is worth the added complexity of keeping it asynchronously in sync with the source-of-truth table.

**Q: How would ranking need to change if the product added paid/sponsored listings that should appear near the top regardless of distance or relevance?**

> **Model Answer:** Sponsored placement would need to be treated as its own explicit signal in the scoring blend, not just folded into rating or relevance, and typically it's applied as a separate boost or a small number of guaranteed top slots layered on top of the organic ranked list, rather than mixed indistinguishably into the same weighted score. This keeps organic ranking honest and auditable while still letting the business logic control where sponsored results appear.

callout.title: Core Architectural Principle
callout.text: The hard part isn't choosing a single clever geospatial data structure, it's that 'nearby' and 'matches ramen' are answered by two completely different kinds of index, a **spatial structure** and a **text/inverted index**, and naively running one filter then the other throws away most of the other index's power, so the real design question is how to combine them into one fast query.

lesson.content:
# Design a Delivery Route Optimization System

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `FedEx • Amazon logistics` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> This is a computational problem wearing a distributed systems costume: the optimal ordering of N stops is **combinatorially explosive** to compute exactly, so the real design decision is which **approximate heuristic** to run, how much time to give it, and how to re-run it fast enough to react to a route that's already in progress.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a system that takes a driver's set of assigned delivery stops for
the day and produces an efficient order to visit them in, minimizing total
drive time. New orders can be added mid-route, so the system must be able
to re-optimize a route the driver is already partway through. Design the
system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many stops does a typical route have, and how many drivers are we optimizing for simultaneously?
*Why it matters:* The traveling-salesman problem is **NP-hard**: exact solutions are feasible for maybe 10-15 stops but become ==computationally impossible== past that. A 30-stop delivery route and a 300-driver fleet running that route concurrently decide whether we need exact solving, heuristics, or a managed solver service.

#### Q: Do new orders need to be incorporated into a route the driver has already started, or only planned before the driver leaves the depot?
*Why it matters:* Static, pre-departure planning is a **batch problem** solvable in minutes with a slower, higher-quality algorithm. Mid-route re-optimization is a **real-time problem** that needs a fast heuristic that returns in well under a second, since the driver is waiting on their next turn-by-turn instruction.

#### Q: Are there hard constraints beyond distance, like delivery time windows, vehicle capacity, or driver shift-end times?
*Why it matters:* Pure shortest-path TSP is already hard; adding time windows and capacity turns this into a Vehicle Routing Problem with constraints, which needs a fundamentally different class of solver (constraint-aware heuristics, not plain nearest-neighbor).

#### Q: How accurate does drive-time estimation between two stops need to be: straight-line distance, or real road network and live traffic?
*Why it matters:* Straight-line distance is nearly free to compute but can be badly wrong in a city with rivers, highways, and one-way streets. Real routing-graph distances with live traffic are far more accurate but require calling (or hosting) a full routing engine for every pair of stops being considered, which is the dominant cost in the whole system.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Given a driver's list of assigned delivery stops, compute an ordered route minimizing total drive time.
- Support hard constraints: delivery time windows and vehicle capacity limits.
- Re-optimize the remaining, not-yet-visited portion of an in-progress route when a new stop is added.
- Provide turn-by-turn navigation for the currently active leg of the route.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Initial route planning for a full day's stops should complete in at most a few seconds per driver, even at 50+ stops.**
- **Mid-route re-optimization must return in under a second, since the driver is stopped or slowing down waiting for the next instruction.**
- **The system must scale to optimizing thousands of drivers' routes concurrently, especially during a morning dispatch rush.**
- **A returned route must always be valid (respects time windows and capacity) even if it isn't the mathematically optimal one; a slightly-suboptimal-but-correct route beats an optimal-but-late computation.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50,000 active drivers, each with an average of 40 stops per day
- Each driver's route is recomputed once at dispatch and re-optimized roughly 3 times during the day as new orders arrive or stops are completed
- Exact TSP solving is O(n!) or O(n^2 * 2^n) with dynamic programming; both are infeasible past roughly 15-20 stops
- A heuristic like nearest-neighbor plus 2-opt improvement runs in roughly O(n^2) per pass

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Exact solve cost at 40 stops:** Held-Karp dynamic programming is O(n^2 * 2^n): 40^2 * 2^40 ≈ 1,600 * 1.1 trillion ≈ 1.76 quadrillion operations, wildly infeasible for a single route, let alone 50,000 of them
- **Heuristic solve cost at 40 stops:** Nearest-neighbor construction is O(n^2) = 1,600 operations; a 2-opt improvement pass adds roughly O(n^2) per iteration, so even 50 iterations is 80,000 operations, comfortably sub-millisecond per route
- **Daily route computations across the fleet:** 50,000 drivers * 4 computations/day (1 initial + 3 re-optimizations) = 200,000 route computations/day ≈ 2.3/sec average, but concentrated in a morning dispatch spike of maybe 50x that
- **Dispatch-rush peak load:** 50,000 initial routes computed within a 10-minute dispatch window ≈ 83 routes/sec, each needing roughly 40x40 distance-matrix lookups (1,600 pairs), so a distance/ETA service must sustain over 100,000 pairwise lookups/sec at peak

*Capacity Takeaway:* The single fact driving this architecture is that **exact optimal solving** is computationally impossible at real fleet scale (a quadrillion operations for one 40-stop route), which forces every design decision toward fast **approximate heuristics**, and the resulting bottleneck moves from 'solving the route' to ==fetching enough accurate pairwise drive-time estimates fast enough to feed the solver==.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A dispatch service takes a driver's stop list and calls a routing/ETA
engine to build a pairwise drive-time matrix between all stops (cached
where possible by geohash bucket). That matrix feeds a route optimizer
service, which runs a fast construction heuristic (nearest-neighbor) plus
a local-search improvement pass (2-opt or Or-opt) under a strict time
budget, and returns an ordered route. The route is stored, and the driver's
app pulls turn-by-turn legs from it one at a time. When a new stop arrives
mid-route, a re-optimize call is made scoped only to the remaining
not-yet-visited stops plus the driver's current position, keeping the
recomputation small and fast rather than re-solving the whole day.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Route planning and mid-route re-optimization

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    driverapp["Driver App"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    dispatch["Dispatch API"]:::server
    distcache["Distance Cache"]:::cache
    routing["Routing/ETA Engine"]:::server
    optqueue>"Optimize Queue"]:::queue
    optworker["Route Optimizer Workers"]:::server
    routedb[("Routes Store")]:::db
    driverapp --> lb
    lb --> dispatch
    dispatch -->|"pairwise drive times"| distcache
    distcache -.->|"miss -> fetch"| routing
    dispatch -.->|"enqueue solve job"| optqueue
    optqueue -.-> optworker
    optworker -->|"read matrix"| distcache
    optworker -->|"write ordered route"| routedb
    dispatch -->|"read/update route"| routedb
```

#### A new order arrives mid-route

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. New stop assigned to driver's route (order created)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Re-optimize call: current position + remaining stops + new stop (completed stops excluded)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Distance cache lookup for new pairwise legs (cache miss triggers routing engine call)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Heuristic solver re-orders remaining stops (nearest-neighbor + 2-opt, sub-second budget)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Updated route pushed to driver app (next-leg navigation refreshes)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Exact solving vs heuristic: compute cost by stop count

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/routes/plan` | Body: { driver_id, stops: [{ address, lat, lng, time_window?, package_size? }] }. Computes and returns an ordered route for a driver's full stop list. |
| `POST` | `/api/routes/{routeId}/reoptimize` | Body: { new_stop, current_position }. Re-optimizes only the remaining, not-yet-visited stops given the driver's current location and a newly added stop. |
| `GET` | `/api/routes/{routeId}/next-leg` | Returns turn-by-turn navigation instructions for the current active leg of the route. |
| `POST` | `/api/routes/{routeId}/stops/{stopId}/complete` | Marks a stop as delivered, removing it from the remaining route and advancing to the next leg. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `routes`
- `route_id`
- `driver_id (indexed)`
- `status (planned, in_progress, completed)`
- `ordered_stop_ids (an array reflecting current planned visit order)`
- `created_at, last_reoptimized_at`
*Notes:* The ordered_stop_ids array is mutable and gets rewritten on every re-optimization; only the not-yet-visited suffix is ever recomputed, completed stops stay fixed.

### Entity: `stops`
- `stop_id`
- `route_id (indexed)`
- `lat, lng`
- `time_window_start, time_window_end (nullable)`
- `package_size`
- `status (pending, completed, skipped)`
*Notes:* A stop belongs to exactly one route at a time; completed stops are never reordered by future re-optimization passes.

### Entity: `distance_cache`
- `origin_geohash`
- `dest_geohash`
- `drive_time_seconds`
- `computed_at (for staleness / traffic refresh)`
*Notes:* Caches pairwise drive-time estimates between geohash-bucketed locations so the solver doesn't call the routing engine fresh for every pair on every optimization pass.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Exact optimal solving vs heuristic approximation: the central trade-off
The Traveling Salesman Problem is **NP-hard**. Held-Karp dynamic programming finds the exact optimal tour in **O(n^2 * 2^n)** time, which is only practical up to roughly 15-20 stops before it becomes ==computationally infeasible==, as the capacity math shows. Real delivery routes regularly have 30-100+ stops. Heuristics like **nearest-neighbor construction** followed by **2-opt** or Or-opt local search find a tour that's typically within 5-10% of optimal, in polynomial time, fast enough to run repeatedly throughout the day.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Exact (Held-Karp / branch-and-bound): guarantees the mathematically optimal route, but the compute cost explodes exponentially past roughly 15-20 stops, unusable for real route sizes
- Construction heuristic alone (nearest-neighbor): very fast, O(n^2), but can produce noticeably suboptimal tours, especially prone to leaving one far-away stop stranded at the end
- Construction plus local search (nearest-neighbor + 2-opt): the practical middle ground used in production, still fast enough for real-time re-optimization, and closes most of the gap to optimal by swapping pairs of edges that cross or backtrack
- Metaheuristics (simulated annealing, genetic algorithms): can get closer to optimal than 2-opt for very large stop counts, but need more compute time and tuning, better suited to overnight batch planning than real-time re-optimization

### Full re-optimization vs incremental re-optimization when a new stop arrives mid-route
When a new order needs to be inserted into a route the driver is already executing, the system could throw away the whole plan and re-solve from scratch including already-completed stops, or it could keep completed stops fixed and only re-optimize the ordering of the **remaining, not-yet-visited stops** plus the new one.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Full re-optimization: theoretically could find a better global route, but recomputing over already-completed stops is wasted work and any change to their order is meaningless anyway, since the driver already visited them
- Incremental re-optimization (fix completed stops, re-solve only the remainder): much smaller problem size means faster response, well suited to the sub-second budget needed while a driver is waiting, at the small cost of being locked into earlier ordering decisions that a full re-solve might have avoided
- Cheapest-insertion heuristic (insert the new stop at whichever position in the remaining route adds the least extra drive time, without a full re-solve): fastest option of all, good enough when only one stop changes, but degrades in quality if many stops are added over the course of a day without ever doing a fuller re-solve

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The routing/ETA engine (computing drive time between two points) is the true bottleneck: an n-stop route needs roughly n^2 pairwise lookups, so this must be aggressively cached by geohash-bucketed origin/destination pairs and refreshed periodically rather than called fresh on every optimization pass.
- The morning dispatch rush concentrates tens of thousands of route computations into a narrow time window; the optimizer service needs to be horizontally scaled as stateless workers pulling jobs off a queue, not a single synchronous compute path per request.
- Time-window and capacity constraints make the search space harder to satisfy, not just optimize; a heuristic that ignores constraints and only fixes them up afterward can produce an invalid route, so constraints should be built into the construction step (e.g. only inserting a stop where its time window is still satisfiable), not bolted on after.
- Live traffic conditions change the drive-time matrix throughout the day; stale cached distances silently degrade route quality, so the distance cache needs a reasonable TTL and periodic refresh, especially during peak traffic hours.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Trying to find the mathematically optimal route with an exact algorithm, not realizing it becomes ==computationally impossible== well before real-world stop counts.
- ⚠️ Re-solving the entire route including already-visited stops on every mid-route update, wasting compute on stops that can no longer be reordered.
- ⚠️ Treating drive-time estimation as free or instantaneous, when in practice it's the dominant cost, especially at n^2 pairwise lookups per route.
- ⚠️ Ignoring time-window and capacity constraints until after generating a distance-optimal route, then discovering the route is ==infeasible== and needing an expensive repair pass.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you just find the actual optimal route for a 50-stop delivery run?**

> **Model Answer:** Because exact TSP solving with dynamic programming is **O(n^2 * 2^n)**; at 50 stops that's on the order of 2^50 (over a quadrillion) operations, ==computationally impossible== to run per route, let alone for tens of thousands of drivers. This forces the use of polynomial-time heuristics like nearest-neighbor plus 2-opt, which trade a small amount of optimality for a solve that completes in milliseconds.

**Q: How would you handle a driver's route needing to incorporate 3 new stops added at different times throughout the day, without the route quality degrading badly by the end of the day?**

> **Model Answer:** Each individual insertion can use a fast cheapest-insertion or incremental re-optimization pass for immediate responsiveness, but the system should also periodically run a fuller local-search re-optimization (2-opt over the full remaining route, not just around the newly inserted stop) on a slightly longer cadence, say every 30-60 minutes, to correct for the accumulated suboptimality of many small incremental insertions without blocking the driver's real-time navigation.

pages.content:
# Design a Delivery Route Optimization System

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `FedEx • Amazon logistics` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> This is a computational problem wearing a distributed systems costume: the optimal ordering of N stops is **combinatorially explosive** to compute exactly, so the real design decision is which **approximate heuristic** to run, how much time to give it, and how to re-run it fast enough to react to a route that's already in progress.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a system that takes a driver's set of assigned delivery stops for
the day and produces an efficient order to visit them in, minimizing total
drive time. New orders can be added mid-route, so the system must be able
to re-optimize a route the driver is already partway through. Design the
system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many stops does a typical route have, and how many drivers are we optimizing for simultaneously?
*Why it matters:* The traveling-salesman problem is **NP-hard**: exact solutions are feasible for maybe 10-15 stops but become ==computationally impossible== past that. A 30-stop delivery route and a 300-driver fleet running that route concurrently decide whether we need exact solving, heuristics, or a managed solver service.

#### Q: Do new orders need to be incorporated into a route the driver has already started, or only planned before the driver leaves the depot?
*Why it matters:* Static, pre-departure planning is a **batch problem** solvable in minutes with a slower, higher-quality algorithm. Mid-route re-optimization is a **real-time problem** that needs a fast heuristic that returns in well under a second, since the driver is waiting on their next turn-by-turn instruction.

#### Q: Are there hard constraints beyond distance, like delivery time windows, vehicle capacity, or driver shift-end times?
*Why it matters:* Pure shortest-path TSP is already hard; adding time windows and capacity turns this into a Vehicle Routing Problem with constraints, which needs a fundamentally different class of solver (constraint-aware heuristics, not plain nearest-neighbor).

#### Q: How accurate does drive-time estimation between two stops need to be: straight-line distance, or real road network and live traffic?
*Why it matters:* Straight-line distance is nearly free to compute but can be badly wrong in a city with rivers, highways, and one-way streets. Real routing-graph distances with live traffic are far more accurate but require calling (or hosting) a full routing engine for every pair of stops being considered, which is the dominant cost in the whole system.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Given a driver's list of assigned delivery stops, compute an ordered route minimizing total drive time.
- Support hard constraints: delivery time windows and vehicle capacity limits.
- Re-optimize the remaining, not-yet-visited portion of an in-progress route when a new stop is added.
- Provide turn-by-turn navigation for the currently active leg of the route.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Initial route planning for a full day's stops should complete in at most a few seconds per driver, even at 50+ stops.**
- **Mid-route re-optimization must return in under a second, since the driver is stopped or slowing down waiting for the next instruction.**
- **The system must scale to optimizing thousands of drivers' routes concurrently, especially during a morning dispatch rush.**
- **A returned route must always be valid (respects time windows and capacity) even if it isn't the mathematically optimal one; a slightly-suboptimal-but-correct route beats an optimal-but-late computation.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50,000 active drivers, each with an average of 40 stops per day
- Each driver's route is recomputed once at dispatch and re-optimized roughly 3 times during the day as new orders arrive or stops are completed
- Exact TSP solving is O(n!) or O(n^2 * 2^n) with dynamic programming; both are infeasible past roughly 15-20 stops
- A heuristic like nearest-neighbor plus 2-opt improvement runs in roughly O(n^2) per pass

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Exact solve cost at 40 stops:** Held-Karp dynamic programming is O(n^2 * 2^n): 40^2 * 2^40 ≈ 1,600 * 1.1 trillion ≈ 1.76 quadrillion operations, wildly infeasible for a single route, let alone 50,000 of them
- **Heuristic solve cost at 40 stops:** Nearest-neighbor construction is O(n^2) = 1,600 operations; a 2-opt improvement pass adds roughly O(n^2) per iteration, so even 50 iterations is 80,000 operations, comfortably sub-millisecond per route
- **Daily route computations across the fleet:** 50,000 drivers * 4 computations/day (1 initial + 3 re-optimizations) = 200,000 route computations/day ≈ 2.3/sec average, but concentrated in a morning dispatch spike of maybe 50x that
- **Dispatch-rush peak load:** 50,000 initial routes computed within a 10-minute dispatch window ≈ 83 routes/sec, each needing roughly 40x40 distance-matrix lookups (1,600 pairs), so a distance/ETA service must sustain over 100,000 pairwise lookups/sec at peak

*Capacity Takeaway:* The single fact driving this architecture is that **exact optimal solving** is computationally impossible at real fleet scale (a quadrillion operations for one 40-stop route), which forces every design decision toward fast **approximate heuristics**, and the resulting bottleneck moves from 'solving the route' to ==fetching enough accurate pairwise drive-time estimates fast enough to feed the solver==.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A dispatch service takes a driver's stop list and calls a routing/ETA
engine to build a pairwise drive-time matrix between all stops (cached
where possible by geohash bucket). That matrix feeds a route optimizer
service, which runs a fast construction heuristic (nearest-neighbor) plus
a local-search improvement pass (2-opt or Or-opt) under a strict time
budget, and returns an ordered route. The route is stored, and the driver's
app pulls turn-by-turn legs from it one at a time. When a new stop arrives
mid-route, a re-optimize call is made scoped only to the remaining
not-yet-visited stops plus the driver's current position, keeping the
recomputation small and fast rather than re-solving the whole day.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Route planning and mid-route re-optimization

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    driverapp["Driver App"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    dispatch["Dispatch API"]:::server
    distcache["Distance Cache"]:::cache
    routing["Routing/ETA Engine"]:::server
    optqueue>"Optimize Queue"]:::queue
    optworker["Route Optimizer Workers"]:::server
    routedb[("Routes Store")]:::db
    driverapp --> lb
    lb --> dispatch
    dispatch -->|"pairwise drive times"| distcache
    distcache -.->|"miss -> fetch"| routing
    dispatch -.->|"enqueue solve job"| optqueue
    optqueue -.-> optworker
    optworker -->|"read matrix"| distcache
    optworker -->|"write ordered route"| routedb
    dispatch -->|"read/update route"| routedb
```

#### A new order arrives mid-route

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. New stop assigned to driver's route (order created)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Re-optimize call: current position + remaining stops + new stop (completed stops excluded)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Distance cache lookup for new pairwise legs (cache miss triggers routing engine call)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Heuristic solver re-orders remaining stops (nearest-neighbor + 2-opt, sub-second budget)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Updated route pushed to driver app (next-leg navigation refreshes)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Exact solving vs heuristic: compute cost by stop count

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/routes/plan` | Body: { driver_id, stops: [{ address, lat, lng, time_window?, package_size? }] }. Computes and returns an ordered route for a driver's full stop list. |
| `POST` | `/api/routes/{routeId}/reoptimize` | Body: { new_stop, current_position }. Re-optimizes only the remaining, not-yet-visited stops given the driver's current location and a newly added stop. |
| `GET` | `/api/routes/{routeId}/next-leg` | Returns turn-by-turn navigation instructions for the current active leg of the route. |
| `POST` | `/api/routes/{routeId}/stops/{stopId}/complete` | Marks a stop as delivered, removing it from the remaining route and advancing to the next leg. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `routes`
- `route_id`
- `driver_id (indexed)`
- `status (planned, in_progress, completed)`
- `ordered_stop_ids (an array reflecting current planned visit order)`
- `created_at, last_reoptimized_at`
*Notes:* The ordered_stop_ids array is mutable and gets rewritten on every re-optimization; only the not-yet-visited suffix is ever recomputed, completed stops stay fixed.

### Entity: `stops`
- `stop_id`
- `route_id (indexed)`
- `lat, lng`
- `time_window_start, time_window_end (nullable)`
- `package_size`
- `status (pending, completed, skipped)`
*Notes:* A stop belongs to exactly one route at a time; completed stops are never reordered by future re-optimization passes.

### Entity: `distance_cache`
- `origin_geohash`
- `dest_geohash`
- `drive_time_seconds`
- `computed_at (for staleness / traffic refresh)`
*Notes:* Caches pairwise drive-time estimates between geohash-bucketed locations so the solver doesn't call the routing engine fresh for every pair on every optimization pass.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Exact optimal solving vs heuristic approximation: the central trade-off
The Traveling Salesman Problem is **NP-hard**. Held-Karp dynamic programming finds the exact optimal tour in **O(n^2 * 2^n)** time, which is only practical up to roughly 15-20 stops before it becomes ==computationally infeasible==, as the capacity math shows. Real delivery routes regularly have 30-100+ stops. Heuristics like **nearest-neighbor construction** followed by **2-opt** or Or-opt local search find a tour that's typically within 5-10% of optimal, in polynomial time, fast enough to run repeatedly throughout the day.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Exact (Held-Karp / branch-and-bound): guarantees the mathematically optimal route, but the compute cost explodes exponentially past roughly 15-20 stops, unusable for real route sizes
- Construction heuristic alone (nearest-neighbor): very fast, O(n^2), but can produce noticeably suboptimal tours, especially prone to leaving one far-away stop stranded at the end
- Construction plus local search (nearest-neighbor + 2-opt): the practical middle ground used in production, still fast enough for real-time re-optimization, and closes most of the gap to optimal by swapping pairs of edges that cross or backtrack
- Metaheuristics (simulated annealing, genetic algorithms): can get closer to optimal than 2-opt for very large stop counts, but need more compute time and tuning, better suited to overnight batch planning than real-time re-optimization

### Full re-optimization vs incremental re-optimization when a new stop arrives mid-route
When a new order needs to be inserted into a route the driver is already executing, the system could throw away the whole plan and re-solve from scratch including already-completed stops, or it could keep completed stops fixed and only re-optimize the ordering of the **remaining, not-yet-visited stops** plus the new one.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**

- Cheapest-insertion heuristic (insert the new stop at whichever position in the remaining route adds the least extra drive time, without a full re-solve): fastest option of all, good enough when only one stop changes, but degrades in quality if many stops are added over the course of a day without ever doing a fuller re-solve

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions

- Live traffic conditions change the drive-time matrix throughout the day; stale cached distances silently degrade route quality, so the distance cache needs a reasonable TTL and periodic refresh, especially during peak traffic hours.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Trying to find the mathematically optimal route with an exact algorithm, not realizing it becomes ==computationally impossible== well before real-world stop counts.
- ⚠️ Re-solving the entire route including already-visited stops on every mid-route update, wasting compute on stops that can no longer be reordered.
- ⚠️ Treating drive-time estimation as free or instantaneous, when in practice it's the dominant cost, especially at n^2 pairwise lookups per route.
- ⚠️ Ignoring time-window and capacity constraints until after generating a distance-optimal route, then discovering the route is ==infeasible== and needing an expensive repair pass.

This forces the use of polynomial-time heuristics like nearest-neighbor plus 2-opt, which trade a small amount of optimality for a solve that completes in milliseconds.
