# Design WhatsApp

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `WhatsApp / Meta` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The hard part of WhatsApp isn't sending a message, it's that every single user might be connected right now on a flaky mobile network or not connected at all, so the entire architecture is really a distributed system for tracking '**who is reachable this instant**' and queuing for everyone who isn't.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a messaging system like WhatsApp: users exchange text messages
one-on-one, messages are delivered even if the recipient is offline when
they're sent, and the sender can see whether a message was sent, delivered
to the device, and read. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is this one-on-one messaging only, or do we need group chats too?
*Why it matters:* Group chats turn a single delivery into a fan-out problem, similar in shape to timeline fan-out. Scoping to one-on-one first keeps the interview focused on connection management and delivery guarantees, which are the genuinely hard parts.

#### Q: Does the server need to be able to read message content, or is this end-to-end encrypted?
*Why it matters:* End-to-end encryption means the server can only ever store and forward opaque ciphertext blobs, it can never search, moderate, or generate previews of message content server-side. That constraint shapes the entire storage design, not just a security checkbox.

#### Q: What delivery guarantees do we need: sent, delivered to device, and read receipts, or just best-effort delivery?
*Why it matters:* Three distinct message states (sent, delivered, read) each require their own acknowledgment round trip and their own piece of state to track, which materially changes both the client protocol and the server's per-message bookkeeping.

#### Q: How long should messages be held for an offline recipient before we give up?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether the offline queue is a lightweight, bounded buffer or a durable long-term store, and it directly drives the storage capacity estimate.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can send a text message to another user.
- A message sent while the recipient is offline is queued and delivered once they reconnect.
- The sender can see message status: sent, delivered (reached the recipient's device), and read (opened by the recipient).
- A user can see their conversation history when they open a chat.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Message delivery must be near-real-time (sub-second) when both parties are online.**
- **The system must sustain hundreds of millions of concurrent open connections without falling over.**
- **No message should be silently lost: if the server accepted it, it must eventually be delivered or clearly reported as undeliverable.**
- **The system must tolerate a huge fraction of users being offline or on unreliable mobile networks at any given moment, without that degrading the experience for connected users.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 500 million daily active users, each with a persistent connection open while the app is in the foreground
- Average user sends 40 messages a day
- Peak concurrent connections are roughly 40% of DAU at once (evening peak across time zones)
- Each message (with metadata, before encryption overhead) is roughly 150 bytes

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Concurrent open connections at peak:** 500,000,000 * 0.4 = 200 million concurrent persistent connections to hold open at once
- **Connection gateway servers needed:** A single well-tuned server can hold roughly 500,000 to 1 million idle WebSocket connections; 200,000,000 / 500,000 = 400 gateway servers minimum, just to hold the sockets open
- **Messages sent per day and per second:** 500,000,000 * 40 = 20 billion messages/day ≈ 231,000 messages/sec average, several times that at peak
- **Daily storage for message history:** 20,000,000,000 * 150 bytes ≈ 3 TB/day of message data, ignoring media, which needs its own object storage path entirely

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that actually drives this architecture isn't message throughput, it's the **200 million simultaneously open connections**: that single fact forces a horizontally sharded fleet of stateful gateway servers plus a routing layer that tracks which gateway holds which user's socket, which is a fundamentally different problem than a stateless request/response API.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Every client holds one persistent connection to a gateway server chosen by
a connection-aware load balancer. On connect, the gateway registers the
user's id against its own server id in a shared connection registry. When
user A sends a message to user B, A's gateway writes the message to
durable storage, then looks up B in the connection registry: if B is
connected somewhere, the message is pushed directly to B's gateway and
forwarded down B's socket in real time; if B is offline, the message id is
placed on B's offline queue instead. When B later reconnects, their
gateway drains the offline queue and pushes everything that piled up.
Delivered and read receipts flow back the same way, as small status
updates routed through the same registry back to A.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Connection gateways, routing registry, and offline queue

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    clienta["Client A"]:::client
    clientb["Client B (offline)"]:::client
    gwa["Gateway (A's socket)"]:::server
    gwb["Gateway (B's socket)"]:::server
    registry["Connection Registry"]:::cache
    msgdb[("Messages Store")]:::db
    offlineq>"Offline Queue"]:::queue
    clienta -->|"persistent WS"| gwa
    clientb -->|"persistent WS (down)"| gwb
    gwa -->|"store message"| msgdb
    gwa -->|"lookup recipient"| registry
    registry -->|"B offline"| gwa
    gwa -.->|"enqueue for B"| offlineq
    gwb -.->|"drain on reconnect"| offlineq
```

#### A message from send to read receipt

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. A sends message (over open socket to A's gateway)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Server stores message (status: sent, ack returned to A)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Registry lookup for B (online, or offline)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Push to B, or enqueue (delivered live, or queued for later)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. B's client acks delivered (status flows back to A)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. B opens the chat (status: read, flows back to A)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### Message status transitions

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  write["Server stores message"] -->|"ack to A"| sent["sent"]
  sent -->|"pushed to B's device"| delivered["delivered"]
  delivered -->|"B opens chat"| read["read"]
  sent -->|"B offline"| queued["queued"]
  queued -->|"B reconnects"| delivered
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `WS` | `wss://gateway/connect` | Upgrades to a persistent WebSocket connection, authenticates the user, and registers this connection in the presence/routing layer. |
| `POST` | `/api/messages` | Body: { recipient_id, ciphertext, client_message_id }. Sent over the open socket (or as a fallback HTTP call); the server acks with sent status and a server-assigned message_id. |
| `POST` | `/api/messages/{messageId}/ack` | Body: { status: 'delivered' | 'read' }. Sent by the recipient's client to report a status transition back to the server, which relays it to the original sender. |
| `GET` | `/api/conversations/{userId}/history` | Returns paginated message history for the conversation with userId, newest first, for populating the chat screen on open. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `messages`
- `message_id (unique, time-sortable)`
- `sender_id`
- `recipient_id`
- `ciphertext (opaque blob, server cannot read it)`
- `status (sent | delivered | read)`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
*Notes:* Sharded by conversation (a stable function of the two user IDs) so a whole conversation's history lives together for fast range reads.

### Entity: `offline_queue`
- `recipient_id (key)`
- `message_id`
- `enqueued_at`
*Notes:* A bounded, per-user queue of message IDs awaiting delivery. Drained and cleared the moment that user's client reconnects and acks receipt.

### Entity: `connection_registry`
- `user_id (key)`
- `gateway_server_id`
- `connected_at`
*Notes:* The routing table: which gateway server currently holds a given user's live socket. Kept in a fast in-memory store since it's read on every message send and rewritten on every connect/disconnect.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you route a message to a specific user when they could be connected to any one of thousands of gateway servers?
A stateless load balancer picking a random backend, as in a typical HTTP API, doesn't work here, because the recipient's live socket is pinned to one specific machine. The system needs a shared connection registry (commonly backed by something like Redis) mapping user_id to the gateway server holding their socket, so any gateway that needs to deliver to that user knows exactly which other gateway to forward to.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- **Shared connection registry** (lookup table in a fast store): any gateway can route to any user in one hop, but the registry itself must be highly available and consistent, since a stale entry means a message gets forwarded to a gateway that no longer holds that socket
- Consistent hashing of users to gateways (no lookup needed, user id determines gateway deterministically): removes the registry as a moving part, but rebalancing when gateways are added or removed forces many users to reconnect at once
- In practice, most large systems use the registry approach because connection churn (users reconnecting on flaky mobile networks constantly) makes a stable hash assignment hard to maintain cleanly

### How do sent, delivered, and read receipts actually work without adding a full extra round trip to every message?
Sent is acknowledged the moment the server durably stores the message, independent of the recipient. Delivered is acknowledged when the message reaches the recipient's device (their client sends a small ack back over its own socket the instant it receives the push). Read is acknowledged separately, only when the recipient actually opens that chat thread, which the client reports as its own event. Each status is a separate one-way ack message, not a blocking round trip on the original send.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Three independent async acks (current real-world approach): the sender's send is never blocked waiting on the recipient, each status update is just a small message flowing back through the same routing path
- A single synchronous 'confirm delivery before returning success' call: simpler mental model, but ties the sender's request latency to the recipient's network conditions, which is unacceptable when the recipient might be offline for hours
- Batching receipt acks (e.g. flush read receipts every few seconds instead of instantly): reduces small-message volume at high scale, at the cost of the sender's read receipt lagging by a few seconds, a trade-off most products accept for group chats but not for one-on-one

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The connection registry is read on every message send and written on every connect/disconnect, at hundreds of millions of entries; it needs to be sharded (by user_id) and run as a cluster, not a single instance, or it becomes the system's central bottleneck.
- A gateway server crashing instantly drops however many hundreds of thousands of connections it was holding; clients need exponential-backoff reconnect logic, and the registry must quickly detect and evict stale entries for that dead gateway so messages aren't routed into a black hole.
- The offline queue must be bounded per user (both in size and retention time), or a user who never reopens the app becomes an ever-growing storage liability; old queued messages past some retention window are dropped or the account is flagged.
- Because content is end-to-end encrypted, the server can't deduplicate, compress, or inspect messages meaningfully, so raw storage and bandwidth scale linearly with message volume with none of the usual content-aware optimizations available.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing this as if it were a stateless HTTP API== and forgetting that routing a message to a specific online user requires knowing exactly which server is holding their socket right now.
- ⚠️ ==Assuming delivered and read receipts can share a single status field==, when they're genuinely two separate events that happen at different times and need to be tracked and communicated independently.
- ⚠️ Not accounting for end-to-end encryption early, then proposing server-side features (search, spam filtering on content) that are simply impossible once the server can't read message bodies.
- ⚠️ Treating the offline queue as unbounded, which quietly becomes a storage time bomb for accounts that uninstall the app without ever reconnecting.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't a normal stateless load balancer route messages the way it routes typical API requests?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a typical stateless API request can be handled by any backend instance, but delivering a message to a specific online user requires reaching the exact gateway server that is holding that user's live socket right now. That requires a shared, fast-lookup registry mapping user to gateway, which a stateless load balancer has no concept of.

**Q: How would you handle a gateway server crashing with 500,000 open connections?**

> **Model Answer:** Clients detect the dropped socket and reconnect with exponential backoff (to avoid a reconnect stampede) to a newly assigned gateway via the load balancer. The connection registry needs a heartbeat or TTL mechanism so entries pointing at the dead gateway expire quickly, otherwise other gateways will keep trying to forward messages to a server that no longer exists.

lesson.content:
# Design Slack

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Slack` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Slack looks like WhatsApp with channels bolted on, but the real design shift is that a channel isn't a conversation between two people, it's a **broadcast target** whose size varies from 2 to 50,000, and the right delivery strategy for a DM ==actively falls apart== at the top of that range.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a workspace-based team chat system like Slack: users belong to
organizations ("workspaces"), workspaces contain channels, users post
messages in channels or send direct messages, and messages must be
searchable across a user's history. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the range of channel sizes we need to support, a handful of teammates or company-wide channels with tens of thousands of members?
*Why it matters:* Fan-out to 5 people and fan-out to 50,000 people are different engineering problems, similar to the celebrity-account problem in a social feed. This decides whether one delivery strategy suffices or whether large channels need special handling.

#### Q: Does search need to cover full message history across every channel a user is in, in near real time as new messages arrive?
*Why it matters:* Real-time, full-history search means every message needs to be indexed into a search system on write, not batched, which adds a whole second write path alongside the primary message store.

#### Q: Do we need real-time presence and typing indicators, or is that out of scope?
*Why it matters:* Presence and typing indicators are high-frequency, low-value-per-event data (a typing indicator might fire on every keystroke). Treating them the same as durable messages would massively and needlessly inflate the storage and delivery pipeline.

#### Q: Is message history required to load instantly on channel open, including for a channel with years of history?
*Why it matters:* This decides between loading the full channel history eagerly versus paginating recent messages first, which changes both the API shape and the read-path caching strategy.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can post a message to a channel they're a member of, or send a direct message.
- All members of a channel receive new messages in near real time while they're active in the workspace.
- A user can search their message history across all channels they belong to.
- A user can see, on joining or scrolling, the recent message history of a channel.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Message delivery to active channel members must be near-real-time (well under a second).**
- **The system must handle extreme skew in channel size, from a 2-person DM to a 50,000-member company-wide channel, without the largest channels degrading delivery for everyone.**
- **Search must return relevant results quickly even across years of accumulated workspace history.**
- **The system must remain available for reads (viewing channel history) even during a spike in write traffic.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 million daily active users across 500,000 workspaces
- Average user posts 20 messages a day and is a member of 15 channels
- A typical channel has 30 members, but the largest company-wide channels reach 50,000
- Each message with metadata is roughly 300 bytes before search indexing overhead

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Messages posted per day and per second:** 10,000,000 * 20 = 200 million messages/day ≈ 2,300 messages/sec average
- **Fan-out writes for an average message:** 1 message * 30 average channel members = 30 delivery pushes, trivial to do live per message
- **Fan-out writes for a company-wide channel message:** 1 message * 50,000 members = 50,000 near-simultaneous pushes for a single post, the number that forces special handling for large channels
- **Daily storage for message history:** 200,000,000 * 300 bytes ≈ 60 GB/day of raw message data, before the roughly equal amount of index data search needs

*Capacity Takeaway:* Average-case fan-out (30 members) is trivial and can be pushed live to every connected member on every message, but the same architecture applied naively to a 50,000-member channel turns one post into a ==delivery storm==, so **channel size** is the single fact that decides whether a channel gets live push fan-out or a pulled/batched delivery strategy.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A client holds a persistent connection to a gateway server and subscribes
to the channels currently relevant to it. When a user posts a message, the
app server writes it to the sharded message store, then, for
ordinary-sized channels, immediately pushes it to every currently
connected member through the gateway layer, the same live fan-out-on-write
pattern as a small group chat. In parallel and asynchronously, the message
is placed on a queue that feeds the search index, so it becomes searchable
within moments without adding latency to the send itself. Very large
channels (tens of thousands of members) skip full live push fan-out and
instead rely on connected clients pulling recent messages when they're
actively viewing that channel, since pushing to fifty thousand sockets at
once for every message is not a cost worth paying for a channel most
members are not actively watching at any given moment.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Channel fan-out and async search indexing

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    gw["Gateway Servers"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    msgdb[("Messages Store")]:::db
    idxqueue>"Indexing Queue"]:::queue
    idxworker["Indexing Workers"]:::server
    searchidx["Search Index"]:::server
    members[("Channel Members")]:::db
    client -->|"persistent WS"| gw
    gw --> app
    app -->|"write message"| msgdb
    app -->|"fan-out list"| members
    app -.->|"push to members"| gw
    app -.->|"enqueue for indexing"| idxqueue
    idxqueue -.-> idxworker
    idxworker -.->|"update index"| searchidx
```

#### A message posted to a channel, step by step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. User posts message (POST to app server)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Written to message store (durable, source of truth)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Fan-out to connected members (live push over sockets)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Enqueued for search (async, off the critical path)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Indexed and searchable (usually within a second)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Delivery strategy decision, per channel

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  post["New message posted"] --> check{"Is channel size huge?"}
  check -->|"no, typical channel"| push["Live push to every connected member"]
  check -->|"yes, 50k+ members"| viewing{"Is member viewing now?"}
  viewing -->|"yes"| pushnow["Push to that socket now"]
  viewing -->|"no"| pull["Pick up on next channel open"]
```

#### Fan-out cost vs channel size

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/channels/{channelId}/messages` | Body: { text }. Posts a message to channelId from the authenticated user, who must be a member. |
| `WS` | `wss://gateway/connect` | Opens a persistent connection scoped to a workspace; the client subscribes to the channels it's currently viewing or a member of, and receives live message pushes. |
| `GET` | `/api/channels/{channelId}/history` | Returns paginated message history for channelId, newest first, for populating the channel view. |
| `GET` | `/api/search` | Query params: q, workspace_id, channel_id? Returns ranked matching messages across the channels the authenticated user is a member of. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `messages`
- `message_id (unique, time-sortable)`
- `channel_id (indexed)`
- `author_id`
- `text`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
*Notes:* Sharded by channel_id so a whole channel's history lives together for fast range reads on channel open.

### Entity: `channel_members`
- `channel_id`
- `user_id`
- `joined_at`
*Notes:* Needs efficient lookup both directions: 'who is in this channel' (for fan-out) and 'which channels is this user in' (for the client's channel list and for scoping search), typically indexed both ways.

### Entity: `search_index`
- `message_id`
- `channel_id`
- `author_id`
- `text (tokenized/inverted)`
*Notes:* A separate inverted-index store (e.g. Elasticsearch-style), updated asynchronously off a queue after a message is durably written, deliberately decoupled from the write path so search indexing latency never blocks a message send.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How should message delivery differ between a small channel and a 50,000-member company-wide channel?
For a normal channel (tens of members), live fan-out-on-write, pushing the new message to every connected member's socket the instant it's posted, is cheap and keeps the experience real-time. For a channel with tens of thousands of members, most of whom are not actively looking at that channel right now, pushing to every one of their open sockets for every message is enormous wasted work. Instead, large channels can push only to clients that have that channel currently open and visible, while everyone else picks up new messages the normal way, on next channel open or via a lower-frequency badge/unread-count update.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- **Live push to all members** regardless of channel size: simplest mental model and truly instant for everyone, but a single post in a 50,000-member channel becomes 50,000 simultaneous pushes, a real load spike concentrated in one instant
- **Push only to actively-viewing clients, pull for everyone else**: bounds the worst-case push fan-out to however many people currently have that channel open (usually a small fraction), at the cost of members not actively watching seeing the message slightly later, on their next open
- This mirrors the fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read tension from a social feed, just triggered by channel size instead of follower count, which is worth naming explicitly since it's the same underlying trade-off

### How does search stay current without slowing down message sends?
Indexing a message into a full-text search system (tokenizing, building or updating an inverted index) is meaningfully slower than a simple database write, and doing it synchronously on the send path would add that latency to every single message. Instead, the message is written durably first (the send completes and the sender gets their ack), and only then is it placed on a queue that a separate indexing worker fleet consumes to update the search index, decoupled entirely from the send.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Synchronous indexing on send: search is always instantly up to date, but every message send now pays the latency cost of a search-index write, which is unacceptable at high message volume
- Asynchronous indexing via a queue: message sends stay fast and are unaffected by indexing load, at the cost of a small window (typically well under a second, but not zero) where a just-sent message isn't yet searchable
- The async approach is the correct trade-off here because a brief indexing lag is invisible to users, while slow message sends are immediately and universally noticeable

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Very large channels remain the sharpest edge case; the threshold for switching from live-push to pull-on-open fan-out needs to be tuned against actual gateway push throughput, similar to the celebrity-account threshold in a feed system.
- The channel_members table can grow into the billions of rows across all workspaces; it needs sharding (commonly by channel_id, since fan-out reads 'who is in this channel') and a separate index for the reverse 'which channels is this user in' lookup.
- The search index is a separate system from the primary message store and needs its own horizontal scaling story (sharded by workspace, typically, since search queries are almost always scoped to one workspace).
- A workspace with unusually high message volume (a very active large company) can create hot shards if messages are sharded purely by channel_id within one workspace; splitting the hottest channels across additional shards or partitioning by time as well as channel avoids a single overloaded shard.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Applying the same live-push fan-out strategy uniformly== regardless of channel size, then having the design collapse under an interviewer's 'what about the company-wide 50,000-person channel' follow-up.
- ⚠️ ==Putting search indexing synchronously in the message send path==, adding avoidable latency to the single most frequent operation in the whole system.
- ⚠️ Treating a workspace's channels as if they all belong to one global namespace, instead of scoping data (and especially search) per workspace, which is both a correctness and a scaling requirement.
- ⚠️ Ignoring typing indicators and presence as 'just a small feature' when at scale they can generate more raw event volume than actual messages, and need their own lightweight, non-durable delivery path.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't the celebrity-account fan-out problem from a social feed map exactly onto Slack's large-channel problem?**

> **Model Answer:** The shape of the trade-off is the same, but the fix differs. A feed handles the celebrity case by merging their tweets in at read time. A large channel instead limits live push to members who currently have the channel open, since most members simply haven't opened it recently, and lets everyone else pick up new messages the normal way on next open, which is a cheaper and simpler fix given that channel activity is naturally bursty and localized to whoever's actively working in it.

**Q: How would you make search results relevant, not just present, across years of workspace history?**

> **Model Answer:** Beyond basic text matching, a real system ranks by signals like recency, whether the message is in a channel the searching user is active in, and engagement (replies, reactions), and typically restricts results to only channels the user is currently a member of for both relevance and access-control reasons, since showing content from a channel a user isn't in would be a real security bug, not just a UX flaw.

# Design a Video Conferencing System (Zoom)

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a video conferencing system like Zoom: multiple participants join a
call and can see and hear each other in near real time, with support for
calls ranging from a two-person conversation to a meeting with hundreds of
participants. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the maximum number of participants in a single call we need to support?
*Why it matters:* A handful of participants can be handled by a fundamentally different, much simpler architecture (direct peer-to-peer) than hundreds of participants can, similar to how follower count decides feed architecture. This single number decides the whole media-routing strategy.

#### Q: Do participants need to see everyone at once, or typically just the active speaker plus a few others?
*Why it matters:* If clients only ever render a small number of video feeds at a time (active speaker view), the server doesn't need to forward every participant's video to every other participant, only the ones actually being displayed, which changes the bandwidth math substantially.

#### Q: Does the call need to be recorded, and do participants join from wildly different network conditions (mobile 4G vs office fiber)?
*Why it matters:* Recording adds a whole separate media-capture and storage pipeline. Mixed network quality means the system needs per-participant bandwidth adaptation, sending a lower-resolution stream to a participant on a weak connection rather than one fixed quality for everyone.

#### Q: Is this browser-based (WebRTC) or a native app, and does it need to interoperate with regular phone dial-in?
*Why it matters:* This affects the client-side codec and signaling assumptions, and phone dial-in requires an entirely separate telephony gateway component bridging PSTN audio into the same call.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Multiple users can join a shared call and see and hear each other in near real time.
- The system supports calls from 2 participants up to several hundred.
- A participant's video quality adapts to their available bandwidth without freezing the call for others.
- A user can mute/unmute audio and turn their camera on or off.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **End-to-end audio/video latency must stay low, generally under 300-500ms, or conversation starts to feel unnatural.**
- **The system must degrade gracefully for participants on poor connections (lower resolution, not a frozen or dropped call) rather than degrading the call for everyone.**
- **The system must scale participant count without each participant's own upload bandwidth becoming the bottleneck.**
- **A single participant's device or network failure must not disrupt the call for other participants.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 million concurrent calls at peak, averaging 4 participants each
- Each participant's video stream, sent at a moderate adaptive bitrate, is roughly 1 Mbps
- A meeting server (SFU node) can comfortably handle around 500 participant-streams of combined inbound and outbound media before needing to add capacity
- Active speaker view means a client typically renders 1 to 4 incoming video streams, not all participants at once

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Concurrent participants at peak:** 10,000,000 calls * 4 participants = 40 million concurrent participants across the platform
- **Bandwidth if the server had to relay every stream to every participant (naive mesh-style forwarding):** In a 4-person call, mesh means each participant uploads to 3 others and downloads from 3 others: 4 * 3 = 12 stream-relationships per call * 1 Mbps = 12 Mbps of total media movement for just one small call
- **SFU nodes needed at peak:** 40,000,000 participants / 500 participant-streams per node ≈ 80,000 SFU server instances needed platform-wide at peak, the number that makes efficient media routing, not just correctness, the central design problem
- **Per-participant upload cost with an SFU vs mesh:** With an SFU, each participant uploads exactly 1 stream (1 Mbps) regardless of call size, instead of uploading a separate stream to every other participant, which is the entire reason mesh doesn't scale past a handful of people

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that drives this architecture is that a participant's upload bandwidth stays **flat with an SFU** (always 1 stream out) but ==grows linearly with call size under peer-to-peer mesh==, which is exactly why mesh works for a 3-person call and falls apart by the time a call reaches even 6-8 participants.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
When a call starts, a signaling server assigns it to a specific SFU
(selective forwarding unit) cluster, geographically close to the
participants to keep latency low. Each participant establishes one media
connection to that SFU, uploading exactly one video/audio stream
regardless of how many other participants are on the call. The SFU
receives every participant's stream and selectively forwards each one to
whichever other participants currently need to see it (typically the
active speaker plus a few others, not necessarily everyone to everyone),
adapting the forwarded resolution per recipient based on their measured
bandwidth. Signaling (who's in the call, connection setup, mute state)
flows over a separate lightweight WebSocket channel, decoupled from the
actual media path, which is why a signaling hiccup doesn't necessarily
freeze the video itself.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### SFU-based media routing for a multi-party call

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    clienta["Participant A"]:::client
    clientb["Participant B"]:::client
    clientc["Participant C"]:::client
    signaling["Signaling Server"]:::server
    sfu["SFU Node"]:::server
    callmeta[("Call Metadata")]:::db
    recorder["Recording Worker"]:::server
    clienta -->|"join/signal"| signaling
    clientb -->|"join/signal"| signaling
    clientc -->|"join/signal"| signaling
    signaling -->|"assign media session"| sfu
    clienta -->|"upload 1 stream"| sfu
    clientb -->|"upload 1 stream"| sfu
    clientc -->|"upload 1 stream"| sfu
    sfu -->|"forward needed streams"| clienta
    sfu -->|"forward needed streams"| clientb
    sfu -->|"forward needed streams"| clientc
    sfu -.->|"tap stream"| recorder
    signaling -->|"call/participant state"| callmeta
```

#### Mesh vs SFU vs MCU

| Peer-to-peer mesh | SFU (used by Zoom and most modern systems) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Zero server media cost, lowest latency | Each participant uploads exactly one stream always |
| Upload bandwidth grows linearly with participants | Server forwards without decoding, relatively cheap |
| Breaks down past roughly 4-6 people | Clients still decode multiple incoming streams |

#### Per-participant upload bandwidth: mesh vs SFU

#### Media routing choice by call size

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  start["New call created"] --> size{"How many participants?"}
  size -->|"2-6, latency critical"| mesh["Peer-to-peer mesh"]
  size -->|"typical call"| sfu["SFU forwards streams"]
  size -->|"weak client or dial-in"| mcu["MCU mixes to one stream"]
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/calls` | Creates a new call/meeting room and returns a join token and the assigned SFU cluster/region for that call. |
| `POST` | `/api/calls/{callId}/join` | Body: { participant_id }. Registers the participant with the call's signaling server, which returns SFU connection details and the current participant list. |
| `WS` | `wss://signaling/{callId}` | Signaling channel for exchanging session descriptions (SDP) and ICE candidates between each client and the SFU to establish the actual media connection. |
| `POST` | `/api/calls/{callId}/leave` | Removes the participant from the call, notifying the SFU to stop forwarding their stream and notifying other participants they've left. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `calls`
- `call_id (unique)`
- `host_id`
- `sfu_cluster_id (which media server cluster is handling this call)`
- `started_at (timestamp)`
- `status (active | ended)`
*Notes:* The source of truth for which SFU cluster owns a given call's live media routing; short-lived, mostly relevant only while the call is active.

### Entity: `participants`
- `call_id`
- `user_id`
- `joined_at`
- `left_at (nullable)`
- `connection_quality (rolling estimate, for adaptive bitrate decisions)`
*Notes:* Tracks who's currently in a call and their live connection quality, which the SFU uses to decide what bitrate to send them.

### Entity: `call_recordings`
- `call_id`
- `recording_url`
- `duration_seconds`
*Notes:* Only populated if recording was enabled; written by a separate recording pipeline that consumes the same media streams the SFU is already routing, never on the live call's critical path.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Peer-to-peer mesh vs SFU vs MCU: how should video actually get from one participant to the others?
Peer-to-peer mesh means every participant sends their video directly to every other participant, no server media routing at all. An SFU (selective forwarding unit) means every participant uploads one stream to a central server, which forwards (without decoding or re-encoding) each participant's stream to whichever others need it. An MCU (multipoint control unit) goes further: the server actually decodes every incoming stream, mixes them into a single combined video (like a pre-built grid layout), and sends each participant one lightweight combined stream back.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- **Mesh**: zero server media cost and the lowest possible latency for a small call, but each participant's upload bandwidth and CPU scale linearly with the number of other participants, which makes it fall apart past roughly 4-6 people
- **SFU**: a participant always uploads exactly one stream no matter the call size, and the server does comparatively cheap forwarding (no decode/re-encode), which is why nearly all modern video conferencing products use this; the cost is that clients still need enough bandwidth and CPU to decode multiple incoming streams
- MCU: the lightest possible client, since it receives one pre-mixed stream and does almost no work, which matters for weak devices or dial-in phone participants, but the server pays a heavy decode/mix/re-encode cost per participant, making MCU infrastructure far more expensive to run at scale than an SFU
- Most real products (Zoom included) use an SFU by default and fall back to MCU-style mixing only for specific weak clients (like a phone dialing in over audio-only), getting SFU's scalability for the common case and MCU's simplicity where it's actually needed

### How does bandwidth adaptation work so one participant's bad connection doesn't freeze the call for everyone else?
Because the SFU forwards streams individually rather than mixing them, it can send a different quality version of the same source stream to different recipients. A sender typically encodes their outgoing video as multiple simulcast layers (say, low, medium, and high resolution) simultaneously, and the SFU picks which layer to forward to each recipient based on that specific recipient's currently measured bandwidth, without needing to re-encode anything itself.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Simulcast (sender encodes multiple quality layers, SFU picks per-recipient): no server-side transcoding cost, degrades gracefully per-recipient, but costs the sender extra upload bandwidth and CPU to produce multiple layers at once
- Server-side transcoding (SFU receives one stream, re-encodes it into multiple qualities itself): saves the sender's upload bandwidth, but is CPU-expensive for the server and adds encode latency, which works against the low-latency requirement
- Simulcast is the dominant real-world choice because sender-side encoding capacity is usually more available than server-side transcoding capacity at the scale a video conferencing platform operates at

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single SFU node has a ceiling on total participant-streams it can forward before CPU/bandwidth saturate; very large calls (hundreds of participants) need to be split across multiple SFU nodes in a cascade, forwarding between SFUs as well as to clients.
- Geographic latency is a hard physical constraint; SFU clusters need to be deployed regionally close to where participants actually are, and a call's participants spread across continents forces a trade-off between routing through one region (adding latency for some) or cascading across regions (adding complexity).
- The signaling layer, while lightweight, still needs to scale to millions of concurrent calls' worth of connection setup and mute/state events; it should be horizontally sharded per call, similar to the connection registry pattern in a messaging system.
- Recording pipelines that consume the same live streams for storage must never be allowed to add backpressure to the live media path; they should tap the stream asynchronously, never sit in the critical forwarding path.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Defaulting to peer-to-peer mesh== for a general-purpose video conferencing system without checking the maximum participant count, then having the design fall over the moment the interviewer asks about a 20-person call.
- ⚠️ Assuming the server needs to decode and re-encode every stream (MCU-style) by default, when an SFU achieves the same multi-party experience far more cheaply for the common case.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that bandwidth adaptation needs to be per-recipient, not per-call, since different participants have different network conditions simultaneously on the very same call.
- ⚠️ Treating signaling and media as one combined path, when keeping them separate is exactly what lets the system recover from a brief signaling hiccup without dropping the actual audio/video.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does peer-to-peer mesh work fine for a 3-person call but not a 30-person call?**

> **Model Answer:** In mesh, each participant uploads a separate stream directly to every other participant, so required upload bandwidth and CPU scale linearly with the number of other participants. At 3 people that's 2 outgoing streams per participant, manageable on typical connections; at 30 people it's 29 outgoing streams per participant simultaneously, which exceeds what almost any consumer upload connection or device CPU can sustain, which is exactly the scaling wall an SFU is designed to remove by capping every participant's upload at exactly one stream.

**Q: How would you decide when to cascade a call across multiple SFU nodes instead of using just one?**

> **Model Answer:** Once a single SFU node's combined inbound and outbound stream load approaches its CPU or bandwidth ceiling (a number you'd determine from load testing that node), or once participants are spread across geographic regions far enough apart that routing everyone through one region adds unacceptable latency for some of them, the call needs to be split across multiple SFU nodes that forward streams between each other as well as to their local clients.

> Presence looks like a tiny piece of state (online or not) but the actual engineering problem is **fan-out**: naively broadcasting every status flip to everyone who might care would generate more traffic than the messages themselves, so the whole design is about ==narrowing who gets told and how often==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design the presence system behind a messaging app: every user's client
shows a green dot next to their contacts who are currently online, and a
"last seen" timestamp for those who aren't. Hundreds of millions of users
may be connected at once, and their status changes constantly. Design the
system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Who actually needs to be notified when a user's status changes: everyone on the platform, or only that user's contacts/open chats?
*Why it matters:* Broadcasting to the whole platform is a fan-out explosion at scale. Restricting delivery to an 'interest set' (contacts, or people with an open chat window) shrinks the fan-out by orders of magnitude and is the single biggest lever in this design.

#### Q: How is 'online' actually detected: a persistent connection, periodic heartbeats, or both?
*Why it matters:* A persistent connection alone tells you a socket is open, not that the app is foregrounded or the network hasn't silently died. Heartbeats on top of the connection give a way to detect a session going stale even when the socket hasn't formally closed, which changes what infrastructure is needed.

#### Q: Do we need exact real-time status, or is a small delay (a few seconds) acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Exact real-time status for every flicker of connectivity forces sending an update on every single blip. Tolerating a short delay enables debouncing, which cuts update volume dramatically for the common case of someone's connection dropping and reconnecting within a second or two.

#### Q: Should we show a precise 'last seen 2 minutes ago' or just a coarse offline state?
*Why it matters:* Precise last-seen timestamps require durably persisting a write on every disconnect for every user, whereas a coarse state can often be served from an in-memory store alone, which is a much cheaper storage design.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user's client can query the current online/offline status of a list of other users (their contacts).
- When a user comes online or goes offline, their contacts who are actively viewing that status are notified in near real time.
- A user who is offline shows a 'last seen at [timestamp]' instead of a live status.
- A user can go idle (app backgrounded but connection still alive) as a distinct third state from fully online and fully offline.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Status changes must propagate to interested viewers within a couple of seconds, not minutes.**
- **The system must **not broadcast** a status change to the entire user base; fan-out must be limited to genuinely interested viewers.**
- **The system must tolerate flaky mobile connections without ==flapping== a user's visible status between online and offline every few seconds.**
- **The system must scale to hundreds of millions of concurrently connected users without the presence layer itself becoming the bottleneck for the rest of the messaging platform.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 300 million users with an open persistent connection at peak
- Average user has 150 contacts, but only a small fraction (say 5) have that user's profile or chat open at any given moment
- Each user's connection state flips (connect/disconnect/reconnect) roughly 20 times a day on average, mobile networks being what they are
- A status update message is small, roughly 50 bytes

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Naive broadcast-to-all-contacts fan-out per flip:** 300,000,000 users * 20 flips/day * 150 contacts = 900 billion notification sends/day, clearly unworkable
- **Fan-out limited to actively-viewing subscribers:** 300,000,000 * 20 flips/day * 5 active viewers = 30 billion sends/day, a 30x reduction just from narrowing the interest set
- **Sends per second at peak (assume 3x average during evening peak):** 30,000,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 347,000 sends/sec average, roughly 1 million/sec at peak, still large but now tractable with a pub/sub fan-out layer
- **In-memory presence table size:** 300,000,000 users * roughly 100 bytes per entry (status, last_seen, gateway_id) ≈ 30 GB, comfortably fits a sharded in-memory cluster

*Capacity Takeaway:* The single driving fact is that broadcasting to a user's entire contact list is **30x more expensive** than broadcasting only to contacts who currently have that user's status on screen, so subscription-scoped fan-out (not raw connection count) is what makes this system affordable at all.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Every client holds a persistent connection to a presence gateway and sends
periodic heartbeats over it. The gateway writes an online entry with a
**short TTL** into a sharded in-memory presence store, refreshed on every
heartbeat; if heartbeats stop, the TTL expires and the user is treated as
offline without any explicit disconnect message needed. Separately,
clients **subscribe** to the specific set of users they're currently watching
(an open chat list, a visible profile). When a user's status changes, a
==debounce window== holds the change briefly to absorb rapid flapping, then a
pub/sub fan-out layer pushes the update only to that user's active
subscribers, not their entire contact list.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Heartbeats, TTL presence store, and scoped fan-out

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    clienta["Client A"]:::client
    clientb["Client B (subscriber)"]:::client
    gw["Presence Gateway"]:::server
    presencestore["Presence Store (TTL)"]:::cache
    pubsub>"Pub/Sub Fan-out"]:::queue
    subs["Subscription Registry"]:::cache
    lastseen[("Last Seen Store")]:::db
    clienta -->|"heartbeat"| gw
    gw -->|"refresh TTL"| presencestore
    gw -.->|"on disconnect"| lastseen
    presencestore -.->|"status changed"| pubsub
    pubsub -->|"lookup subscribers"| subs
    pubsub -.->|"push update"| clientb
    clientb -->|"subscribe to A"| subs
```

#### A goes offline, only subscribed viewers find out

#### A user's presence state transitions

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  offline["Offline"] -->|"connects"| online["Online"]
  online -->|"app backgrounded"| idle["Idle"]
  idle -->|"foregrounded again"| online
  online -->|"heartbeat TTL expires"| offline
  idle -->|"heartbeat TTL expires"| offline
```

#### Debounce window vs connection blips absorbed

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `WS` | `wss://presence/connect` | Opens the persistent connection used for both heartbeats and receiving presence push updates; on connect, the server marks this user online and starts the heartbeat timer. |
| `POST` | `/api/presence/subscribe` | Body: { user_ids: [...] }. Registers the authenticated user's interest in receiving live status updates for this set of users (e.g. contacts currently visible in the open chat list). |
| `GET` | `/api/presence/status` | Query param userIds: batch lookup of current status (online | idle | offline) and last_seen for a list of users, used to paint initial state on app open before live updates arrive. |
| `POST` | `/api/presence/heartbeat` | Sent periodically over the open socket (or as a fallback ping) to refresh the user's online TTL; missing heartbeats past a threshold flips the user to offline. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `presence_state`
- `user_id (key)`
- `status (online | idle | offline)`
- `last_heartbeat_at`
- `gateway_id`
*Notes:* Lives entirely in an in-memory, sharded key-value store with a TTL per entry; a missed heartbeat lets the entry naturally expire to offline instead of requiring an explicit disconnect event.

### Entity: `last_seen`
- `user_id (key)`
- `last_seen_at (timestamp)`
*Notes:* The only piece of presence data that needs durable storage, since it must survive the in-memory entry expiring; written once per disconnect, not on every heartbeat.

### Entity: `subscriptions`
- `subscriber_id`
- `target_user_id`
- `expires_at`
*Notes:* The interest graph: who is currently watching whose status. Short-lived by design, refreshed while a chat list or profile is on screen and dropped when it's closed, which is what keeps fan-out bounded.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you avoid flooding subscribers when a user's connection is flapping on a bad mobile network?
A raw connect/disconnect event stream would fire a status change every time a phone briefly loses signal in an elevator, even though the user reconnects two seconds later. A debounce window delays marking a user offline until their connection has actually been down past a short threshold (say 5-10 seconds), and coalesces rapid flip-flops into a single, stable update instead of a burst of contradictory ones.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- No debounce, instant status propagation: technically most accurate, but generates a stream of ==flickering online/offline updates== for anyone on a marginal connection, which is worse UX and wastes fan-out capacity
- **Fixed debounce window** (delay before flipping to offline): absorbs brief blips cleanly, at the cost of a small, bounded lag before genuinely offline users show as offline
- Adaptive debounce based on recent flap frequency for that user (longer delay for a user who's flapped repeatedly in the last minute): more resilient to genuinely bad connections, but adds per-user state and tuning complexity that a fixed window avoids

### How do you scope fan-out so a status change doesn't get pushed to a user's entire contact list?
The naive design treats presence like a broadcast: any contact might care, so notify all of them. The fix is to only fan out to a short-lived subscription set, populated the moment a client actually renders that user's status (an open chat list, a visible profile) and dropped when that view closes or after a short expiry. This turns fan-out size from 'total contact count' into 'currently-watching count', which is dramatically smaller in practice.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Broadcast to full contact graph: simple to reason about, but the fan-out volume scales with total relationships, not actual attention, and becomes the dominant cost in the whole system at this user count
- **Subscription-scoped fan-out** (subscribe when visible, unsubscribe when not): fan-out volume scales with what people are actually looking at right now, but requires clients to actively manage subscribe/unsubscribe calls as views open and close, adding client-side complexity
- Polling instead of push (client periodically re-fetches status for visible contacts): removes the need for a subscription registry entirely, but trades push's low latency for polling interval lag, and still costs server load proportional to polling frequency times visible contacts

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The in-memory presence store is read and written on nearly every heartbeat across hundreds of millions of connections; it must be sharded by user_id across a cluster, since a single instance cannot hold that write rate.
- The subscription registry needs fast expiry and cleanup, or stale subscriptions (from crashed clients that never unsubscribed) accumulate and quietly inflate fan-out volume back toward the broadcast case this design is trying to avoid.
- A large group of mutual contacts all opening the same popular user's profile at once (a mini celebrity effect) can spike that one user's fan-out fan-in disproportionately; the pub/sub layer needs to handle a skewed subscriber count per target user gracefully.
- Presence gateways dying takes down their held connections at once, similar to a chat gateway; heartbeat TTL expiry naturally self-heals affected users to offline rather than requiring an explicit failure-detection pass.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Broadcasting every status change to a user's entire contact list==, ignoring that most contacts aren't currently looking, which multiplies fan-out volume for no user-facing benefit.
- ⚠️ ==Treating connection drop as an instant, un-debounced offline signal==, causing visible status to flicker on any user with a shaky connection.
- ⚠️ Storing full presence history durably on every heartbeat, when only the current state and last-seen timestamp actually need to persist beyond an in-memory TTL.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that subscriptions need their own expiry; stale subscriptions from clients that closed without unsubscribing quietly grow fan-out back toward broadcast levels over time.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is TTL-based expiry preferred over explicit disconnect events for detecting offline status?**

> **Model Answer:** A clean disconnect message assumes the client gets a chance to send one, which isn't true for a crashed app, a killed process, or a gateway server that dies mid-connection. **TTL expiry** treats 'absence of a recent heartbeat' as the ground truth instead, so a user is correctly marked offline within one TTL window regardless of how the connection actually ended, with no separate failure-detection system required.

**Q: How would you handle a user with an unusually large number of active subscribers, like a public figure whose status page many people have open at once?**

> **Model Answer:** This is a smaller-scale version of the celebrity fan-out problem: cap or batch fan-out delivery for high-subscriber targets, and consider serving their status via a short-lived cached snapshot refreshed on an interval instead of pushing to every subscriber individually on every flip, trading a little staleness for bounded fan-out cost.

lesson.content:
# Design a Group Chat System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `WhatsApp Groups • Telegram • Discord` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A group chat is Twitter's fan-out problem shrunk down to a **bounded, known-in-advance audience**, and that boundedness is exactly what makes **fan-out-on-write** the right default here, unlike the timeline case where an unbounded, skewed audience forced a hybrid.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Extend a one-on-one messaging system to support group chats: a message
sent to a group must be delivered to every member, each member sees who
has read the message, and groups can range from a handful of friends to
thousands of members. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the group size distribution: mostly small friend groups, or do we need to support large communities of thousands of members?
*Why it matters:* A handful of members and a few thousand members are different engineering problems. Small groups can fan out synchronously and cheaply; large groups start to resemble the celebrity fan-out case and may need the read path involved.

#### Q: Do we need per-member read receipts (who specifically has read the message), or just an aggregate read count?
*Why it matters:* **Per-member receipts** mean tracking one row per (message, member) pair, which for a 500-person group is 500x the bookkeeping of a one-on-one chat. An aggregate count is far cheaper and is what most large-group products actually ship.

#### Q: Can group membership change (people added or removed) while old messages still exist?
*Why it matters:* If a new member should not see history predating their join, delivery and history queries both need to be scoped by 'messages sent after this member joined,' not just 'all messages in this group,' which changes both the write path and the read query.

#### Q: Is delivery ordering required to be identical for every member, or is per-member eventual consistency acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Guaranteeing every member sees messages in the exact same order requires a single ordering authority per group. Accepting minor per-member ordering differences allows a simpler, more parallel fan-out with no shared bottleneck.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create a group and add or remove members (up to some maximum group size).
- A message sent to a group is delivered to every current member, whether they're online now or offline.
- A sender can see delivery and read status for a group message (either per-member or as an aggregate count, depending on group size).
- A member can view the group's message history from whenever they joined onward.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Message delivery to a small group must feel just as instant as one-on-one messaging.**
- **The system must not let a single very large group's fan-out volume degrade delivery latency for every other, smaller group sharing the same infrastructure.**
- **Read receipt bookkeeping must stay bounded even for groups with thousands of members, rather than growing without limit per message.**
- **A member added to a group must never receive messages sent before they joined.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 500 million total users; 100 million active groups; average group size 8 members, with a long tail up to 10,000 members for large community groups
- An average group sends 30 messages/day; a large (max-size) group sends 500 messages/day
- 99% of groups are under 50 members; the remaining 1% account for most of the total fan-out volume
- Each message is roughly 200 bytes of text plus metadata

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Fan-out writes for an average small group:** 30 messages/day * 8 members = 240 fan-out deliveries/day per group, trivial to do synchronously per send
- **Fan-out writes for a large (10,000-member) group:** 500 messages/day * 10,000 members = 5 million fan-out deliveries/day for a single group, the same shape of problem a celebrity tweet creates
- **Total fan-out deliveries across all groups per day:** 99,000,000 small groups * 240 ≈ 23.8 billion, plus 1,000,000 large groups * up to 5,000,000 ≈ 5 trillion in the worst case if every large group is maxed out; in practice large-group volume dominates the total by orders of magnitude
- **Read receipt rows for a single message in a 500-member group:** 1 message * 500 members = 500 read-state rows if tracked per-member; switching to an aggregate counter for groups over some threshold turns this into 1 row instead of 500

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving fact is the same shape as Twitter's celebrity problem but inverted in scale: even a small number of very large groups can generate fan-out volume that dwarfs the long tail of small groups combined, so large groups need the same fan-out-on-write-with-a-ceiling treatment, while per-member read receipts must ==degrade to an aggregate count== past a size threshold to keep bookkeeping bounded.

A message sent to a group is written once to the group's message store,
then handed to a fan-out step that looks up the group's current member
list and pushes a delivery to each member's connection gateway, the same
live-or-queued delivery mechanism as one-on-one messaging. For small and
medium groups this fan-out happens synchronously and immediately, since
the member count is small enough to be cheap. Groups above a size
threshold route through an async fan-out queue instead, so one large
group's delivery burst can't stall message sends for every other group
sharing the same gateway fleet. Read receipts follow member count too:
small groups track a receipt row per member, large groups collapse to a
single incrementing read counter.

```

| :--- | :--- |

| Only the largest groups need an async fan-out queue, not a different read strategy | Requires a genuinely different read-time merge strategy above a threshold |

#### Fan-out deliveries per message vs group size

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["Message read by member"] --> b{"Group size over threshold?"}

  b -->|"yes, large group"| d["Atomically increment read_count"]
```

| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/groups` | Body: { name, member_ids: [...] }. Creates a new group with an initial member list. |
| `POST` | `/api/groups/{groupId}/members` | Body: { user_id }. Adds a member to the group; delivery of future messages starts from this point, not retroactively. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `groups`
- `group_id`
- `name`
- `created_at`
- `member_count`
*Notes:* member_count is denormalized on the group row so the fan-out path can cheaply decide whether to use per-member receipts or an aggregate counter without a separate count query.

### Entity: `group_members`
- `group_id`
- `user_id`
- `joined_at`
*Notes:* joined_at is what scopes history visibility; a member's history query and the fan-out target list are both filtered by it.

### Entity: `group_messages`
- `message_id (time-sortable)`
- `group_id`
- `sender_id`
- `text`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Sharded by group_id so a group's full history lives together for fast range reads, the same reasoning as conversation-sharded one-on-one messages.

### Entity: `read_state`
- `group_id`
- `message_id`
- `reader_id (nullable for aggregate mode)`
- `read_count (used instead of reader_id for large groups)`
*Notes:* Small groups store one row per (message_id, reader_id) for exact per-member receipts; groups past a size threshold switch to a single incrementing read_count per message instead.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Why does group chat default to fan-out-on-write when Twitter needed a hybrid?
Twitter's fan-out audience is a follower graph that can range from zero to tens of millions, entirely open-ended and highly skewed, which is what forced fan-out-on-read for the largest accounts. A group's membership is capped (products typically enforce a max group size, commonly in the low thousands) and known exactly at send time, so even the worst case is bounded and small compared to a celebrity's follower count. That boundedness is why fan-out-on-write works as the default for essentially all group sizes, with only the largest groups needing an async queue rather than a fundamentally different read-time strategy.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Fan-out-on-write for all groups regardless of size: simplest mental model, but a synchronous fan-out to a 10,000-member group on the same code path as a 3-person group risks blocking the sender's request on a slow delivery burst
- **Sync fan-out** for small/medium groups, **async queued fan-out** for groups past a size threshold: keeps the common case (small groups, the vast majority) instant, while isolating large-group fan-out load so it can't stall the shared gateway fleet
- Fan-out-on-read for large groups (members pull recent messages on open instead of being pushed): avoids the burst write entirely, but group chat's expectation of near-real-time delivery to everyone makes this a worse fit than it is for a browsed timeline

### How do read receipts stay affordable for a 5,000-member group without either dropping the feature or writing 5,000 rows per message?
Per-member read receipts are genuinely useful in small groups (seeing exactly which 4 friends have seen a message) but provide diminishing value and linearly growing cost as membership grows into the thousands. The fix is a size-based split: below a threshold, track one row per (message, member); above it, collapse to a single incrementing counter updated atomically as members read, sacrificing the 'who exactly' detail that's rarely useful at that scale anyway.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Always per-member receipts: maximum fidelity, but ==storage and write volume scale with group size times message count==, becoming the single largest storage cost in the system for large communities
- Always aggregate count: cheap and bounded regardless of group size, but loses a feature (seeing who specifically has read) that users genuinely want in small, intimate groups
- Size-based threshold switch: matches cost to where the feature actually matters, at the cost of the product behaving slightly differently (and needing separate UI) above and below the threshold

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A small number of extremely large groups can dominate total fan-out volume; these need to route through a dedicated async queue so their delivery bursts don't add latency to the far more common small-group sends sharing the same infrastructure.
- group_members lookups happen on every single message send (to know who to fan out to); this table needs to be indexed by group_id and cached aggressively, since it's read far more often than it's written.
- Per-member read receipts for large groups, if not capped by the aggregate-counter threshold, become the single largest storage and write-throughput consumer in the whole system, growing as group_size times message_count.
- Removing a member from a large, active group must invalidate their pending fan-out and queued deliveries promptly, or a former member can keep receiving messages briefly after being removed.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Copying Twitter's full hybrid fan-out-on-read design wholesale, when group membership being bounded and known in advance makes fan-out-on-write sufficient for the vast majority of groups.
- ⚠️ ==Tracking per-member read receipts unconditionally==, letting storage and write cost scale linearly with group size times message count for even the largest communities.
- ⚠️ ==Forgetting to scope message history and fan-out by joined_at==, causing newly added members to see (or need delivery of) messages sent before they joined.
- ⚠️ Treating all groups as the same size for fan-out purposes, letting one very large group's delivery burst add latency to the far more common, much smaller groups sharing the same gateway fleet.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't group chat need Twitter's fan-out-on-read strategy for its largest groups?**

> **Model Answer:** Twitter's problem is an open-ended, unbounded audience where a single account can have tens of millions of followers with no ceiling. **Group membership is capped** by product design, so even the worst-case group is a known, bounded fan-out size. That's small enough to still fan out on write, just routed through an async queue instead of done synchronously, rather than needing a fundamentally different read-time merge strategy.

**Q: How would you redesign read receipts if a product wanted to support 100,000-member groups?**

> **Model Answer:** Per-member receipts at that scale are both prohibitively expensive and not particularly useful to a sender anyway. I'd switch to an aggregate read counter (and maybe a sampled 'seen by X and 40,000 others' style summary) for any group past a size threshold, and reserve exact per-member receipts for small groups where users actually care who specifically has seen a message.

lesson.content:
# Design an Email System (Gmail)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Gmail • Outlook` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Email is really two different systems duct-taped together: a federated, decades-old delivery protocol you don't control (**SMTP**, talking to every other mail server on earth) and a storage-and-search problem you fully control (one mailbox per user, at a scale where a single power user's history can hit millions of messages), and almost every hard decision here is about ==not letting the first system's unreliability leak into the second system's guarantees==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design an email system like Gmail: a user can compose and send an email to
any address on the internet (not just other users of your system), receive
email from any address on the internet, organize a mailbox of potentially
hundreds of thousands of messages, and search across their entire mail
history instantly. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we need to interoperate with the broader internet's email system (send to and receive from any external address), or is this a closed system where all users are on our own domain?
*Why it matters:* Interoperating with the real internet means implementing **SMTP** as both a sending and receiving party, dealing with other servers' queuing, retries, and rejections, an entirely different and much harder problem than a closed messaging app that owns both ends of every conversation.

#### Q: What's the expected mailbox size and retention? Are we designing for a mailbox that keeps everything forever, like Gmail's 'never delete' philosophy?
*Why it matters:* **Unlimited retention** turns storage from 'recent hot data' into a problem with a long tail of cold, rarely-accessed data spanning years, which changes the storage tier strategy and the cost model entirely.

#### Q: Does full-text search need to cover the entire mailbox instantly, including attachments, or just recent mail and subject lines?
*Why it matters:* Instant full-text search across a user's entire multi-year history requires a dedicated search index kept in sync with every mailbox mutation, which is a substantial subsystem on its own, not a side feature.

#### Q: How aggressive does spam and phishing filtering need to be, and can it introduce a small amount of delivery latency?
*Why it matters:* A spam pipeline that must complete before a message reaches the inbox adds a processing stage to the critical delivery path, and the accuracy-versus-latency trade-off there shapes whether filtering happens inline or asynchronously after initial delivery.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can compose and send an email to one or more recipients, on this system or any external domain.
- A user can receive email sent to their address from any sender, internal or external.
- A user can organize mail into folders/labels (inbox, sent, spam, trash, custom labels) and mark messages read, starred, or archived.
- A user can search their full mail history by sender, subject, body text, and attachment name, and get results in well under a second.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Delivery must be reliable: a message accepted for sending must eventually be delivered or the sender must be reliably notified of failure, never silently dropped.**

Design a push notification service that lets any client application (a
ride-sharing app, a social app, a news app) send a notification to a
specific user's phone or browser, even when that app isn't open. The

are offline, and avoid overwhelming a single user with too many
notifications at once. Design the system end to end.

#### Q: What happens when a device is offline: should the notification be dropped, retried, or queued until the device reconnects?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether the system needs any durable per-device queue at all versus a fire-and-forget model, and directly shapes the retry and TTL strategy for undeliverable notifications.

#### Q: Can a single user have multiple registered devices (phone, tablet, browser), and should a notification go to all of them or just the most recently active one?

- The system supports multiple devices per user and can deliver to some or all of them.
- The system handles offline devices by retrying delivery, with the platform gateway's own store-and-forward semantics, up to a bounded time-to-live.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Delivery latency should be low, typically under a few seconds from request to arrival at the device, for time-sensitive notifications.**
- **The system must scale to hundreds of millions of registered devices and tens of thousands of notification sends per second at peak.**
- **The system must gracefully handle a constantly churning set of device tokens (tokens expire, rotate, or become invalid when an app is uninstalled) without accumulating dead weight.**

### Assumptions:
- 500 million registered devices across iOS, Android, and web
- Average device receives 20 notifications/day, but distribution is heavily skewed by app category
- Each notification payload is small, roughly 1 KB including title, body, and data
- Peak traffic (e.g. a breaking news push to a large segment) can be 50x the average sustained rate for short bursts

- **Notifications sent per day:** 500,000,000 * 20 = 10 billion notifications/day ≈ 116,000 sends/sec average

app server writes a durable notification_request and enqueues it. A pool
of platform-specific dispatch workers (one pool per gateway: APNs, FCM, web

| Method | Endpoint | Description |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `device_tokens`
- `device_id (unique)`
- `user_id (indexed)`
- `platform (ios | android | web)`
- `token (opaque string issued by the platform gateway)`
- `last_seen_at / registered_at`

- `request_id`
- `target_user_id or target_device_id`
- `payload (title, body, data)`
- `status (queued, sent, delivered, failed)`

- `device_id`
- `gateway (apns | fcm | web_push)`
- `attempt_number / result / attempted_at`

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Fan-out to multiple devices per user: per-device queue items or a single job expanded at dispatch time?
