**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- **Eager expansion** (one queue item per device at enqueue time): dispatch workers are simple and stateless, but a large campaign fan-out (millions of users, several devices each) creates a huge burst of queue writes upfront, and a device registered/unregistered mid-flight can cause a stale send
- **Lazy expansion** (one queue item per user, expanded at dispatch time): queue writes stay proportional to requests, not devices, and device lookup happens right before sending so it reflects the freshest token list, at the cost of dispatch workers needing to do a device lookup on every job instead of a pure send
- For large campaigns specifically, lazy expansion is the better default since campaign volume is dominated by device count, not request count, and freshness of the token lookup matters more the longer a campaign takes to fully process

### How do you prevent notification storms and respect each platform gateway's own rate limits?
APNs and FCM both throttle senders, and a naive dispatch worker that blasts requests as fast as it can dequeue them will start getting throttled or, worse, temporarily blocked by the gateway. Each gateway's dispatch worker pool needs its own **token-bucket rate limiter** tuned below that gateway's published limits, and separately, the system should apply a per-user notification cap (e.g. no more than N notifications in a rolling window) so one chatty upstream client can't spam an individual user even if the gateway itself would accept the volume.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Rate limiting only at the gateway-pool level: protects the relationship with Apple/Google, but does nothing to stop one user being spammed by a single misbehaving upstream integration
- Rate limiting only per-user: protects the end-user experience, but a burst across many users can still trip the platform gateway's sender-level limits
- Both layers together: gateway-pool rate limiting protects infrastructure-level standing with each platform, per-user capping protects the individual experience; running only one leaves the other failure mode uncovered

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Each platform gateway enforces its own rate limits per sender identity, so the dispatch worker pools must scale and rate-limit independently per gateway, a burst on iOS traffic should never starve or slow down Android/web dispatch.
- Device token churn (rotation, app uninstalls, token expiry) means a naive 'send and assume delivered' model accumulates dead tokens over time; gateways report invalid tokens back on send attempts, and that feedback loop must prune device_tokens or retries silently waste capacity sending into the void.
- Large campaign fan-outs (millions of users at once) can dominate the queue and starve smaller, latency-sensitive individual sends (like a chat message notification); separating campaign traffic and individual sends into distinct queues with different priority lets latency-sensitive sends skip the line.
- The device_tokens lookup, hit on every single dispatch, needs to be a fast key-value store sharded by user_id, a relational table with a full table scan pattern will not keep up at hundreds of thousands of sends per second.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing a single generic 'send to device' path that ignores that iOS, Android, and web each require talking to a completely different gateway with different protocols and rate limits.
- ⚠️ ==Treating gateway acceptance of a send as proof of on-device delivery==, when most gateways only confirm they've accepted responsibility for delivery, not that the device actually received it.
- ⚠️ Not rate-limiting per gateway, leading to a sender being throttled or temporarily blocked by Apple or Google during a traffic spike.
- ⚠️ Expanding a large campaign into millions of individual queue items eagerly at request time instead of lazily at dispatch time, causing a massive write burst and stale device lookups for a campaign that takes minutes to fully process.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't this system guarantee real-time delivery the way a chat message between two logged-in users can?**

> **Model Answer:** Because delivery to the actual device is delegated to a platform-owned gateway that has its own connection model, retry policy, and offline handling that this system doesn't control; the service's own guarantee stops at 'successfully handed off to the gateway,' and treating gateway acceptance as equivalent to confirmed on-device delivery is a design mistake, not just an implementation detail.

**Q: How would you handle a single upstream client accidentally sending the same notification a thousand times in a loop due to a bug?**

> **Model Answer:** A per-user (or per-user-per-notification-type) rate limit or dedup window catches this before it reaches the device, for example rejecting or coalescing requests with identical payload and target within a short time window, combined with per-upstream-client quotas so a buggy integration is throttled at the source rather than only at the final gateway hop.

# Design a Live Chat Support System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Intercom • Zendesk Chat` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The hard part isn't sending chat messages, it's the **routing layer** sitting in front of them: deciding which of possibly many available agents (with different skills, languages, and current loads) should get this specific incoming chat, and doing it fast enough that a visitor doesn't sit staring at 'connecting you to an agent' for a noticeable amount of time.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a live chat support system like Intercom: a visitor on a website
opens a chat widget and is connected to either a bot or a human support
agent. The system must route incoming chats to an available agent (or a
queue if none are free), support handoff from bot to human mid-conversation
without losing context, and let whichever agent picks up a chat see the
full history and any context gathered so far. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Should routing be purely 'first available agent' or skill-based, matching a chat to an agent who speaks the visitor's language or handles a specific product area?
*Why it matters:* Pure round-robin to any available agent is a much simpler matching problem than skill-based routing, which needs agents tagged with capabilities and a matching/scoring step before assignment, and changes what 'available' even means (available for this specific chat, not just available in general).

#### Q: Can a chat start with a bot and hand off to a human, and if so, does the human need the full bot conversation history and any structured data the bot collected?
*Why it matters:* If handoff needs to preserve context, the conversation and any bot-collected metadata (like 'order number: 1234') must live in **one continuous record** from the start, not two disconnected systems, which affects the core data model, not just the routing logic.

#### Q: What should happen to an incoming chat when every matching agent is currently busy: queue it, offer a callback, or route to a lower-priority agent?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether the system needs a durable, ordered per-skill-group queue with wait-time estimation, which is a real subsystem, versus a simpler design that always finds someone, even at the cost of an imperfect skill match.

#### Q: How many concurrent chats can a single agent realistically handle, one at a time or several in parallel?
*Why it matters:* If agents handle multiple chats concurrently (common in real support tools), 'agent availability' becomes a capacity threshold rather than a boolean, which changes the routing algorithm from simple assignment to load-aware assignment.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A visitor can open a chat widget and start a conversation, which is routed to a bot, then optionally handed off to a human agent.
- The system routes an incoming chat to an available agent, considering skill/language match and current agent load, or queues it if no agent is available.
- Whichever agent (bot or human) picks up a conversation can see its full message history and any context/metadata collected so far.
- An agent can see their queue of assigned and waiting conversations and respond to messages in real time.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Message delivery within an active chat must feel real-time, well under a second of perceived delay.**
- **Routing an incoming chat to an agent (or into a queue) must happen quickly, within a couple seconds, since a visitor deciding whether to wait is happening in that window.**
- **The system must remain available and continue routing chats even if a subset of agent-facing app servers fail, no visitor should be stuck with an unroutable chat.**
- **Conversation history and context must never be lost across a bot-to-human handoff or an agent-to-agent transfer.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10,000 businesses using the platform, average 50 concurrent chats per business at peak across all of them combined ≈ 500,000 concurrent chats platform-wide at peak
- Average conversation has 20 messages exchanged over 10 minutes
- Each message is small, roughly 500 bytes including sender metadata
- 10% of chats require bot-to-human handoff; average wait time in queue when no agent is available is 90 seconds

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Peak concurrent chats:** 500,000 concurrent conversations, each needing an open real-time connection (WebSocket) held by the visitor and, if assigned, the agent
- **Message throughput at peak:** 500,000 chats * (20 messages / 600 seconds) ≈ 16,700 messages/sec at peak across the platform
- **Routing decisions per second:** New chats arriving: assuming average chat duration 10 min, 500,000 concurrent / 600 sec ≈ 833 new chats/sec needing a routing decision, each of which must complete in low seconds
- **Daily message storage:** 833 new chats/sec * 86,400 sec/day * 20 messages * 500 bytes ≈ 833*86,400 ≈ 72 million chats/day * 20 * 500 bytes ≈ 720 GB/day, easily handled by a sharded store

*Capacity Takeaway:* The system is bottlenecked by two very different things at once: real-time message fan-out to hundreds of thousands of concurrently open connections, and a routing decision that has to run for every one of the roughly 800+ new chats arriving per second, which is why the architecture splits cleanly into a **messaging/connection layer** and a separate **routing/queueing layer** rather than one monolithic chat server.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A visitor's message goes to a bot service by default, over a persistent
WebSocket connection held by a real-time messaging layer. When a bot
can't help (or a visitor explicitly asks for a human), a handoff request
goes to a routing service, which evaluates currently available agents
against required skills and current load, and either assigns the
conversation to an agent directly (pushing it into their live queue over
the same WebSocket layer) or, if none qualify, places it into a durable
per-skill-group priority queue until an agent frees up. All messages,
regardless of bot or human sender, are appended to one shared conversation
history, so whichever party picks up the chat next reads the same
continuous record.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Routing service assigns chats between bot, queue, and agents

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    visitor["Visitor (Widget)"]:::client
    gateway["Realtime Gateway (WS)"]:::server
    bot["Bot Service"]:::server
    router["Routing Service"]:::server
    agentstatus["Agent Status Store"]:::cache
    waitqueue>"Wait Queue"]:::queue
    agent["Agent Client"]:::client
    convodb[("Conversation Store")]:::db
    visitor --> gateway
    gateway -->|"default routing"| bot
    bot -->|"append message"| convodb
    bot -.->|"handoff request"| router
    router -->|"check availability"| agentstatus
    router -.->|"no match yet"| waitqueue
    router -->|"assign to agent"| gateway
    gateway --> agent
    agent -->|"read history + append"| convodb
```

#### A chat, from visitor message to human agent pickup

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Visitor sends first message (over WebSocket)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Bot service handles conversation (appended to shared conversation record)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Bot triggers handoff request (can't resolve, or visitor asks for human)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Routing service scores available agents (skills + current load)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Match found: assign, or none: enter wait queue (queue is durable, ordered)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Agent picks up, reads full shared history (including bot-collected context)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### Skill matching with graceful degradation

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["Chat needs handoff"] --> b{"Skill-matched agent free?"}
  b -->|"yes"| c["Assign to matched agent"]
  b -->|"no"| d["Enter wait queue"]
  d --> e{"Waited over 60s?"}
  e -->|"no"| d
  e -->|"yes"| f["Widen pool, assign best available"]
```

#### Queue depth during a support traffic spike

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/conversations` | Body: { visitor_id, initial_message, metadata? }. Starts a new conversation, routes it to a bot by default. |
| `POST` | `/api/conversations/{conversationId}/messages` | Body: { sender_type (visitor|bot|agent), text }. Appends a message to an active conversation and pushes it to connected participants. |
| `POST` | `/api/conversations/{conversationId}/handoff` | Body: { required_skills?, reason }. Requests routing of the conversation from bot to a human agent, entering the routing/queue system. |
| `PUT` | `/api/agents/{agentId}/status` | Body: { status (available|busy|away), skills? }. Updates an agent's availability and skill tags, used by the router to compute eligible agents. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `conversations`
- `conversation_id`
- `visitor_id / assigned_agent_id (nullable)`
- `status (bot_handling, queued, assigned, closed)`
- `required_skills (list, nullable)`
- `created_at / last_message_at`
*Notes:* One continuous record spans the entire lifecycle including bot handling and any handoff, so context is never split across separate bot and human systems.

### Entity: `messages`
- `message_id`
- `conversation_id (indexed)`
- `sender_type / sender_id`
- `text / structured_data (nullable, e.g. bot-collected fields)`
- `sent_at`
*Notes:* Includes bot-collected structured data (like an order number extracted during the bot phase) inline in the same timeline a human agent reads, so handoff context isn't a separate lookup.

### Entity: `agents`
- `agent_id`
- `status (available | busy | away)`
- `skills (list, e.g. languages, product areas)`
- `current_chat_count / max_concurrent_chats`
*Notes:* current_chat_count and max_concurrent_chats together define real-time capacity, not just a boolean available flag, which is what the router actually reads.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Skill-based routing: match strictly or degrade gracefully under load?
A router that only ever assigns a chat to an agent with a perfect skill match (right language, right product area) is simple to reason about but can leave a visitor waiting a long time if the only matching agents are all busy while less-perfectly-matched agents sit idle. The alternative is a scored match: rank available agents by how well they fit, and after a wait threshold, relax the requirement and assign to the best available agent even if imperfect.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Strict matching only: guarantees every assigned agent is fully qualified, but can ==strand visitors in queue== during uneven load even when other agents are free, hurting wait-time SLAs
- Scored matching with graceful degradation after a wait threshold: keeps wait times bounded by trading off match quality only when necessary, but adds real complexity (scoring function, threshold tuning) and risk of misrouting a chat too eagerly if the threshold is set too low
- The practical answer: strict matching as the default, with a time-boxed escalation (e.g. after 60 seconds unmatched, widen the eligible agent pool), giving most chats a good match while bounding worst-case wait time

### How does an agent (or the next bot turn) get full context instantly on pickup, including anything the bot already learned?
Because bot and human messages live in **one shared conversation timeline** (not two separate systems bridged at handoff time), 'get context' is just 'load the conversation's message history and structured_data fields,' the same read path regardless of whether the previous turn was a bot or a person. The alternative, where bot conversations live in a separate transcript system that gets summarized and attached at handoff, avoids one shared schema but introduces a lossy translation step exactly at the moment context matters most.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Unified conversation record from the start: handoff is a status change, not a data migration; the receiving agent's UI just renders the same timeline; nothing to lose in translation
- Separate bot transcript summarized at handoff: keeps the bot system decoupled and independently deployable, but risks losing detail in the summarization step at precisely the moment a human needs full fidelity
- Unified record is the stronger choice specifically because handoff fidelity is a functional requirement here, not just an implementation preference; the coupling cost is worth paying for the guarantee

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The real-time messaging layer (WebSocket connections) needs to scale horizontally across many connection-handling servers, with a pub/sub layer (like Redis pub/sub or a message broker) routing a message to whichever server currently holds the recipient's connection, since sender and recipient are rarely on the same server.
- The routing decision itself, run on every new chat and every handoff, must read fresh agent availability; a stale or slow agent-status read causes ==double-assignment== (two chats routed to an agent who just went busy), so agent status needs to be a fast, low-latency store (in-memory, not a general-purpose relational table) with **atomic claim semantics**.
- The per-skill-group wait queue can grow long during traffic spikes (e.g. an outage causing a support surge); the queue needs to be durable (survives a router restart) and support estimated-wait-time computation so the widget can show the visitor something better than silence.
- Conversation history storage grows linearly with chat volume and needs to be partitioned by conversation_id or business_id so one large business's chat volume doesn't degrade lookup performance for everyone else on the platform.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing routing as simple round-robin or first-available without considering that under real load, strict skill matching can strand visitors in queue while mismatched agents sit idle.
- ⚠️ ==Building the bot conversation and the human agent conversation as two separate systems== bridged only by a summary at handoff time, losing fidelity exactly when a human needs full context.
- ⚠️ ==Treating agent availability as a boolean flag== instead of a load threshold, causing over-assignment once agents are expected to handle multiple concurrent chats.
- ⚠️ Not making the wait queue durable, so a routing service restart during a traffic spike silently drops visitors who were waiting.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is it important that agent availability be read from a fast, low-latency store with atomic claim semantics rather than a general relational table?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the routing decision happens on every new chat and handoff, and a slow or non-atomic read-then-write on agent status creates a **race window** where two chats can both be assigned to the same agent right as they go from available to busy; an atomic claim (e.g. compare-and-swap on current_chat_count against max_concurrent_chats) in a fast in-memory store closes that race, which a slower or non-atomic relational update would not reliably do under concurrent routing requests.

**Q: What's the trade-off in relaxing skill-matching requirements after a wait threshold instead of always requiring a perfect match?**

> **Model Answer:** Always requiring a perfect match guarantees every agent assignment is fully qualified but can leave a visitor waiting a long time if the only matching agents are busy while other, less-matched agents are idle, hurting wait-time SLAs and visitor experience. Relaxing the requirement after a bounded wait trades a small amount of match quality for a bounded worst-case wait time, which is usually the better trade-off since an imperfectly matched but fast human response beats a perfectly matched but very slow one for most support scenarios.

- Conversation history storage grows linearly with chat volume and needs to be partitioned by conversation_id or business_id so one large business's chat volume doesn't degrade lookup performance for everyone else on the platform.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing routing as simple round-robin or first-available without considering that under real load, strict skill matching can strand visitors in queue while mismatched agents sit idle.
- ⚠️ ==Building the bot conversation and the human agent conversation as two separate systems== bridged only by a summary at handoff time, losing fidelity exactly when a human needs full context.
- ⚠️ ==Treating agent availability as a boolean flag== instead of a load threshold, causing over-assignment once agents are expected to handle multiple concurrent chats.
- ⚠️ Not making the wait queue durable, so a routing service restart during a traffic spike silently drops visitors who were waiting.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is it important that agent availability be read from a fast, low-latency store with atomic claim semantics rather than a general relational table?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the routing decision happens on every new chat and handoff, and a slow or non-atomic read-then-write on agent status creates a **race window** where two chats can both be assigned to the same agent right as they go from available to busy; an atomic claim (e.g. compare-and-swap on current_chat_count against max_concurrent_chats) in a fast in-memory store closes that race, which a slower or non-atomic relational update would not reliably do under concurrent routing requests.

**Q: What's the trade-off in relaxing skill-matching requirements after a wait threshold instead of always requiring a perfect match?**

> **Model Answer:** Always requiring a perfect match guarantees every agent assignment is fully qualified but can leave a visitor waiting a long time if the only matching agents are busy while other, less-matched agents are idle, hurting wait-time SLAs and visitor experience. callout.title: Core Architectural Principle
callout.text: The hard part isn't sending chat messages, it's the **routing layer** sitting in front of them: deciding which of possibly many available agents (with different skills, languages, and current loads) should get this specific incoming chat, and doing it fast enough that a visitor doesn't sit staring at 'connecting you to an agent' for a noticeable amount of time.

# Design Discord

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Discord` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Discord is really two different real-time systems wearing one UI: **durable, ordered text messaging** per channel, and ==lossy, latency-obsessed voice transport== per channel, and the entire architecture is about keeping those two very different delivery models from being forced through the same pipe.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a system like Discord: users organize into servers (communities),
each server contains multiple text and voice channels, members can send
persistent text messages per channel and join low-latency live voice
calls per channel, and servers have a role-based permission system
controlling who can do what. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Are text and voice genuinely separate subsystems, or does the design need to unify them into a single message/event pipeline?
*Why it matters:* Text needs **durability, ordering, and history**; voice needs ==sub-100ms latency== and can drop packets without anyone caring. Forcing both through one delivery mechanism optimizes for neither, so this decision shapes the entire system split.

#### Q: How large do servers and channels get: is this closer to a few hundred members, or communities with hundreds of thousands?
*Why it matters:* A 200-person server and a 500,000-member server need very different text fan-out and voice-routing strategies. This decides whether we can treat 'channel' as a small bounded audience or need the same large-group handling as a group chat system.

#### Q: For voice, are we relaying audio through our own servers, or can clients connect peer-to-peer for small calls?
*Why it matters:* Peer-to-peer works for a handful of participants but doesn't scale past a small group and has no server-side moderation hook. A server-relayed model (SFU) is what makes large voice channels, recording, and moderation possible at all, at the cost of running real-time media infrastructure.

#### Q: How granular does the permission system need to be: per-server roles only, or per-channel overrides on top of roles?
*Why it matters:* Per-channel overrides on top of server-wide roles is a materially more complex authorization model (effective permission = role permissions merged with channel-specific overrides) than a flat per-server role, and it needs to be checked on every single message send and channel join.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create a server, and the server can contain multiple text channels and voice channels.
- A member can send a text message in a channel, visible to all members with access to that channel, with persistent history.
- A member can join a voice channel and talk with other members in that same channel in near real time.
- Server owners can define roles with specific permissions (send messages, join voice, manage channels) and assign them to members, with optional per-channel overrides.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Voice audio must have very low, consistent latency (well under 150ms end to end) since gaming and live conversation are unusable otherwise.**
- **Text messages must never be lost or silently reordered within a channel, even if delivered a moment late.**
- **Permission checks must be fast enough to run on every message send and channel action without adding noticeable latency.**
- **The system must isolate a large, extremely active server (a viral community) from degrading performance for every other server sharing the same infrastructure.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 150 million monthly active users; 5 million concurrent voice participants at peak across all servers
- Average server has 50 members and 8 text channels; average text channel gets 500 messages/day
- Voice audio is Opus-encoded at roughly 32 kbps per participant stream
- Average voice call has 4 concurrent speakers per channel at any instant

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Text messages per day and per second:** Assume 10 million active servers * 8 channels * 500 messages/day = 40 billion messages/day ≈ 463,000 messages/sec average, several times that at peak, in the same ballpark as a large-scale group chat system
- **Voice bandwidth per participant (SFU model, receiving N-1 streams):** In a 4-person active voice channel, each client downloads 3 other streams * 32 kbps = 96 kbps down, while uploading 1 stream at 32 kbps, i.e. the server (not the client) bears the N-way fan-out cost
- **Total SFU relay bandwidth at peak concurrency:** 5,000,000 concurrent voice participants * roughly 32 kbps upload received by the SFU = 160 Gbps of inbound audio alone, before the SFU re-distributes it back out to listeners, which roughly doubles again in aggregate egress
- **Voice server (SFU instance) capacity:** A single SFU box handles roughly a few thousand concurrent streams before CPU/bandwidth limits; 5,000,000 / 3,000 ≈ 1,700 SFU instances needed at peak, geographically distributed to keep round-trip latency low

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving fact is that voice bandwidth and text message volume are two independent scaling problems with different bottlenecks (voice is bounded by **real-time relay bandwidth** and geographic latency, text is bounded by message throughput and storage), which is exactly why the architecture treats them as two separate backend systems rather than one unified pipeline.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Text and voice run as two independent backend paths that only share the
server/channel/permission data model. Text messages flow through a
gateway that checks the sender's effective permission (role bitfield
merged with channel overrides), writes to a channel-sharded message
store, and pushes to the small set of currently-connected members of that
channel, essentially a bounded group chat fan-out. Voice works
differently: joining a voice channel routes the client to a
geographically nearby **SFU** (selective forwarding unit) instance, which
receives each speaker's audio stream once and forwards it to every other
participant, so N participants cost the SFU roughly N inbound and
N*(N-1) outbound relayed streams rather than requiring every client to
connect to every other client directly. Permission checks and channel
membership are the only things both paths depend on.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Two independent paths sharing one permission model

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    gw["Text Gateway"]:::server
    sfu["Voice SFU"]:::server
    permcache["Permission Cache"]:::cache
    msgdb[("Messages Store")]:::db
    serverdb[("Servers/Roles Store")]:::db
    voicereg["Voice Session Registry"]:::cache
    client -->|"send message"| gw
    client -->|"voice stream"| sfu
    gw -->|"check permission"| permcache
    sfu -->|"check permission"| permcache
    permcache -.->|"refresh on miss"| serverdb
    gw -->|"store message"| msgdb
    sfu -->|"register session"| voicereg
```

#### Text channel delivery vs voice channel delivery

| Text | Voice |
| :--- | :--- |
| Durable, ordered, stored history | Lossy, best-effort, no history requirement |
| Tolerates a moment of delay | Cannot tolerate more than ~150ms latency |
| Delivered via gateway fan-out, group-chat-shaped | Delivered via SFU relay, media-transport-shaped |

#### SFU outbound relay streams grow quadratically with speakers

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/servers/{serverId}/channels` | Body: { name, type: 'text' | 'voice' }. Creates a new channel in a server, subject to the creator's permissions. |
| `POST` | `/api/channels/{channelId}/messages` | Body: { text }. Sends a text message to a channel; server checks the sender's effective permission (role plus channel overrides) before accepting. |
| `GET` | `/api/channels/{channelId}/messages` | Returns paginated message history for a text channel, newest first. |
| `WS` | `wss://voice/{channelId}/join` | Establishes a real-time media connection to the voice channel's assigned SFU instance; the server first checks voice-join permission, then returns SFU connection details. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `servers`
- `server_id`
- `owner_id`
- `name`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* The top-level community container; roles and channels both belong to a server.

### Entity: `channels`
- `channel_id`
- `server_id`
- `type (text | voice)`
- `name`
- `permission_overrides (per-role overrides scoped to this channel)`
*Notes:* A channel's effective permissions are the server role's base permissions merged with any channel-specific overrides, computed at check time, not pre-materialized.

### Entity: `messages`
- `message_id (time-sortable)`
- `channel_id`
- `author_id`
- `text`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Sharded by channel_id, same reasoning as group chat: a channel's full history should live together for fast range reads.

### Entity: `roles_and_members`
- `server_id`
- `user_id`
- `role_ids (assigned roles)`
- `role permissions (bitfield of allowed actions per role)`
*Notes:* Permissions are stored as a bitfield per role for a fast bitwise check on every action, rather than a database join on every message send.

### Entity: `voice_sessions`
- `channel_id`
- `user_id`
- `sfu_instance_id`
- `joined_at`
*Notes:* Ephemeral, in-memory routing state, same shape as the connection registry in a messaging system: which SFU instance currently holds this user's live audio stream.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Why relay voice through a server (SFU) instead of connecting participants directly (mesh)?
A full mesh, where every participant sends their audio directly to every other participant, requires each client to upload N-1 separate streams, which falls apart past a handful of people (an 8-person call would need each client uploading 7 simultaneous streams). An SFU (selective forwarding unit) has each client upload just one stream to the server, which then forwards it to everyone else, moving the N-way fan-out cost off constrained client uplinks and onto server infrastructure built for it, and giving the server a place to apply moderation, recording, or bandwidth-adaptive forwarding.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Peer-to-peer mesh: lowest possible latency (no relay hop) and zero server bandwidth cost, but upload bandwidth per client scales with participant count, making it unusable past roughly 4-6 people, and offers no server-side moderation hook
- SFU (selective forwarding, server relays without decoding): each client uploads once regardless of channel size, server bears the relay bandwidth cost, and this is what makes large voice channels and moderation features possible at all
- MCU (server decodes and mixes all streams into one combined stream per listener): minimizes client download bandwidth further since each listener gets one mixed stream instead of N separate ones, but costs significant server-side CPU to decode and re-encode audio for every participant, a cost SFU avoids by only forwarding, not transcoding

### How do per-channel permission overrides interact with server-wide roles without a database join on every message?
A member's effective permission in a specific channel is computed by starting from their role's base permission bitfield (say, 'can send messages' is bit 3) and then applying that channel's specific overrides (which might deny bit 3 for a particular role in a specific announcements channel), producing a final allow/deny per action. Storing permissions as bitfields lets this merge happen as a couple of fast bitwise operations in the gateway process, entirely in memory, rather than a database round trip on every single message send.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Bitfield roles with in-memory channel override merge: extremely fast per-action check (no database hit on the hot path), but requires roles and overrides to be cached and invalidated correctly whenever a permission changes, or a stale cache briefly grants access that was just revoked
- Database join computing effective permission on every action: always reflects the latest permission state with no cache invalidation risk, but adds a database round trip to the highest-frequency operation in the whole system (every message send), which doesn't scale
- Pre-materializing effective permissions per (user, channel) pair on every role/override change: keeps the hot path cache-only like the bitfield approach, but multiplies write amplification on every permission change, since one role edit can touch effective-permission rows for every member and every channel that role applies to

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- SFU instances need geographic distribution, since voice latency is dominated by round-trip network distance; a user routed to a far-away SFU will have noticeably worse call quality regardless of how well the SFU itself scales.
- A viral, extremely active server (tens of thousands of members) puts unusual load on both text fan-out (many concurrently connected members per channel) and permission checks (large role/member tables); this server needs to be isolated or the shared gateway fleet degrades for smaller, unrelated servers.
- Voice channel capacity is bounded per SFU instance by both CPU (packet forwarding) and bandwidth (N*(N-1) relayed streams growing quadratically with participants); very large voice channels need either a participant cap or a cascaded multi-SFU relay topology.
- Permission cache invalidation across a distributed gateway fleet must be fast and reliable, since a stale cached permission can incorrectly grant or deny access after a role change, and role changes happen far less often than message sends but must never be silently ignored.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing one unified message pipeline for both text and voice, when their durability, ordering, and latency requirements are different enough to need separate systems entirely.
- ⚠️ Proposing a peer-to-peer mesh for voice without a participant cap, not realizing per-client upload bandwidth scales with participant count and becomes unusable well before typical voice channel sizes.
- ⚠️ Computing effective permissions with a database join on the message-send hot path, adding a round trip to the single highest-frequency operation in the system.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that a role change needs to invalidate cached permissions across every gateway instance, or a revoked permission stays effectively granted until caches happen to expire.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't voice channels use the same fan-out mechanism as text channels?**

> **Model Answer:** Text fan-out tolerates a small delay and needs durable, ordered delivery, which fits a queue-and-push model well. Voice needs sub-150ms round-trip latency and has no durability requirement at all, dropped packets are simply lost audio, not a bug. Routing voice through the same durable, queued pipeline as text would add latency voice can't tolerate, so it needs its own real-time media relay (SFU) infrastructure instead.

**Q: How would you scale voice channels to support significantly larger participant counts, like a 500-person community voice channel?**

> **Model Answer:** A single SFU's relay cost grows roughly with N participants for upload and N*(N-1) for the total forwarded output, so past some size a single instance can't keep up. Options include cascading multiple SFUs (each handling a subset of participants and relaying a summarized stream between SFU instances), or, more commonly for very large voice audiences, switching listen-only participants to a much cheaper one-way broadcast model rather than full bidirectional relay for everyone.

lesson.content:
# Design a Real-Time Collaborative Cursor/Presence System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Figma • Google Docs` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A chat message that arrives late or slightly out of order is a bug; a cursor position that arrives late or gets dropped is invisible a fraction of a second later anyway, and that single difference is what lets this system trade away every ==durability guarantee== a messaging system treats as non-negotiable in exchange for **raw speed**.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design the system behind the colored cursors and name labels you see
moving around live in tools like Figma or Google Docs: every user viewing
the same document sees every other viewer's live cursor position, updated
many times per second, with minimal visible lag. Design the system end
to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Does a dropped or out-of-order cursor update need to be retried or corrected, or can it simply be superseded by the next one?
*Why it matters:* If the answer is 'just superseded,' the system can use **unreliable, unordered, fire-and-forget delivery**, which is dramatically cheaper and lower-latency than anything with retries or ordering guarantees. This single answer determines the entire transport choice.

#### Q: How many simultaneous collaborators does a single document or room need to support?
*Why it matters:* Broadcasting every cursor move to every other viewer is an **N-to-N fan-out** within the room; a 5-person document and a 500-person live workshop board need very different fan-out strategies, the same way group size drove the fan-out design in a group chat system.

#### Q: Do cursor updates need to be persisted anywhere, or do they only matter for the instant they're displayed?
*Why it matters:* If nobody needs cursor history after the fact, the system needs ==zero durable storage== for this data at all, only a live in-memory broadcast path, which is a fundamentally simpler and cheaper design than anything storing state.

#### Q: Is this purely cursor position, or does it also need to broadcast selections, live edits, and other presence signals through the same channel?
*Why it matters:* Live document edits (the actual content changes) typically need a real **conflict-resolution protocol like OT or CRDTs**, a much heavier guarantee than cursor position. Scoping this to cursor and presence broadcast only keeps the interview focused on the fan-out and freshness problem rather than merging into full collaborative editing.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Every user viewing a document sees a live, moving cursor for every other user currently viewing that same document.
- Each cursor is labeled with the viewer's name or a distinguishing color.
- A cursor disappears promptly when that user closes the document or loses connection.
- Cursor updates feel smooth and immediate, not choppy or laggy, even with several concurrent collaborators.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **End-to-end latency for a cursor update should be **well under 100ms** so movement feels live rather than delayed.**
- **The system must tolerate dropped or out-of-order updates gracefully, since a stale cursor position is meaningless the moment a newer one exists.**
- **Bandwidth and server cost must stay low even at high update rates (many updates per second per user), since this data has no long-term value once displayed.**
- **The system must scale **fan-out within a single room** to at least a few hundred concurrent viewers without degrading update latency for everyone in that room.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 million documents open concurrently at peak; average of 3 concurrent viewers per open document, with some documents (workshops, large reviews) having up to 200
- An actively-moving client sends a cursor update roughly 20 times per second, but only a fraction of open viewers are moving their mouse at any instant, say 20% at once
- Each cursor update payload is tiny, roughly 40 bytes (x, y, user_id, color reference)
- The server does not persist any cursor data, only relays it live, so there is no storage growth over time

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Concurrent open documents needing an active broadcast room:** 10,000,000 documents, each an independent fan-out scope; a cursor update from one document's room never needs to reach any other room
- **Inbound update rate across all documents:** 10,000,000 documents * 3 viewers avg * 20% actively moving * 20 updates/sec = 12 million inbound updates/sec system-wide
- **Outbound fan-out rate for an average 3-viewer document:** 1 update from 1 mover is relayed to 2 other viewers = 2 outbound sends per inbound update, roughly doubling the average document's traffic, a small, cheap multiplier at this room size
- **Outbound fan-out rate for a 200-viewer workshop document:** 1 update from 1 mover is relayed to 199 other viewers = 199 outbound sends per inbound update, a ~100x larger fan-out multiplier than the average document, purely from room size

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving fact is that this system is **bandwidth-and-fan-out bound**, not storage bound: 12 million tiny, disposable updates per second with zero persistence needed is only affordable because nothing here is written to disk, and the fan-out multiplier per update scales directly with how many viewers share a room, which is why large rooms (not total document count) are the real scaling risk.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Each open document maps to a lightweight, **ephemeral broadcast room** held
entirely in memory on one gateway instance (or a small shard of
instances for very large rooms). A client sends cursor position updates
over an open WebSocket using fire-and-forget, unordered, unacknowledged
delivery: no retry, no queue, no durable write. The gateway holding that
room simply overwrites the sender's last-known position in an in-memory
map and immediately broadcasts the new position to every other connected
member of the same room. If an update is dropped, nothing recovers it,
the next update a fraction of a second later simply supersedes it. When
a client disconnects, the gateway removes their entry and broadcasts a
"cursor left" event, and the room itself is discarded once its last
member leaves.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Ephemeral room broadcast, no durable writes

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    clienta["Client A (moving)"]:::client
    clientb["Client B (viewing)"]:::client
    gw["Room Gateway"]:::server
    roomstate["In-memory Room State"]:::cache
    registry["Room Membership Registry"]:::cache
    clienta -->|"cursor update (fire-and-forget)"| gw
    gw -->|"overwrite last position"| roomstate
    gw -.->|"broadcast (batched tick)"| clientb
    gw -->|"track room membership"| registry
```

#### A cursor update travels from mouse move to another viewer's screen

#### Outbound fan-out grows linearly with room size

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `WS` | `wss://rooms/{documentId}/connect` | Joins the live broadcast room for a document; the server assigns the client a color/identity and immediately sends the current set of active cursors in that room. |
| `WS` | `wss://rooms/{documentId}/cursor` | **Fire-and-forget** message sent over the open socket with the client's latest { x, y } position; no acknowledgment is sent back, and only the most recent position per user matters. |
| `GET` | `/api/rooms/{documentId}/active` | Fallback HTTP snapshot of who's currently active in the room (used for initial paint before the socket finishes connecting, or for clients that don't need live cursors, only a viewer count). |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `active_room_state`
- `document_id (key)`
- `user_id`
- `x, y (last known position)`
- `color`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* Entirely **in-memory**, held only for the lifetime of the room being active; never written to durable storage, since a cursor position has no value once superseded or once the last viewer leaves.

### Entity: `room_membership`
- `document_id (key)`
- `user_id`
- `gateway_id`
- `connected_at`
*Notes:* Tracks which broadcast gateway instance holds a given room's connections, so the room can be torn down cleanly the moment the last member disconnects.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Why is unreliable, unordered, fire-and-forget delivery the right choice here when it would be unacceptable for chat messages?
A chat message is meaningful forever: losing one is a permanent, visible gap in the conversation, so messaging systems pay for durability, retries, and strict ordering. A cursor position's value ==decays to zero== within a fraction of a second, since a newer position immediately supersedes it. Retrying a dropped cursor update after the fact would deliver a position that's already stale and wrong, actively worse than just letting it be superseded by whatever the next update says. This is the core reason the transport can drop the guarantees a messaging system treats as load-bearing.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Reliable, ordered delivery (like a message queue with acks and retries): guarantees every update arrives, but adds latency and complexity for data that's obsolete within milliseconds of being generated, actively counterproductive here
- Unreliable, unordered, fire-and-forget (e.g. plain WebSocket sends, or UDP-based transport where available): lowest possible latency and server overhead, occasional dropped or reordered updates are invisible since only the latest position ever matters
- Client-side interpolation/extrapolation on top of unreliable delivery: smooths out visible jumps from dropped updates by estimating motion between the last two known points, adding a little client complexity in exchange for the appearance of smoothness even under real-world packet loss

### How do you keep a 200-person room's fan-out from overwhelming the gateway or flooding every client's bandwidth?
Naively broadcasting every single cursor update at full frequency to every other member scales as roughly **(active movers) times (room size)**, which grows fast for large rooms. Two levers bring this down: throttling how often a client sends updates (e.g. capping to 10-20/sec regardless of raw mouse event rate) and batching/coalescing outbound broadcasts per room on a fixed tick (e.g. broadcast the latest known state of all movers every 50ms as one batched message, rather than relaying each individual update immediately as it arrives).

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Broadcast every update immediately, unbatched: lowest possible per-update latency, but fan-out volume scales directly with both room size and per-user update frequency, becoming expensive fast in large rooms
- Client-side send throttling only: reduces the inbound update rate cleanly, but doesn't address outbound fan-out multiplying by room size for large rooms
- Server-side batched broadcast ticks (coalesce all changes in a room into one message every fixed interval): caps outbound message count regardless of how many individual cursors moved, trading a small, usually imperceptible fixed delay (the tick interval) for a large reduction in total messages sent, especially valuable in large rooms

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single very large room (a workshop with hundreds of live viewers) can ==flood== one gateway instance with fan-out traffic; large rooms may need to be sharded across multiple gateway instances with a lightweight relay between them, rather than assuming one room always fits on one machine.
- Because no cursor state is durably persisted, a gateway instance crashing simply drops that room's live state entirely; clients reconnect, rejoin the room, and rebuild presence from scratch, which is acceptable precisely because none of this data had lasting value to begin with.
- Update frequency per client must be **capped server-side** (not just trusted client-side), or a single misbehaving or malicious client can flood a room's fan-out well past its intended rate.
- As concurrent document count grows into the tens of millions, the total number of ephemeral in-memory rooms (even if each is individually cheap) becomes a fleet-wide memory and connection-count planning problem, similar in shape to the persistent-connection scaling challenge in a chat gateway fleet.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Reaching for a reliable, ordered message queue== for cursor updates out of habit, adding latency and complexity for data that's obsolete within milliseconds regardless.
- ⚠️ ==Broadcasting every raw mouse-move event unthrottled==, generating far more update traffic than a smooth-looking cursor actually requires.
- ⚠️ Persisting cursor positions to a database, mistaking 'real-time' data for data that needs to survive past the moment it's displayed.
- ⚠️ Assuming small and large rooms have the same fan-out cost, and not accounting for the fact that fan-out volume grows with room size, not with total number of open documents.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is it acceptable for this system to drop updates that a messaging system would never be allowed to drop?**

> **Model Answer:** A chat message has permanent value: losing it is a visible, permanent gap. A cursor position's value is entirely tied to being **the most recent one**; the instant a newer position exists, the old one is worthless, whether or not it was ever delivered. Retrying a dropped cursor update would just deliver stale, wrong data late, which is worse than doing nothing, so the system is designed to let newer updates simply supersede lost ones rather than guarantee delivery of every single one.

**Q: How would you handle a room with hundreds of concurrent live viewers without overwhelming the gateway?**

> **Model Answer:** Two levers: **throttle** how often each client is allowed to send updates regardless of raw mouse event rate, and switch the server's outbound broadcast from per-update relay to a fixed-interval **batched tick** that coalesces every room member's latest position into one message. Both cap the fan-out multiplier that would otherwise grow linearly with room size, at the cost of a small, generally imperceptible fixed delay from the batching interval.

# Design Amazon (Product Catalog & Checkout)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Amazon` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Amazon isn't one system, it's several services (catalog, cart, order, inventory, payment) stitched together, and the entire design hinges on one non-negotiable rule: ==never let two customers both believe they bought the last unit of the same item==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a simplified version of Amazon: users can search and browse a
product catalog, add items to a cart, and place an order. Assume payment
processing exists as a separate concern you can call into. Design the
system end to end, including how you'd decompose it into services.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How large is the catalog, and how often does it change (price, stock, new listings)?
*Why it matters:* Hundreds of millions of SKUs with constant price and stock churn from third-party sellers demands a search-optimized read store separate from the transactional source of truth, rather than one database serving both browse and checkout.

#### Q: Is this a single-seller store or a multi-seller marketplace where third parties list and fulfill their own inventory?
*Why it matters:* A marketplace means the catalog and inventory services need a seller_id dimension throughout, and order fulfillment may need to fan out to different sellers' warehouses, which changes both the data model and the checkout flow.

#### Q: What consistency guarantee do we need on stock counts? Is it acceptable to occasionally overbook and cancel, or must we never oversell?
*Why it matters:* Never-oversell requires strongly consistent, often pessimistic, locking on inventory at checkout time. Tolerating rare oversells (with an apology and refund) allows a much faster, eventually-consistent stock model. This single answer decides the entire checkout architecture.

#### Q: Do we need to support real-time price changes, flash sales, and personalized recommendations, or just a static browsable catalog?
*Why it matters:* Personalization and flash sales each add their own subsystems (a recommendation service, a surge-aware rate limiter) on top of the core browse-and-buy loop. Scoping them out keeps the interview focused on catalog, cart, and order correctness.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can search and browse the product catalog by keyword and category.
- A user can view a product detail page showing price, description, and current stock availability.
- A user can add items to a cart and adjust quantities before checkout.
- A user can place an order, which charges payment and decrements inventory atomically from the user's point of view.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Catalog browsing and search must be fast, well under a second, since slow product pages directly cost the business money.**
- **Inventory correctness is the hardest requirement: the system must never sell more units of an item than physically exist, even under thousands of concurrent purchase attempts on the same popular item.**
- **The system must remain available for browsing even if the order-placement path is degraded, browsing and buying should fail independently.**
- **Order placement must be durable: once a customer sees 'order confirmed,' that order can never silently disappear, even if a downstream service crashes mid-request.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 300 million monthly active users, 50 million daily active users
- Average user views 10 product pages per session, 1 session per day for active browsers
- 2% of daily sessions result in a completed order; average order has 2 line items
- 500 million SKUs in the catalog, each catalog record roughly 2 KB (title, description, images metadata, price, category)

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Product page views per day:** 50,000,000 users * 10 views = 500 million views/day ≈ 5,800 views/sec average, several times higher at peak (holidays)
- **Orders placed per day:** 50,000,000 * 2% = 1 million orders/day ≈ 12 orders/sec average, but each order touches inventory, payment, and order-creation, so it's disproportionately expensive per request
- **Inventory decrement operations per day:** 1,000,000 orders * 2 line items = 2 million stock-decrement operations/day, each one requiring a strongly consistent check-and-decrement, not just a simple write
- **Catalog storage:** 500,000,000 SKUs * 2 KB ≈ 1 TB for catalog metadata alone, comfortably shardable, and this excludes product images which live in blob storage behind a CDN

*Capacity Takeaway:* Browsing outnumbers buying by roughly 500 to 1, so browsing scales like any read-heavy content site with caching and a search index, but the 12 orders/sec average hides the real difficulty: a hot product (a doorbuster deal) can spike thousands of concurrent purchase attempts against a single row of stock, and ==that contention, not raw QPS, is the number that actually drives the architecture==.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
The system is decomposed into independent services behind an API gateway:
a Catalog Service (backed by a search index for browse/search and a
relational store as source of truth) serves the read-heavy browsing path
and is cached aggressively since prices and descriptions change
infrequently relative to how often they're read. A Cart Service holds
lightweight, non-authoritative cart state per user. An Order Service
orchestrates checkout: it calls an Inventory Service to atomically reserve
stock, calls a Payment Service to charge the customer, and only then
writes the confirmed order, using a saga-style flow so a failure partway
through triggers compensating actions (release the reservation, void the
charge) instead of leaving the system in an inconsistent state. Splitting
these into separate services means a catalog search slowdown never blocks
someone else's checkout, and a payment provider outage never takes down
product browsing.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Service decomposition: browse path and checkout path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    gateway["API Gateway"]:::server
    catalog["Catalog Service"]:::server
    search["Search Index"]:::server
    cart["Cart Service"]:::server
    cartdb["Cart Store"]:::cache
    order["Order Service"]:::server
    inventory[("Inventory Store")]:::db
    payment["Payment Service"]:::server
    orderdb[("Orders DB")]:::db
    client --> gateway
    gateway -->|"browse/search"| catalog
    catalog --> search
    gateway --> cart
    cart --> cartdb
    gateway -->|"checkout"| order
    order -->|"reserve stock"| inventory
    order -->|"charge"| payment
    order -->|"create order"| orderdb
```

#### Placing an order, step by step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Client submits checkout (cartId, paymentMethodId)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Order service reserves inventory (conditional decrement, fails fast if sold out)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Order service charges payment (idempotency key prevents double charge)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Order record created (status: confirmed)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Reservation released or confirmed order returned (on any failure, compensating rollback fires)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Picking a concurrency strategy for one SKU

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["How contended is this SKU?"] --> b["Rarely concurrent"]
  a --> c["Occasionally concurrent"]
  a --> d["Flash sale / doorbuster"]
  b --> e["Plain optimistic UPDATE"]
  c --> f["Optimistic + retry on conflict"]
  d --> g["In-memory atomic counter"]
  g --> h["Async write-back to DB"]
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/products/search` | Query params: q, category, page. Returns paginated product results from the search index, not the transactional database. |
| `GET` | `/api/products/{productId}` | Returns product detail: price, description, images, and a cached (slightly stale) stock availability indicator. |
| `POST` | `/api/cart/items` | Body: { productId, quantity }. Adds or updates an item in the authenticated user's cart. |
| `POST` | `/api/orders` | Body: { cartId, paymentMethodId, shippingAddress }. Places an order: reserves inventory, charges payment, and creates the order record. |
| `GET` | `/api/orders/{orderId}` | Returns order status and details for the authenticated user. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `products`
- `product_id (unique, primary key)`
- `seller_id (which seller owns this listing)`
- `title, description, category, images (metadata only, images in blob storage)`
- `price (current price, source of truth)`
*Notes:* The transactional source of truth. A separate denormalized copy lives in the search index for browse/search, updated asynchronously via events, so search never blocks on or slows down catalog writes.

### Entity: `inventory`
- `product_id (indexed)`
- `warehouse_id`
- `available_quantity`
- `reserved_quantity (held during in-flight checkouts)`
*Notes:* Deliberately separate from the products table. This is the single most contention-heavy table in the system and is optimized for fast, safe check-and-decrement, not for descriptive fields.

### Entity: `orders`
- `order_id (unique)`
- `user_id (indexed)`
- `status (pending, confirmed, shipped, cancelled)`
- `line_items (product_id, quantity, price_at_purchase)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* price_at_purchase is stored (not looked up live) so an order's total never changes if the catalog price later changes.

### Entity: `cart`
- `cart_id (keyed by user_id for logged-in users)`
- `items (product_id, quantity)`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* Cart contents are not inventory reservations, adding to cart never holds stock, only checkout does. This is what keeps browsing cheap.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Preventing overselling: optimistic vs pessimistic locking on inventory
When two customers try to buy the last unit of a product at the same instant, the system must guarantee only one succeeds. **Pessimistic locking** takes a row-level lock (e.g. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) on the inventory row before checking stock, so the second request physically waits until the first transaction commits or rolls back. **Optimistic locking** instead does a conditional update (UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE product_id = ? AND available > 0) and checks the affected row count, no lock held, but the request must be prepared to retry or fail if the condition no longer holds.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Pessimistic locking: simple to reason about, guarantees correctness, but under a flash-sale spike on one product, ==thousands of requests queue up waiting for the same row lock, and throughput on that item collapses==
- Optimistic locking (conditional update): much higher throughput under contention since no request blocks another, but a losing request must handle failure gracefully (fast retry or immediate 'sold out'), and heavy contention still means many wasted retries
- The production answer for hot items: neither directly at the database. Instead, decrement a fast **in-memory counter** (Redis, atomic DECR) as the point of truth for availability, with the relational database updated asynchronously for durability, trading a small window of eventual consistency for orders-of-magnitude higher throughput on the hottest SKUs.

### Service decomposition: one monolith vs separate catalog/cart/order/payment services
A monolithic e-commerce backend puts catalog browsing, cart management, order placement, and payment handling in one codebase and one database. Splitting them into separate services means each can be scaled, deployed, and made resilient independently: the catalog service can be read-replicated and cached hard since it's read-heavy, while the order service is optimized for strong consistency on writes.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Monolith: simpler to build and operate initially, transactions across catalog/cart/order can use one local database transaction, but a slow catalog query or a bug in cart logic can degrade or take down checkout, and scaling means scaling everything together even though browsing and buying have very different load profiles
- Microservices (catalog/cart/order/payment split): each service scales and fails independently, a catalog outage doesn't block existing checkouts in flight, but a checkout now spans multiple services and can no longer use one local database transaction, requiring a saga pattern with compensating actions instead of a simple rollback
- In practice, the boundary is drawn around consistency needs: services that must be strongly consistent together (order + inventory reservation) are often kept closer, while services that only need eventual consistency (catalog search index) are split off more aggressively

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single wildly popular product (a doorbuster deal) creates hot-row contention on its inventory record no matter how the rest of the system scales; mitigate with an in-memory atomic counter per SKU rather than relying on the relational database's row locking under that load.
- The catalog's search index (not the transactional database) must absorb almost all browse traffic; it needs to be a dedicated search cluster (like Elasticsearch), sharded by category or product_id, kept eventually consistent with the source-of-truth catalog via an async event stream.
- Checkout, being the one path that must coordinate inventory, payment, and order-creation across services, is the most failure-prone request in the system; a saga with compensating transactions (and idempotency keys so a client retry never double-charges or double-reserves) is required, not just a best-effort multi-service call chain.
- Product images and static assets must be served from a CDN, never from application servers, since they're a large fraction of page weight and don't change per-request.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Using the same database table and simple UPDATE statements for both catalog browsing and inventory checkout==, causing hot-product contention to slow down unrelated product page views.
- ⚠️ Treating checkout as one big local database transaction across services, then having no answer for what happens when the payment call succeeds but the order-write call fails.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that adding to a cart must not reserve inventory, if it did, popular items would appear sold out just from people browsing with items sitting unpurchased in abandoned carts.
- ⚠️ Designing for average order volume (12/sec) without separately reasoning about worst-case contention on a single SKU during a flash sale, which is a concurrency problem, not a throughput problem.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is inventory the hardest part of this system, harder than search or the catalog?**

> **Model Answer:** Because inventory correctness is a **concurrency** problem, not a scale problem: catalog and search can be made fast by caching and denormalizing freely since staleness is tolerable, but inventory cannot tolerate staleness at the moment of purchase without risking overselling, which is a direct financial and trust cost. That forces at least one part of the system (the final stock check) to be strongly consistent even while everything around it is optimized for eventual consistency.

**Q: What happens if payment succeeds but the order-creation write fails right after?**

> **Model Answer:** This is exactly why checkout needs a saga with idempotency keys rather than a single transaction: the payment charge is tagged with an idempotency key tied to the checkout attempt, so if the order-creation step fails, a retry (or a reconciliation job) can safely re-attempt order creation using the same key without double-charging, and if the whole checkout is ultimately abandoned, a compensating refund is issued instead of leaving a customer charged with no order.

**Q: How would you decide whether a product's inventory check needs pessimistic locking, optimistic locking, or an in-memory counter?**

> **Model Answer:** By how contended that specific SKU is expected to be. Long-tail products with rarely-concurrent purchases are fine with a simple optimistic conditional update against the database. Extremely hot products (flash sales, doorbusters) need the in-memory atomic counter approach to survive the contention spike, with the database catching up asynchronously. Pessimistic locking is rarely the right default at this scale since it turns contention into queued latency rather than resolving it.

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single wildly popular product (a doorbuster deal) creates hot-row contention on its inventory record no matter how the rest of the system scales; mitigate with an in-memory atomic counter per SKU rather than relying on the relational database's row locking under that load.
- The catalog's search index (not the transactional database) must absorb almost all browse traffic; it needs to be a dedicated search cluster (like Elasticsearch), sharded by category or product_id, kept eventually consistent with the source-of-truth catalog via an async event stream.
- Checkout, being the one path that must coordinate inventory, payment, and order-creation across services, is the most failure-prone request in the system; a saga with compensating transactions (and idempotency keys so a client retry never double-charges or double-reserves) is required, not just a best-effort multi-service call chain.
- Product images and static assets must be served from a CDN, never from application servers, since they're a large fraction of page weight and don't change per-request.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Using the same database table and simple UPDATE statements for both catalog browsing and inventory checkout==, causing hot-product contention to slow down unrelated product page views.
- ⚠️ Treating checkout as one big local database transaction across services, then having no answer for what happens when the payment call succeeds but the order-write call fails.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that adding to a cart must not reserve inventory, if it did, popular items would appear sold out just from people browsing with items sitting unpurchased in abandoned carts.
- ⚠️ Designing for average order volume (12/sec) without separately reasoning about worst-case contention on a single SKU during a flash sale, which is a concurrency problem, not a throughput problem.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is inventory the hardest part of this system, harder than search or the catalog?**

> **Model Answer:** Because inventory correctness is a **concurrency** problem, not a scale problem: catalog and search can be made fast by caching and denormalizing freely since staleness is tolerable, but inventory cannot tolerate staleness at the moment of purchase without risking overselling, which is a direct financial and trust cost. That forces at least one part of the system (the final stock check) to be strongly consistent even while everything around it is optimized for eventual consistency.

**Q: What happens if payment succeeds but the order-creation write fails right after?**

> **Model Answer:** This is exactly why checkout needs a saga with idempotency keys rather than a single transaction: the payment charge is tagged with an idempotency key tied to the checkout attempt, so if the order-creation step fails, a retry (or a reconciliation job) can safely re-attempt order creation using the same key without double-charging, and if the whole checkout is ultimately abandoned, a compensating refund is issued instead of leaving a customer charged with no order.

**Q: How would you decide whether a product's inventory check needs pessimistic locking, optimistic locking, or an in-memory counter?**

> **Model Answer:** By how contended that specific SKU is expected to be. Long-tail products with rarely-concurrent purchases are fine with a simple optimistic conditional update against the database. Extremely hot products (flash sales, doorbusters) need the in-memory atomic counter approach to survive the contention spike, with the database catching up asynchronously. Pessimistic locking is rarely the right default at this scale since it turns contention into queued latency rather than resolving it.
